subject: geography

Each pool = 20 items spread across difficulty 1 (recall ~30%) / 2 (apply ~40%) / 3 (evaluate ~30%). LIGHT-VISUAL: stimulus is text or inline data tables (data-interpret); diagram-label items reference a one-time SVG library by image_refs (e.g. 'atmosphere_structure'); no sourced maps/orthophotos/graphs. Input types reuse existing engine templates: choice, true-false, cloze, scenario, match, sort-buckets, sequence, data-interpret, diagram-label, highlight-source. FET rule: no timer, 60% pass mark (12 of 20 correct). v1.1: ALL THREE GRADES authored — Grade 10 (20 pools), Grade 11 (21 pools), Grade 12 (23 pools) = 64 pools, 1,280 items. GEO.G10.MAP.A1.title: Map calculations
GEO.G10.MAP.A1.description: Given-number calculations on a 1:50 000 map: scale, distance, gradient, magnetic bearing and declination, area, vertical exaggeration. No map image needed.
GEO.G10.MAP.A1.recovery_strategy: On a 1:50 000 map, 1 cm = 0,5 km = 500 m. Distance: cm × 0,5 = km. Gradient: VI ÷ HD with both in metres, written 1:n. Magnetic bearing = true bearing + magnetic declination. Convert units to match BEFORE dividing.

questions.question: A map has a scale of 1:50 000. What does this ratio mean?
options: 1 unit on the map equals 50 000 of the same units on the ground
1 cm on the map equals 50 000 km on the ground
The map is 50 000 times bigger than the area shown
questions.expected: 1 unit on the map equals 50 000 of the same units on the ground
questions.memo: A ratio scale has no units: 1 of anything on the map = 50 000 of the same thing on the ground. So 1 cm = 50 000 cm = 500 m = 0,5 km.

questions.question: On a 1:50 000 topographic map, 1 cm on the map represents how much real distance on the ground?
On a 1:50 000 map, 1 cm represents _______ metres on the ground.
questions.memo: 1 cm = 50 000 cm = 500 m. (Divide cm by 100 to get metres.)

questions.question: True or false: a 1:50 000 map shows more detail of a small area than a 1:250 000 map of the same region.
questions.memo: 1:50 000 is a LARGER scale (smaller number on the bottom), so it shows a smaller area in greater detail. 1:250 000 shows a bigger area with less detail.

questions.question: Two trig beacons are 8 cm apart in a straight line on a 1:50 000 map. What is the real distance between them?
questions.memo: Distance = map cm × 0,5 km. 8 × 0,5 = 4 km.

questions.question: On a 1:50 000 map two points are 5 cm apart. What is the ground distance in kilometres?
A river measured with string is 14 cm long on a 1:50 000 map. What is its real length?
questions.memo: Curved-line distance still uses the scale: 14 cm × 0,5 km = 7 km.

questions.question: Which is the correct formula for the average gradient between two points?
questions.memo: Gradient = VI ÷ HD, with both values in the SAME unit (metres), written as a ratio 1:n.

questions.question: Before working out a gradient, the vertical interval is 120 m and the horizontal distance is 3 cm on a 1:50 000 map. What is the horizontal distance in metres?
questions.memo: 3 cm × 500 m = 1 500 m. You must convert the map distance to metres before dividing for gradient.

questions.question: Point A is 150 m above sea level and point B is 0 m. They are 3 000 m apart on the ground. What is the average gradient?
questions.memo: Gradient = VI ÷ HD = 150 ÷ 3 000 = 1/20, written 1:20. For every 20 m along the ground you rise 1 m.

questions.question: The vertical interval between two points is 50 m and the horizontal distance is 2 000 m. The average gradient is _______.
A true bearing is 135°. The magnetic declination is 23° WEST of true north. What is the magnetic bearing? (Magnetic bearing = true bearing + western declination)
questions.memo: With a WEST declination you ADD: 135° + 23° = 158°.

questions.question: A bearing is measured clockwise from which direction?
questions.memo: A bearing is the angle measured CLOCKWISE from north (0°/360°), through east (90°), south (180°) and west (270°).

questions.question: True or false: 'true north' and 'magnetic north' point in exactly the same direction everywhere on Earth.
questions.memo: Magnetic north differs from true north by the magnetic declination, which changes with place and slowly over time — that is why we correct bearings.

questions.question: A rectangular farm measures 4 km by 3 km. What is its area?
questions.memo: Area of a rectangle = length × breadth = 4 × 3 = 12 km². Area is always in square units (km²).

questions.question: On a 1:50 000 map a field measures 6 cm long and 2 cm wide. What is its real area? (1 cm = 0,5 km)
questions.memo: Convert sides first: 6 cm = 3 km, 2 cm = 1 km. Area = 3 × 1 = 3 km². Convert THEN multiply.

questions.question: What is the 'vertical interval' on a topographic map?
options: the height difference between two points
the distance walked along a path
questions.expected: the height difference between two points
questions.memo: Vertical interval (VI) is the difference in height (altitude) between two points — found by subtracting their two elevations.

questions.question: The contour interval on a map is 20 m. Point X sits on the 3rd contour line above the 100 m line. What is its height?
questions.memo: Each contour up adds 20 m: 100 + (3 × 20) = 100 + 60 = 160 m.

questions.question: Put the steps for calculating average gradient in the correct order.

items.text: Find the vertical interval (subtract the two heights)
Measure the horizontal distance on the map in cm
Convert the horizontal distance to metres using the scale
Divide VI by HD and write the answer as 1:n

questions.memo: Heights first (VI), then map distance, then convert to metres so units match, then divide VI ÷ HD and express as a ratio.

questions.question: A road is 12 cm long on a 1:50 000 map. A learner says it is 'about 60 km' on the ground. What mistake did they make?
options: They multiplied by 5 km instead of 0,5 km per cm
They forgot the road is curved
They measured in the wrong units
questions.expected: They multiplied by 5 km instead of 0,5 km per cm
questions.memo: Correct: 12 × 0,5 = 6 km. The learner used 5 km per cm (a 1:500 000 scale) instead of 0,5 km, giving an answer ten times too big.

GEO.G10.MAP.A2.title: Map & GIS concepts
GEO.G10.MAP.A2.description: Position in degrees/minutes/seconds, map symbols and contours, the difference between topographic maps, aerial photos and orthophotos, and the core ideas of GIS.
GEO.G10.MAP.A2.recovery_strategy: Topographic map = drawn to scale with symbols and contours. Aerial photo = raw picture (edge distortion). Orthophoto = aerial photo corrected to true scale (you can measure on it). GIS = layered, queryable DATA, not just a picture.

questions.question: Lines of latitude measure distance north or south of which line?
questions.memo: Latitude is measured north/south from the Equator (0°). Longitude is measured east/west from the Greenwich Meridian (0°).

questions.question: A position is given as 33°55'30"S. What does the 30" (30 seconds) part measure?
options: A fraction of a minute of latitude
questions.expected: A fraction of a minute of latitude
questions.memo: Positions use degrees (°), minutes (') and seconds ("). 60 seconds = 1 minute; 60 minutes = 1 degree. Seconds give the most precise part of the position.

questions.question: One degree is divided into 60 _______.
questions.memo: 1 degree = 60 minutes; 1 minute = 60 seconds. (Same names as time, but here they are angles.)

questions.question: On a topographic map, contour lines that are very close together show what?
questions.memo: Closely-spaced contours mean height changes quickly over a short distance — a steep slope. Widely-spaced contours mean a gentle slope.

questions.question: True or false: on a topographic map, blue symbols usually show water features such as rivers and dams.
questions.memo: Standard map colours: blue = water, green = vegetation/cultivation, brown = contours/relief, black = constructed features, red = roads/built-up.

questions.question: What is the main difference between an ordinary aerial photograph and an orthophoto map?
options: An orthophoto is corrected to true scale, so you can measure on it accurately
An orthophoto is taken from the ground, not the air
An aerial photograph is always in black and white
questions.expected: An orthophoto is corrected to true scale, so you can measure on it accurately
questions.memo: A raw aerial photo has scale distortion (worse at the edges). An orthophoto has been corrected so its scale is uniform — measurements are reliable, like a map.

questions.question: Which product is drawn with symbols and contours rather than being a photograph?
questions.memo: A topographic map is a DRAWING that uses symbols, colours and contour lines. The other three are image-based.

questions.question: Match each map product to its best description.
questions.memo: 1 Topographic map → B drawn to scale with symbols/contours. 2 Aerial photograph → C raw picture with edge distortion. 3 Orthophoto → A photo corrected to true scale. (Prompt: 1=Topographic map, 2=Aerial photograph, 3=Orthophoto; A=corrected photo you can measure on, B=symbols and contours, C=raw picture with distortion.)

questions.question: What does GIS stand for?
questions.memo: GIS = Geographic Information System: software that stores, displays and analyses geographic data in layers.

questions.question: Which statement best describes how a GIS stores information?
options: As separate layers of data that can be switched on/off and combined
As a single fixed picture that cannot be changed
As a list of place names only
questions.expected: As separate layers of data that can be switched on/off and combined
questions.memo: GIS keeps data in LAYERS (e.g. roads, rivers, population, land use). You overlay and query them — it is data you can analyse, not just a picture.

questions.question: In GIS, what is the difference between raster and vector data?
options: Raster data is made of a grid of pixels; vector data is made of points, lines and polygons
Raster data is paper; vector data is digital
Raster data shows only water; vector data shows only roads
questions.expected: Raster data is made of a grid of pixels; vector data is made of points, lines and polygons
questions.memo: RASTER = a grid of cells/pixels (like a photo or satellite image). VECTOR = points, lines and polygons (like roads, rivers, boundaries).

questions.question: What is 'remote sensing'?
options: Collecting information about the Earth from a distance, e.g. by satellite or aircraft
questions.expected: Collecting information about the Earth from a distance, e.g. by satellite or aircraft
questions.memo: Remote sensing gathers data WITHOUT direct contact — satellites and aircraft capture images and measurements used to build and update GIS layers.

questions.question: A town planner wants to find all houses within 500 m of a river that could flood. Why is GIS better than a paper map for this?
options: GIS can quickly query and combine layers to select exactly those houses
A paper map cannot show rivers
questions.expected: GIS can quickly query and combine layers to select exactly those houses
questions.memo: GIS can buffer the river (a 500 m zone) and overlay the housing layer to instantly select matching houses — analysis a static paper map cannot do.

questions.question: True or false: you can always measure exact ground distances directly off any aerial photograph without correction.
questions.memo: Raw aerial photos have scale distortion (tilt and relief), worst at the edges. You need an orthophoto (corrected) or a map to measure accurately.

questions.question: Sort each item as VECTOR data or RASTER data in a GIS.

items.text: A road shown as a line
A satellite image made of pixels
A town boundary shown as a polygon
A single trig beacon shown as a point
A rainfall heat-map of coloured cells

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Vector = points, lines, polygons (roads, boundaries, beacons). Raster = grids of cells/pixels (satellite images, scans, heat-maps).

questions.question: On a map, the symbol of a small aeroplane most likely shows what?
questions.memo: Map symbols are pictorial shorthand explained in the key/legend. An aeroplane symbol marks an airport or airfield.

questions.question: Why do mapmakers use symbols and a key instead of writing words on every feature?
options: Symbols save space and let many features be shown clearly at small scale
Symbols are only used to make maps look pretty
Words are not allowed on maps
Symbols make the map less accurate
questions.expected: Symbols save space and let many features be shown clearly at small scale
questions.memo: Standardised symbols pack a lot of information into a small space and can be read in any language once you know the key.

questions.question: A contour line on a map joins all points that have the same _______.
questions.memo: A contour line connects points of equal height (altitude). The gap between lines is the contour interval.

questions.question: A disaster team needs a base map that is correct to scale AND looks like the real ground, to plan rescue routes after a flood. Which single product fits best?
questions.memo: An orthophoto combines a real photographic view WITH true, uniform scale — so it both looks like the ground and can be measured for planning.

questions.question: True or false: GIS is only useful for geographers and cannot help with everyday services like emergency response or delivery routing.
questions.memo: GIS is used widely — ambulance and fire dispatch, delivery and ride apps, town planning, farming, conservation and disaster management all rely on it.

GEO.G10.T1.ATM.A1.title: Composition & structure of the atmosphere
GEO.G10.T1.ATM.A1.description: Why the atmosphere matters, its gases, the four layers and their temperatures, the ozone layer, and ozone depletion.
GEO.G10.T1.ATM.A1.recovery_strategy: Layers up from the ground: TROPOsphere (weather) → STRATOsphere (ozone) → MESOsphere (coldest) → THERMOsphere (hot). Ozone depletion (stratosphere, lets in UV) is different from the greenhouse effect (troposphere, traps heat).

questions.question: Which two gases make up most of the atmosphere?
questions.memo: Dry air is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen — together ~99%. The remaining 1% includes argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour.

questions.question: Which layer of the atmosphere is closest to the Earth's surface, where almost all weather happens?
questions.memo: The troposphere is the lowest layer — clouds, weather and most water vapour are here. Temperature falls with height through it.

questions.question: The ozone layer is found mainly in which layer of the atmosphere?
questions.memo: The ozone layer sits in the stratosphere, where it absorbs harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the Sun.

questions.question: Look at the diagram of the atmosphere's layers. Which label points to the layer that contains the ozone layer?
questions.memo: Going up from the ground: A troposphere, B stratosphere (ozone layer), C mesosphere, D thermosphere. The ozone layer is in B.

questions.question: Why is the atmosphere important for life on Earth? (Choose the best single answer.)
options: It supplies gases we breathe, blocks harmful radiation and keeps temperatures liveable
It only provides oxygen and nothing else
It exists to make the sky blue
It has no effect on living things
questions.expected: It supplies gases we breathe, blocks harmful radiation and keeps temperatures liveable
questions.memo: The atmosphere provides oxygen and carbon dioxide, shields us from UV (ozone), burns up meteors, and traps enough heat to keep Earth warm enough for life.

questions.question: Place the four layers in order, starting from the Earth's surface and going up.
questions.memo: From the ground up: Troposphere → Stratosphere → Mesosphere → Thermosphere. A memory aid: 'The Strong Man Throws'.

questions.question: True or false: in the troposphere, temperature generally decreases as you go higher.
questions.memo: In the troposphere temperature drops with height (about 6,5 °C per 1 000 m) because the air is heated from the ground upward.

questions.question: What is the main job of the ozone layer?
options: To absorb harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the Sun
To trap heat and cause global warming
To produce the oxygen we breathe
questions.expected: To absorb harmful ultraviolet (UV) radiation from the Sun
questions.memo: Ozone in the stratosphere absorbs most UV-B radiation, protecting living things from skin cancer, eye damage and harm to plants.

questions.question: Which human-made chemicals were the main cause of ozone depletion?
questions.memo: CFCs (from old fridges, aerosols and foams) release chlorine high up, which destroys ozone. The Montreal Protocol phased them out.

questions.question: A learner says: 'The ozone hole is what causes global warming.' Why is this wrong?
options: Ozone depletion lets in UV; global warming is heat trapped by greenhouse gases — two different problems
Ozone is a greenhouse gas in the troposphere only
The ozone hole and global warming are the same thing
questions.expected: Ozone depletion lets in UV; global warming is heat trapped by greenhouse gases — two different problems
questions.memo: Ozone depletion = less UV protection (stratosphere). Global warming = greenhouse gases trapping heat (troposphere). Different causes, different effects.

questions.question: Which everyday action helps REDUCE ozone depletion?
questions.memo: Choosing CFC-free products and safely disposing of old fridges/air-conditioners cuts the chemicals that destroy ozone.

questions.question: Which layer is the COLDEST, where most meteors burn up?
questions.memo: The mesosphere is the coldest layer (down to about −90 °C) and is where most meteors burn up due to friction.

questions.question: The atmosphere thins with height. This means that as you go up, the air _______.
questions.memo: Gravity holds most air molecules near the surface, so air pressure and density both decrease with altitude.

questions.question: True or false: a thinning ozone layer increases the risk of skin cancer and eye damage for people on the ground.
questions.memo: Less ozone means more UV reaches the surface, raising risks of skin cancer, cataracts and harm to crops and marine life.

questions.question: Which layer contains the satellites in low orbit and shows rising temperature with height?
questions.memo: The thermosphere is very hot (absorbs high-energy solar radiation) and contains the ionosphere; many satellites orbit at this level.

questions.question: Why does temperature INCREASE with height in the stratosphere, unlike in the troposphere?
options: The ozone layer absorbs UV radiation and releases heat high up
It is closer to the hot core of the Earth
Cold air sinks out of it
There is more water vapour higher up
questions.expected: The ozone layer absorbs UV radiation and releases heat high up
questions.memo: Ozone absorbing UV warms the upper stratosphere, so temperature rises with height there — the opposite of the troposphere.

questions.question: Sort each statement as a CAUSE of ozone depletion or an EFFECT of ozone depletion.

items.text: Release of CFCs from old aerosols
More UV radiation reaching the ground
Use of CFC foams and refrigerants

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Causes are the CFC chemicals and the chlorine reaction; effects are the extra UV and the harm it does to health, crops and sea life.

questions.question: The international agreement that successfully phased out ozone-destroying chemicals is the _______ Protocol.
questions.memo: The 1987 Montreal Protocol banned CFCs worldwide; the ozone layer is now slowly recovering. (Kyoto and Paris deal with climate change, not ozone.)

questions.question: Why can the atmosphere be described as a 'blanket' for the Earth?
options: It traps enough heat to keep the surface warm enough for life
It makes the Earth completely airtight
It stops the Earth from spinning
questions.expected: It traps enough heat to keep the surface warm enough for life
questions.memo: Greenhouse gases hold in some of the heat radiated by the surface; without this natural blanket Earth would be about −18 °C and frozen.

questions.question: A study finds the ozone hole over Antarctica is slowly shrinking since the 1990s. What does this best show?
options: Global action to ban CFCs is working
Ozone depletion was never a real problem
The atmosphere is losing its oxygen
questions.expected: Global action to ban CFCs is working
questions.memo: The recovery of the ozone layer is strong evidence that the worldwide CFC ban (Montreal Protocol) is succeeding — a rare environmental success story.

GEO.G10.T1.ATM.A2.title: Heating of the atmosphere
GEO.G10.T1.ATM.A2.description: How the atmosphere is heated, the controls on temperature (latitude, altitude, ocean currents, distance from sea), the greenhouse effect and global warming with reference to Africa.
GEO.G10.T1.ATM.A2.recovery_strategy: The Sun heats the GROUND; the ground heats the air — so air is warmest near the surface. Four controls on temperature: LATITUDE, ALTITUDE, OCEAN CURRENTS, DISTANCE FROM SEA. Greenhouse gases trap heat; too much = global warming.

questions.question: The energy the Earth receives from the Sun is called _______.
questions.memo: Insolation = INcoming SOLar radiATION, the Sun's energy that reaches the Earth.

questions.question: How is the lower atmosphere mainly heated?
options: The Sun heats the Earth's surface, which then heats the air above it
The Sun heats the air directly from the top down
Heat rises from the Earth's core
questions.expected: The Sun heats the Earth's surface, which then heats the air above it
questions.memo: Sunlight passes through the air and heats the GROUND; the warm ground then heats the air by conduction, convection and radiation. So air is warmest near the surface.

questions.question: Why is it usually colder at the top of a high mountain than at its base?
options: Higher altitude means thinner air that holds less heat from the ground
Mountain tops are closer to the Sun, so heat escapes
Cold air is attracted to high places
questions.expected: Higher altitude means thinner air that holds less heat from the ground
questions.memo: Air is heated from the ground up and thins with height, so it holds less heat. Temperature drops about 6,5 °C per 1 000 m of altitude.

questions.question: Which factor explains why places near the Equator are generally hotter than places near the poles?
options: Latitude — the Sun's rays are more concentrated near the Equator
questions.expected: Latitude — the Sun's rays are more concentrated near the Equator
questions.memo: Near the Equator the Sun is high, so its energy is concentrated on a small area. Near the poles the same energy is spread over a larger, angled area, so it is cooler.

questions.question: Sort each as a factor that affects temperature, or NOT a temperature factor.

items.text: The colour of a town's flag

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: The four real controls are latitude, altitude, ocean currents and distance from the sea. Flags and weekdays have nothing to do with temperature.

questions.question: A warm ocean current flows past a coast. What effect does it usually have on that coast's climate?
questions.memo: Warm currents warm the air above them and add moisture, giving warmer, wetter coasts. Cold currents do the opposite.

questions.question: What is the greenhouse effect?
options: Greenhouse gases trapping some of the heat radiated by the Earth's surface
Glass houses being used to grow plants
The Sun getting hotter each year
Holes forming in the ozone layer
questions.expected: Greenhouse gases trapping some of the heat radiated by the Earth's surface
questions.memo: Gases like CO₂, methane and water vapour absorb heat radiated from the surface and re-radiate it, keeping the lower atmosphere warm. A natural amount is essential for life.

questions.question: Which gas is the main human-released greenhouse gas driving recent global warming?
questions.memo: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) from burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) is the main driver. Methane and nitrous oxide also contribute.

questions.question: True or false: the greenhouse effect is entirely bad and the Earth would be better with none of it.
questions.memo: A NATURAL greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough for life (about +15 °C instead of −18 °C). The problem is the EXTRA warming from too many human emissions.

questions.question:
The table shows average yearly temperature for three towns at different altitudes (same latitude). Which trend does it show?

| Town | Altitude (m) | Temp (°C) |
|------|------|------|
| A | 100 | 22 |
| B | 1 000 | 16 |
| C | 1 800 | 11 |
options: Altitude has no effect on temperature
Temperature is highest at the greatest altitude
questions.memo: 100 m → 22 °C, 1 800 m → 11 °C: higher places are colder. This is the altitude control on temperature.

questions.question: Why does the coast often have milder temperatures (cooler summers, warmer winters) than places far inland?
options: The sea heats and cools slowly, moderating nearby air temperatures
The coast is always at a higher altitude
questions.expected: The sea heats and cools slowly, moderating nearby air temperatures
questions.memo: Water changes temperature slowly, so coastal areas have a smaller temperature range. Inland (continental) areas heat and cool quickly, giving bigger extremes.

questions.question: Which of these is EVIDENCE of global warming?
options: Melting glaciers and rising sea levels
questions.expected: Melting glaciers and rising sea levels
questions.memo: Evidence includes rising average temperatures, melting glaciers and ice sheets, rising seas, and more extreme droughts and floods.

questions.question: Conduction, convection and radiation are three ways that _______ moves through the atmosphere.
questions.memo: Heat transfers by CONDUCTION (touch), CONVECTION (rising warm air) and RADIATION (energy through space). All three warm the atmosphere.

questions.question: Reflection of insolation off bright surfaces (like ice or clouds) is called the albedo effect. A region whose ice melts and is replaced by dark ocean will then _______.
options: absorb more heat and warm faster
reflect more heat and cool down
questions.expected: absorb more heat and warm faster
questions.memo: Ice is bright and reflects sunlight (high albedo). Dark ocean absorbs it, so melting ice leads to MORE warming — a feedback loop.

questions.question: Which is a likely consequence of climate change for many parts of Africa?
options: More frequent and severe droughts and floods
An end to all farming difficulties
questions.expected: More frequent and severe droughts and floods
questions.memo: Africa is especially vulnerable: more droughts, floods, heatwaves, shifting rainfall, water stress and threats to food security and health.

questions.question: A learner says: 'Air high up in a hot-air balloon must be hottest because it is nearer the Sun.' Why is this wrong?
options: Air is heated from the ground up, so it gets COLDER with height, not hotter
The Sun is actually very close to balloons
Higher air has more oxygen, which is cold
questions.expected: Air is heated from the ground up, so it gets COLDER with height, not hotter
questions.memo: The few kilometres a balloon rises make no difference to the 150-million-km distance to the Sun. The ground heats the air, so higher = colder in the troposphere.

questions.question: Which action by individuals helps reduce greenhouse-gas emissions?
options: Using public transport, saving electricity and recycling
Driving short distances instead of walking
questions.expected: Using public transport, saving electricity and recycling
questions.memo: Cutting fossil-fuel use — less driving, energy saving, renewables, recycling and planting trees — lowers the CO₂ that drives warming.

questions.question: True or false: rising sea levels caused by global warming threaten low-lying coastal cities and islands.
questions.memo: As ice melts and warmer water expands, seas rise — flooding low coasts, forcing people to move and damaging property and farmland.

questions.question: Two towns are at the same latitude and altitude, but one is on the coast and one is far inland. Which experiences the bigger difference between summer and winter temperatures?
questions.memo: Inland (continental) areas heat and cool quickly, so they have a LARGER temperature range. The sea moderates the coastal town's climate.

questions.question: Why is global warming described as a global problem needing global cooperation?
options: Greenhouse gases mix through the whole atmosphere, so emissions anywhere affect everyone
Only one country produces all the emissions
It only affects the country that causes it
questions.expected: Greenhouse gases mix through the whole atmosphere, so emissions anywhere affect everyone
questions.memo: The atmosphere is shared. CO₂ released in one country warms the whole planet, so agreements like the Paris Agreement need many nations to act together.

GEO.G10.T1.ATM.A3.title: Moisture in the atmosphere
GEO.G10.T1.ATM.A3.description: Water vapour, evaporation, condensation and precipitation; dew point, humidity and relative humidity; cloud formation and types; forms of precipitation; and relief, convectional and frontal rainfall.
GEO.G10.T1.ATM.A3.recovery_strategy: Warm air holds more vapour. Cool it to DEW POINT → condensation → cloud/dew. Relative humidity = how full the air is (% of capacity). Three rainfalls: RELIEF (up a mountain), CONVECTIONAL (hot ground, afternoon storms), FRONTAL (warm air over cold at a front).

questions.question: The process by which liquid water turns into water vapour is called _______.
questions.memo: Evaporation turns liquid water into vapour (needs heat). Condensation is the reverse — vapour back to liquid.

questions.question: What is condensation?
options: Water vapour cooling and turning back into liquid water
questions.expected: Water vapour cooling and turning back into liquid water
questions.memo: Condensation happens when moist air is cooled to its dew point — vapour becomes tiny water droplets, forming cloud, mist or dew.

questions.question: The temperature at which air becomes saturated and water vapour starts to condense is called the _______.
questions.memo: At the dew point the air is 'full' (100% relative humidity) and condensation begins. Cooling below it produces dew, mist or cloud.

questions.question: What does 'relative humidity' measure?
options: How full the air is with water vapour, as a percentage of what it could hold
The total mass of the atmosphere
questions.expected: How full the air is with water vapour, as a percentage of what it could hold
questions.memo: Relative humidity is a %: actual vapour ÷ maximum the air could hold at that temperature. 100% means saturated.

questions.question: Warm air can hold MORE water vapour than cold air. So when warm, moist air is cooled, what happens?
options: It reaches saturation and water vapour condenses into cloud or dew
It can hold even more vapour
questions.expected: It reaches saturation and water vapour condenses into cloud or dew
questions.memo: Cooling lowers how much vapour the air can hold. Once it hits the dew point, excess vapour condenses — this is how clouds, dew and mist form.

questions.question: Look at the diagram of the three rainfall types. Which label shows RELIEF (orographic) rainfall?
options: A — air forced to rise over a mountain
B — hot ground heating air that rises
C — warm air rising over cold air at a front
D — water evaporating from a lake
questions.expected: A — air forced to rise over a mountain
questions.memo: Relief rainfall (A): moist air is forced up the windward slope of a mountain, cools, condenses and rains. B is convectional, C is frontal.

questions.question: On a hot summer afternoon the ground heats up, air rises strongly, and a thunderstorm forms. Which rainfall type is this?
questions.memo: Convectional rainfall: intense surface heating makes air rise rapidly, building tall cumulonimbus clouds and short, heavy afternoon thunderstorms.

questions.question: Rain that forms when a warm air mass rises over a cold air mass along a front is called _______ rainfall.
questions.memo: Frontal rainfall happens where warm and cold air meet: the lighter warm air is forced up over the cold air, cools and rains. Common in the Western Cape in winter.

questions.question: Sort each example into the correct rainfall type.

items.text: Moist sea air forced up a coastal mountain range
A short, heavy afternoon thunderstorm after a hot day
Steady winter rain as a cold front passes Cape Town
Heavy rain on the windward slope, dry air on the leeward side
Towering cumulonimbus building over hot inland plains
Rain where a warm air mass rides over a cold air mass

questions.memo: Relief = forced up a mountain. Convectional = hot ground, rising air, afternoon storms. Frontal = warm air over cold air at a front.

questions.question: Which is NOT a form of precipitation?
questions.memo: Precipitation is water falling from the sky: rain, drizzle, hail, snow, sleet. Wind is moving air, not precipitation.

questions.question: Frost forms when which condition is met?
options: Air is cooled below freezing and water vapour freezes onto surfaces
questions.expected: Air is cooled below freezing and water vapour freezes onto surfaces
questions.memo: Frost is frozen dew: on clear, calm, cold nights surfaces cool below 0 °C and vapour deposits as ice crystals.

questions.question: Why do clouds form when air rises?
options: Rising air cools, reaches dew point, and its vapour condenses on tiny particles
Rising air heats up and dries out
Clouds are blown up from the sea
questions.expected: Rising air cools, reaches dew point, and its vapour condenses on tiny particles
questions.memo: As air rises it expands and cools. At the dew point its vapour condenses onto dust/salt particles, forming the droplets we see as cloud.

questions.question: Tall, dark cumulonimbus clouds are usually a sign of _______.
questions.memo: Cumulonimbus are towering storm clouds linked to heavy rain, lightning, hail and strong gusts. Wispy cirrus or flat stratus bring milder conditions.

questions.question: True or false: dew, frost, rain, hail and snow are all forms of precipitation or condensation involving water in the air.
questions.memo: All involve water changing state in or from the atmosphere — dew and frost form on surfaces; rain, hail and snow fall as precipitation.

questions.question: Hail is most associated with which kind of weather?
questions.memo: Hail forms in cumulonimbus storm clouds: strong updrafts carry droplets up into freezing air repeatedly, building ice layers until they fall.

questions.question: On the leeward (sheltered) side of a mountain, after relief rainfall, the air is usually warm and dry. What is this dry zone called?
questions.memo: Air loses its moisture rising over the windward side; descending on the leeward side it is dry, creating a rain-shadow area.

questions.question: Air at 30 °C currently holds half the water vapour it could hold. Its relative humidity is therefore about _______.
questions.memo: Relative humidity = actual ÷ maximum capacity. Half of capacity = 50%.

questions.question: A learner calls a sudden, heavy afternoon downpour after a hot morning 'relief rainfall'. Why is that the wrong label?
options: It is convectional rainfall — caused by surface heating, not by a mountain
It is frontal rainfall caused by a cold front
Relief rainfall only happens at night
It is not rainfall at all
questions.expected: It is convectional rainfall — caused by surface heating, not by a mountain
questions.memo: Relief rainfall needs air forced up a mountain. A hot-day downpour from rising heated air is convectional.

questions.question: Why does dew often form on grass on a clear, calm night but not on a cloudy, windy one?
options: Clear, calm conditions let the ground cool below dew point so vapour condenses
Clouds add extra dew to the grass
Dew only forms when it is raining
questions.expected: Clear, calm conditions let the ground cool below dew point so vapour condenses
questions.memo: On clear nights heat radiates away freely and surfaces cool to dew point. Cloud traps heat and wind mixes the air, both preventing dew.

questions.question: Put the steps of cloud formation in the correct order.

items.text: Air near the warm surface picks up water vapour
Rising air cools to its dew point
Vapour condenses on tiny particles to form cloud droplets

questions.memo: Moisture in → air rises and cools → reaches dew point → condensation forms cloud. The same rising-and-cooling drives all three rainfall types.

GEO.G10.T1.ATM.A4.title: Reading & interpreting synoptic weather maps
GEO.G10.T1.ATM.A4.description: Weather elements on a synoptic chart, reading station-model data, and interpreting pressure patterns (highs, lows, isobars) and the weather they bring.
GEO.G10.T1.ATM.A4.recovery_strategy: Wind is named by where it comes FROM. Close isobars = strong wind. LOW pressure = rising air = cloud/rain; HIGH pressure = sinking air = clear/dry. Read each station-model value off the key one at a time.

questions.question: A synoptic weather map is a map that shows _______.
options: the state of the weather over a large area at one moment
questions.expected: the state of the weather over a large area at one moment
questions.memo: A synoptic chart gives a 'snapshot' of weather — pressure, fronts, wind, temperature — across a region at a particular time.

questions.question: Lines on a synoptic map that join places of equal atmospheric pressure are called _______.
questions.memo: Isobars join points of equal pressure. (Isotherms join equal temperature; contours join equal height.)

questions.question: Atmospheric pressure is measured in which units on a synoptic chart?
questions.memo: Pressure is given in hectopascals (hPa), the same value as millibars. Average sea-level pressure is about 1 013 hPa.

questions.question: On a synoptic map, what does a 'LOW' (low-pressure cell) usually bring?
options: Sinking air, clear and dry weather
questions.memo: In a low, air rises, cools and condenses — so lows bring cloud, rain and unsettled weather. Highs bring sinking air and clear, dry conditions.

questions.question: What kind of weather is a high-pressure cell (anticyclone) usually linked to?
options: Clear skies and dry, settled weather
questions.expected: Clear skies and dry, settled weather
questions.memo: In a high, air sinks and warms, preventing cloud formation — so highs bring calm, clear, dry weather.

questions.question: When isobars are very close together on a synoptic map, the wind is likely to be _______.
questions.memo: Closely-spaced isobars mean pressure changes sharply over a short distance (a steep pressure gradient) — this produces strong wind. Widely-spaced isobars = light wind.

questions.question: A weather station reports a 'south-easterly wind'. From which direction is the wind blowing?
options: From the north-west only at night
questions.memo: Winds are always named by where they come FROM. A south-easterly blows from the south-east towards the north-west.

questions.question:
The table is a station-model reading. What is the temperature?

| Element | Value |
|------|------|
| Temperature | 18 °C |
| Dew point | 12 °C |
| Cloud cover | 4/8 |
| Wind | NW 15 knots |
| Pressure | 1018 hPa |
questions.memo: Read the temperature row directly: 18 °C. The 12 °C is the dew point, 1018 is pressure, 15 knots is wind speed.

questions.question: Using the same station-model table (temp 18 °C, dew point 12 °C), what does the small gap between temperature and dew point suggest?
options: The air is fairly moist (humid), so cloud or rain is more likely
There is no water vapour at all
questions.expected: The air is fairly moist (humid), so cloud or rain is more likely
questions.memo: When temperature and dew point are CLOSE, the air is near saturation (high relative humidity) — cloud, mist or rain become more likely. A big gap means dry air.

questions.question: Match each synoptic feature to what it shows.
questions.memo: 1 Isobar → C line of equal pressure. 2 'L' symbol → A low-pressure cell (rain). 3 'H' symbol → B high-pressure cell (clear/dry). (Prompt: 1=Isobar, 2='L', 3='H'; A=low-pressure cell, B=high-pressure cell, C=line of equal pressure.)

questions.question: Cloud cover on a station model is shown in eighths (oktas). A reading of 8/8 means the sky is _______.
questions.memo: Oktas measure cloud cover out of 8. 0/8 = clear sky; 8/8 = fully overcast; 4/8 = half covered.

questions.question: True or false: on a synoptic chart, the centre of a high-pressure cell has the highest pressure value, and pressure decreases outwards.
questions.memo: Isobar values rise towards the centre of a HIGH and fall towards the centre of a LOW, just like contour heights rise towards a hilltop.

questions.question: Which weather element is measured with a barometer and shown by isobars?
questions.memo: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure (hPa). Thermometers measure temperature; rain gauges measure rainfall; anemometers measure wind speed.

questions.question: A synoptic map shows a deep low off the Cape coast with tightly-packed isobars. What weather should sailors expect?
options: Strong winds, rough seas and rain
questions.expected: Strong winds, rough seas and rain
questions.memo: A deep low (rising air) brings cloud and rain; tightly-packed isobars mean a steep pressure gradient and strong winds — dangerous sea conditions.

questions.question: Wind speed on older charts is often given in 'knots'. A knot is a measure of _______.
questions.memo: A knot is one nautical mile per hour — a unit of speed used for wind and ships.

questions.question: Why does a weather forecaster look at BOTH the pressure pattern and the spacing of isobars?
options: Pressure shows wet or dry weather; isobar spacing shows wind strength
Both show the same single thing
questions.expected: Pressure shows wet or dry weather; isobar spacing shows wind strength
questions.memo: The TYPE of cell (high/low) predicts cloud and rain; the SPACING of isobars predicts how strong the wind will be. Together they describe the coming weather.

questions.question: True or false: a north wind and a northerly wind both mean wind coming from the north.
questions.memo: Both name the source direction. A north/northerly wind blows from the north towards the south.

questions.question: A learner reads '1004 hPa' at a low's centre and '1024 hPa' at a high's centre and says 'the low has higher pressure'. What is the error?
options: 1004 is LOWER than 1024, so the low correctly has lower pressure
questions.expected: 1004 is LOWER than 1024, so the low correctly has lower pressure
questions.memo: 1004 hPa < 1024 hPa. The low-pressure cell has the lower value — that is why it is called a 'low'.

questions.question: Which instrument and reading would you use to describe how humid the air is at a station?
options: The gap between temperature and dew-point temperature
questions.expected: The gap between temperature and dew-point temperature
questions.memo: A small temperature–dew-point gap = high humidity (air near saturation). A large gap = dry air. This is read straight off the station model.

questions.question: Put these steps for reading a synoptic map in a sensible order.

items.text: Find the high- and low-pressure cells (H and L)
Check the isobar spacing to judge wind strength
Read each station model for temperature, cloud and wind
Describe the overall weather the area will experience

questions.memo: Start with the big picture (pressure cells), then wind (isobar spacing), then local details (station models), then summarise the weather.

GEO.G10.T2.GEO.A1.title: The structure of the Earth
GEO.G10.T2.GEO.A1.description: The internal layers of the Earth (crust, mantle, outer core, inner core), continental vs oceanic crust, and convection currents driven by core heat.
GEO.G10.T2.GEO.A1.recovery_strategy: Outside in: CRUST (thin solid) → MANTLE (hot flowing rock) → OUTER CORE (liquid iron) → INNER CORE (solid, hottest). Oceanic crust = thinner but denser; continental = thicker, lighter. Core heat drives mantle convection that moves the plates.

questions.question: What is the outermost solid layer of the Earth called?
questions.memo: The crust is the thin, solid, rocky outer skin of the Earth — the layer we live on.

questions.question: Order the Earth's layers from the OUTSIDE to the centre.
questions.memo: From the surface inwards: crust → mantle → outer core → inner core. It gets hotter and denser towards the centre.

questions.question: The thick layer of hot, slowly-flowing rock between the crust and the core is the _______.
questions.memo: The mantle is the largest layer — hot, semi-solid rock that flows slowly in convection currents.

questions.question: Look at the cross-section of the Earth. Which label points to the inner core?
options: C — the liquid layer around the centre
questions.memo: A crust, B mantle, C outer core (liquid), D inner core (solid centre, hottest). The inner core is solid because of immense pressure.

questions.question: Which part of the Earth is liquid?
questions.memo: The outer core is liquid iron and nickel; the inner core is solid (squeezed by pressure). Movement in the liquid outer core creates Earth's magnetic field.

questions.question: Which statement correctly compares continental and oceanic crust?
options: Continental crust is thicker but less dense; oceanic crust is thinner but denser
Continental crust is thinner and denser than oceanic crust
Oceanic crust is the thickest layer of the Earth
questions.expected: Continental crust is thicker but less dense; oceanic crust is thinner but denser
questions.memo: Continental crust (granite) is thick (~35 km) and light; oceanic crust (basalt) is thin (~7 km) and dense. That is why oceanic crust sinks beneath continental crust when they collide.

questions.question: What drives the slow movement (convection currents) in the mantle?
questions.memo: Intense heat from the core makes mantle rock rise, cool, and sink in giant loops (convection currents). These currents drag the plates above them.

questions.question: True or false: temperature and pressure both increase as you go deeper into the Earth.
questions.memo: Both rise towards the centre — the inner core is the hottest (about 5 000–6 000 °C) and under the greatest pressure.

questions.question: Match each layer to its key feature.
questions.memo: 1 Crust → C thin solid rock. 2 Mantle → D hot flowing rock. 3 Outer core → A liquid iron/nickel. 4 Inner core → B solid, hottest. (Prompt: 1=Crust, 2=Mantle, 3=Outer core, 4=Inner core; A=liquid iron/nickel, B=solid and hottest, C=thin solid rock, D=hot flowing rock.)

questions.question: Why is the inner core solid even though it is the hottest layer?
options: The enormous pressure there keeps it solid despite the heat
It is actually the coolest layer
It is far from the Sun
questions.expected: The enormous pressure there keeps it solid despite the heat
questions.memo: Pressure rises faster than temperature towards the centre, so the inner core stays solid while the outer core (less pressure) is liquid.

questions.question: The rigid outer shell of the Earth (crust + uppermost mantle), broken into plates, is called the _______.
questions.memo: The lithosphere is the rigid layer that is broken into tectonic plates. It sits on the softer, partly-molten asthenosphere.

questions.question: Roughly how does the thickness of oceanic crust compare with continental crust?
options: Oceanic crust is much thinner (about 7 km vs about 35 km)
They are identical at 100 km each
questions.expected: Oceanic crust is much thinner (about 7 km vs about 35 km)
questions.memo: Oceanic crust averages ~7 km; continental crust averages ~35 km and can exceed 70 km under mountains.

questions.question: Convection currents in the mantle behave most like which everyday example?
options: Boiling water rising, cooling at the top and sinking again in a pot
A ball rolling down a hill
questions.expected: Boiling water rising, cooling at the top and sinking again in a pot
questions.memo: Like boiling soup, hot mantle rock rises, spreads and cools near the top, then sinks — a continuous loop that moves the plates.

questions.question: True or false: oceanic crust is denser than continental crust, so it tends to sink beneath continental crust where they meet.
questions.memo: Because oceanic crust is denser, at a convergent boundary it subducts (dives) under the lighter continental crust, forming trenches and volcanoes.

questions.question: Movement of liquid iron in the outer core is responsible for the Earth's _______.
questions.memo: Swirling liquid iron in the outer core acts like a dynamo, generating Earth's magnetic field — the field a compass needle responds to.

questions.question: Which is the THICKEST layer of the Earth by volume?
questions.memo: The mantle makes up most of the Earth's volume (about 84%). The crust is a thin skin by comparison.

questions.question: A learner says the crust is the thickest, most important layer because we live on it. Evaluate this.
options: The crust is actually the THINNEST layer; we live on it but the mantle is far larger
Correct — the crust is the thickest layer
The crust is hotter than the core
questions.expected: The crust is actually the THINNEST layer; we live on it but the mantle is far larger
questions.memo: Importance to us does not equal size. The crust is the thinnest layer; the mantle is by far the largest.

questions.question: Which two metals mainly make up the Earth's core?
questions.memo: The core is mostly iron and nickel — very dense metals that sank to the centre when the Earth formed.

questions.question: Granite is typical of continental crust and basalt of oceanic crust. Basalt is denser. This helps explain why _______.
options: the ocean floor sits lower and subducts under continents
questions.expected: the ocean floor sits lower and subducts under continents
questions.memo: Denser basaltic oceanic crust rides lower and dives beneath lighter granitic continental crust at convergent boundaries.

questions.question: How does the structure of the Earth connect to plate tectonics?
options: Core heat drives mantle convection, which moves the lithospheric plates
The crust moves because of ocean waves
Plates move because of the Sun's heat on the surface
questions.expected: Core heat drives mantle convection, which moves the lithospheric plates
questions.memo: The internal structure is the engine of plate tectonics: heat from the core → convection in the mantle → dragging of the plates → earthquakes, volcanoes and mountains.

GEO.G10.T2.GEO.A2.title: Plate tectonics
GEO.G10.T2.GEO.A2.description: The theory and evidence of plate tectonics, the three plate boundaries and their landforms and events, and how mantle convection moves the plates.
GEO.G10.T2.GEO.A2.recovery_strategy: Three boundaries: DIVERGENT (apart → ridges, rift valleys, new crust), CONVERGENT (collide → mountains, trenches, volcanoes), TRANSFORM (slide past → earthquakes). The engine is mantle convection dragging the plates.

questions.question: The Earth's outer shell is broken into large moving pieces called _______.
questions.memo: Tectonic plates are huge slabs of lithosphere that slowly move on the mantle below.

questions.question: Which observation is EVIDENCE that continents were once joined?
options: The coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like a jigsaw
questions.expected: The coastlines of South America and Africa fit together like a jigsaw
questions.memo: Matching coastlines, identical fossils and rock types on different continents, all support the idea that the continents drifted apart from one supercontinent (Pangaea).

questions.question: At a DIVERGENT boundary, the plates move _______.
questions.memo: Divergent = diverging = moving apart. Magma rises to fill the gap, creating new crust (mid-ocean ridges, rift valleys).

questions.question: What typically forms where two plates COLLIDE (a convergent boundary)?
options: Fold mountains, ocean trenches and volcanoes
questions.expected: Fold mountains, ocean trenches and volcanoes
questions.memo: Convergent boundaries crumple crust into fold mountains (e.g. Himalayas) and, where oceanic crust subducts, form deep trenches and volcanoes.

questions.question: At a TRANSFORM boundary, plates slide past each other. This mainly produces _______.
questions.memo: Plates grinding past one another (e.g. the San Andreas Fault) build up stress that is released as earthquakes. Little crust is made or destroyed.

questions.question: Sort each landform/event under the plate boundary that produces it.

items.text: A rift valley such as the East African Rift
A deep ocean trench with volcanoes
Plates grinding sideways with no new crust

questions.memo: Divergent = ridges and rift valleys; convergent = fold mountains, trenches, volcanoes; transform = sideways grinding earthquakes.

questions.question: Look at the diagram of a divergent boundary. Which label shows the rising magma that creates new crust?
options: C — magma rising in the gap between the plates
questions.expected: C — magma rising in the gap between the plates
questions.memo: At a divergent boundary plates pull apart and magma (C) rises to fill the gap, hardening into new oceanic crust.

questions.question: The single supercontinent that scientists believe existed about 250 million years ago is called _______.
questions.memo: Pangaea was the supercontinent that later split; its southern part, Gondwana, included today's Africa, South America, India, Australia and Antarctica.

questions.question: True or false: identical fossils found on different continents support the theory of plate tectonics.
questions.memo: The same land-animal and plant fossils on continents now separated by oceans show those lands were once joined.

questions.question: Which process actually moves the plates?
options: Convection currents in the mantle dragging the plates
questions.expected: Convection currents in the mantle dragging the plates
questions.memo: Heat-driven convection currents in the mantle flow beneath the plates and drag them along — the mechanism behind continental drift.

questions.question: When dense oceanic crust dives beneath lighter continental crust at a convergent boundary, the process is called _______.
questions.memo: Subduction is the sinking of one plate beneath another. The descending plate melts, feeding volcanoes, and forms a deep ocean trench.

questions.question: The East African Rift Valley is forming because the African continent is being _______.
options: pulled apart at a divergent boundary
pushed together at a convergent boundary
questions.expected: pulled apart at a divergent boundary
questions.memo: The Rift Valley is a divergent zone on land: the crust is stretching and dropping along faults as Africa slowly splits.

questions.question: Match each boundary type to a real example.
questions.memo: 1 Divergent → B Mid-Atlantic Ridge. 2 Convergent → C Himalayas. 3 Transform → A San Andreas Fault. (Prompt: 1=Divergent, 2=Convergent, 3=Transform; A=San Andreas Fault, B=Mid-Atlantic Ridge, C=Himalayas.)

questions.question: True or false: most of the world's earthquakes and volcanoes occur along plate boundaries.
questions.memo: Plate edges are where stress and magma concentrate, so earthquakes and volcanoes cluster there — for example around the Pacific 'Ring of Fire'.

questions.question: New oceanic crust is created at a mid-ocean ridge and destroyed at a subduction trench. This idea is called _______.
questions.memo: Sea-floor spreading: magma rises at ridges making new crust that moves outward and is eventually recycled at trenches — strong evidence for plate tectonics.

questions.question: The Himalaya mountains are still slowly rising. What does this tell us?
options: The Indian and Eurasian plates are still colliding
The mountains are being eroded only
A divergent boundary runs through them
questions.expected: The Indian and Eurasian plates are still colliding
questions.memo: Ongoing convergence of India into Eurasia keeps pushing the Himalayas higher — plate movement is slow but continuous.

questions.question: Why does South Africa have very few earthquakes and no active volcanoes?
options: It lies in the stable middle of a plate, far from boundaries
questions.expected: It lies in the stable middle of a plate, far from boundaries
questions.memo: Most of South Africa sits in the interior of the African Plate, away from active boundaries, so major tectonic activity is rare (mining tremors aside).

questions.question: At a divergent boundary on the ocean floor, what landform is created?
questions.memo: Rising magma at a spreading boundary builds a long underwater mountain chain — a mid-ocean ridge, such as the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.

questions.question: True or false: plate tectonics explains earthquakes, volcanoes, mountain-building and the slow movement of continents all with one theory.
questions.memo: Plate tectonics is a 'big idea' that ties together many processes — its explanatory power is why it is so widely accepted.

questions.question: A learner claims continents drift because 'the sea pushes them around'. Why is this wrong?
options: Plates are dragged by mantle convection below, not pushed by surface seawater
The sea is too small to move continents
Continents do not move at all
questions.expected: Plates are dragged by mantle convection below, not pushed by surface seawater
questions.memo: The driving force is deep: heat-driven convection in the mantle. Surface seawater has nowhere near the energy to move tectonic plates.

GEO.G10.T2.GEO.A3.title: Folding & faulting
GEO.G10.T2.GEO.A3.description: Folding (anticlines, synclines, fold mountains) from compression, and faulting (normal/reverse faults, fault scarps, horsts/block mountains, grabens/rift valleys) from tension and compression.
GEO.G10.T2.GEO.A3.recovery_strategy: FOLDING = rock BENDS under compression: anticline = arch (up), syncline = trough (down). FAULTING = rock BREAKS along a crack: raised block = horst (block mountain); dropped block = graben (rift valley). Folds bend, faults break.

questions.question: When rock layers are squeezed and BEND without breaking, the process is called _______.
questions.memo: Folding is the bending of rock layers under compression (sideways squeezing). Faulting is when rock breaks instead.

questions.question: An up-fold (arch shape) in rock layers is called a/an _______.
questions.memo: An anticline is an up-arch; a syncline is a down-trough. Tip: antICline points up like a tent.

questions.question: A down-fold (trough shape) is called a/an _______.
questions.memo: A syncline sags downwards like a valley; an anticline arches up. They alternate in folded rock.

questions.question: What force causes folding?
questions.memo: Folding happens where plates push together, compressing and crumpling the rock layers into folds and fold mountains.

questions.question: When rock layers crack and move along the break, the process is called _______.
questions.memo: Faulting is the fracturing of rock and movement of the blocks along the crack (the fault line).

questions.question: Look at the diagram of folded rock. Which label points to the syncline?
questions.memo: A is the anticline (up-arch), B is the syncline (down-trough). Synclines hold the lowest layers in their centre.

questions.question: Large mountain ranges formed by folding are called _______ mountains.
questions.memo: Fold mountains (e.g. the Cape Fold Mountains, the Alps, the Himalayas) form where compression crumples thick rock layers upward.

questions.question: A block of rock that is pushed UP between two faults forms a _______ (block mountain).
questions.memo: A horst is an upthrown block between two faults — a block mountain. A down-dropped block between faults is a graben.

questions.question: A block of rock that DROPS DOWN between two faults forms a _______, often seen as a rift valley.
questions.memo: A graben is a down-thrown block between two faults; large grabens form rift valleys, like the East African Rift.

questions.question: What is the key difference between folding and faulting?
options: Folding bends rock; faulting breaks rock
Folding breaks rock; faulting bends rock
questions.expected: Folding bends rock; faulting breaks rock
questions.memo: Folding = bending (rock is flexible enough to crumple). Faulting = breaking (rock snaps and the blocks shift along the fault).

questions.question: Match each feature to its description.
questions.memo: 1 Anticline → C up-arch fold. 2 Syncline → D down-trough fold. 3 Horst → A up-block between faults. 4 Graben → B down-block between faults. (Prompt: 1=Anticline, 2=Syncline, 3=Horst, 4=Graben; A=raised block, B=dropped block, C=up-arch, D=down-trough.)

questions.question: The steep cliff-like step formed where the land is displaced along a fault is called a fault _______.
questions.memo: A fault scarp is the exposed cliff or step created where one side of a fault is lifted relative to the other.

questions.question: The Cape Fold Mountains in South Africa are an example of landforms created by _______.
questions.memo: The Cape Fold Belt formed when ancient plate compression crumpled the rock layers into long parallel fold ridges.

questions.question: True or false: a rift valley (graben) forms where the crust is pulled apart (tension) and a block drops between two faults.
questions.memo: Tension stretches the crust; the central block slips down between two faults to form a graben/rift valley.

questions.question: A learner labels a down-trough fold as an 'anticline'. What correction would you give?
options: A down-trough is a syncline; an anticline is the up-arch
questions.expected: A down-trough is a syncline; an anticline is the up-arch
questions.memo: Anticline = arch up; syncline = sag down. The learner swapped the two.

questions.question: Which pair of landforms is typical of FAULTING (not folding)?
questions.memo: Faulting produces horsts (block mountains) and grabens (rift valleys). Anticlines and synclines are folding features.

questions.question: Why are folded rock structures important when searching for oil and gas?
options: Oil and gas can collect in the up-arch of an anticline, trapped under impermeable rock
Oil only forms in flat rock
questions.expected: Oil and gas can collect in the up-arch of an anticline, trapped under impermeable rock
questions.memo: Anticlines make good 'traps': lighter oil and gas rise into the crest and are sealed by a cap of impermeable rock above — a key target for drilling.

questions.question: Both folding and faulting are mainly caused by the movement of _______.
questions.memo: Plate movement supplies the compression and tension forces that fold and fault the crust.

questions.question: A region shows alternating ridges and valleys of bent rock layers with no breaks. Is this folding or faulting, and why?
options: Folding — the rock is bent into arches and troughs without breaking
Faulting — the rock has clearly broken
questions.expected: Folding — the rock is bent into arches and troughs without breaking
questions.memo: Continuous bent layers (anticlines and synclines) with no fracture is the signature of folding.

questions.question: True or false: very old fold mountains are usually lower and more rounded than young ones because erosion has worn them down.
questions.memo: Young fold mountains (Himalayas) are high and jagged; old ones (Cape Fold Mountains, Appalachians) are lower and smoother after long erosion.

GEO.G10.T2.GEO.A4.title: Earthquakes
GEO.G10.T2.GEO.A4.description: Causes of earthquakes, focus and epicentre, magnitude vs intensity, where they occur, their effects, and preparation and response.
GEO.G10.T2.GEO.A4.recovery_strategy: FOCUS = where rock slips underground; EPICENTRE = the surface point above it. MAGNITUDE = energy released (one number); INTENSITY = shaking/damage felt at a place (varies). Most quakes are along plate boundaries.

questions.question: What is the main cause of most earthquakes?
options: Sudden release of stress as rocks slip along a fault
questions.expected: Sudden release of stress as rocks slip along a fault
questions.memo: Stress builds as plates move; when rocks suddenly slip along a fault, the stored energy is released as seismic waves — an earthquake.

questions.question: The exact point UNDERGROUND where an earthquake starts is called the _______.
questions.memo: The focus (or hypocentre) is the underground origin. The epicentre is the point on the surface directly above it.

questions.question: The point on the Earth's SURFACE directly above the focus is the _______.
questions.memo: Shaking is usually strongest at the epicentre because it is closest to the focus.

questions.question: What is the difference between magnitude and intensity?
options: Magnitude is the energy released; intensity is the shaking/damage felt at a place
Magnitude is felt damage; intensity is energy
questions.expected: Magnitude is the energy released; intensity is the shaking/damage felt at a place
questions.memo: Magnitude (e.g. Richter) is a single number for total energy. Intensity describes effects at a location and changes with distance, ground and buildings.

questions.question: Earthquake magnitude is measured using the _______ scale.
questions.memo: The Richter (and modern moment-magnitude) scale measures energy. Beaufort measures wind; okta measures cloud cover.

questions.question: Where do most earthquakes occur?
options: In the middle of continents only
questions.memo: Plate boundaries are where stress concentrates, so earthquakes cluster there — for example around the Pacific 'Ring of Fire'.

questions.question: The Richter scale is logarithmic. A magnitude 6 quake releases far more energy than a magnitude 5. This means each step up the scale represents _______.
options: a large jump in energy, not just one unit more
exactly one extra unit of energy
questions.expected: a large jump in energy, not just one unit more
questions.memo: Each whole number is about 32 times more energy. So magnitude 7 is vastly stronger than magnitude 6 — small number changes matter a lot.

questions.question: Sort each item as a PRIMARY effect (directly from the shaking) or a SECONDARY effect (knock-on) of an earthquake.

items.text: Disease spreading in crowded shelters afterwards

questions.memo: Primary effects come straight from the shaking (collapse, ground rupture). Secondary effects follow on (fires, tsunamis, disease, homelessness).

questions.question: A giant sea wave that can be triggered by an undersea earthquake is called a _______.
questions.memo: An undersea quake can suddenly displace huge volumes of water, sending a tsunami racing across the ocean to flood distant coasts.

questions.question: The instrument that records earthquake waves is a _______.
questions.memo: A seismograph (seismometer) records the ground vibrations from an earthquake as a trace called a seismogram.

questions.question: Two cities feel the SAME magnitude-6 quake, but one suffers far more damage. Which is the most likely reason?
options: It is closer to the epicentre or has weaker buildings and softer ground
It was further from the focus and had stronger buildings
questions.expected: It is closer to the epicentre or has weaker buildings and softer ground
questions.memo: Magnitude is fixed for one quake, but INTENSITY (damage) depends on distance, building quality and ground type — so damage varies between places.

questions.question: Which is a good way to PREPARE for earthquakes in a high-risk area?
options: Construct buildings to earthquake-resistant standards and run drills
Build only on the worst faults
Ignore building codes to save money
questions.expected: Construct buildings to earthquake-resistant standards and run drills
questions.memo: Preparation includes strict building codes, retrofitting, early-warning systems, emergency drills and public education — these save lives.

questions.question: True or false: the focus of an earthquake is on the surface and the epicentre is deep underground.
questions.memo: It is the other way round: the focus is underground (the origin); the epicentre is the surface point directly above it.

questions.question:
The table shows quake intensity felt at increasing distance from one epicentre. What pattern does it show?

| Distance from epicentre (km) | Intensity felt |
|------|------|
| 0 | Very strong |
| 50 | Strong |
| 150 | Moderate |
| 400 | Weak |
options: Intensity decreases as distance from the epicentre increases
Distance has no effect on intensity
questions.expected: Intensity decreases as distance from the epicentre increases
questions.memo: Shaking is felt most strongly near the epicentre and fades with distance as the seismic waves lose energy.

questions.question: Which countries are most at risk of major earthquakes?
options: Those located on active plate boundaries, like Japan and Chile
Those in the centre of the African Plate
questions.expected: Those located on active plate boundaries, like Japan and Chile
questions.memo: Japan, Chile, Turkey, Indonesia and others lie on active boundaries, so they face frequent, strong earthquakes.

questions.question: During strong shaking indoors, the safest immediate action is usually to _______.
options: drop, cover under sturdy furniture, and hold on
stand in a doorway and push others
use the lift to leave quickly
questions.expected: drop, cover under sturdy furniture, and hold on
questions.memo: 'Drop, cover and hold on' protects you from falling objects. Running outside during shaking and using lifts are both dangerous.

questions.question: Why do poorer communities often suffer more deaths in an earthquake of the same magnitude than wealthier ones?
options: Weaker buildings, less preparation and slower emergency response increase the toll
They are always nearer the focus
questions.expected: Weaker buildings, less preparation and slower emergency response increase the toll
questions.memo: Vulnerability depends on building quality, planning, warning systems and rescue capacity — so the human cost is partly social, not just natural.

questions.question: Seismic waves travel outwards from the focus in all directions. What does this cause at the surface?
options: Ground shaking that weakens with distance
questions.expected: Ground shaking that weakens with distance
questions.memo: The energy spreads as seismic waves, shaking the ground; the further from the focus/epicentre, the weaker the shaking.

questions.question: True or false: a coastal early-warning system can give people minutes to evacuate before a tsunami arrives.
questions.memo: Sensors detect the offshore quake and the wave; warnings broadcast to coasts can give crucial minutes to move to higher ground.

questions.question: Why might a magnitude-5 quake in a dense, poorly-built city cause more deaths than a magnitude-7 quake in an empty desert?
options: Impact depends on people and buildings exposed, not only on magnitude
Magnitude 5 always releases more energy than magnitude 7
questions.expected: Impact depends on people and buildings exposed, not only on magnitude
questions.memo: Disaster = hazard × exposure × vulnerability. A smaller quake where many vulnerable people and weak buildings are concentrated can be deadlier than a bigger one in an empty area.

GEO.G10.T2.GEO.A5.title: Volcanoes
GEO.G10.T2.GEO.A5.description: How volcanoes form and erupt, their parts, types and landforms, where they occur, and their negative and positive effects.
GEO.G10.T2.GEO.A5.recovery_strategy: MAGMA is molten rock UNDERGROUND; once it erupts it is LAVA. Volcanoes cluster at plate boundaries and hotspots. They are dangerous (ash, lava, gases) BUT bring benefits: fertile soil, geothermal energy, minerals, tourism.

questions.question: Molten rock BELOW the Earth's surface is called _______.
questions.memo: Underground molten rock is magma. Once it erupts onto the surface it is called lava.

questions.question: Molten rock that has erupted ONTO the surface is called _______.
questions.memo: Lava is erupted magma. The name change marks where it crosses the surface.

questions.question: The opening at the top of a volcano through which lava and ash erupt is the _______.
questions.memo: Magma rises through the central vent and erupts at the crater. The store of magma below is the magma chamber.

questions.question: Look at the cross-section of a volcano. Which label points to the magma chamber?
options: D — the underground store of molten rock
A — the crater at the top
questions.expected: D — the underground store of molten rock
questions.memo: A crater, B vent, C ash cloud, D magma chamber (the underground reservoir feeding the eruption).

questions.question: Where are most volcanoes found?
options: Along plate boundaries and over hotspots
Only in the middle of oceans far from boundaries
questions.expected: Along plate boundaries and over hotspots
questions.memo: Volcanoes cluster where magma can reach the surface: at plate boundaries (e.g. the Ring of Fire) and over mantle hotspots (e.g. Hawaii).

questions.question: A learner says 'magma flows down the outside of the volcano'. What is the correction?
options: Once it flows on the surface it is called lava, not magma
questions.expected: Once it flows on the surface it is called lava, not magma
questions.memo: Magma is the underground form; the same material flowing on the surface is lava. The learner used the wrong term.

questions.question: Sort each item as a NEGATIVE effect or a POSITIVE effect of volcanoes.

items.text: Lava and ash destroying homes and crops
Very fertile volcanic soils for farming
People forced to evacuate and lose livelihoods

questions.memo: Volcanoes harm (lava, ash, gases, evacuation) AND help (fertile soils, geothermal power, minerals, tourism). They are a hazard and a resource.

questions.question: Why is the soil around many volcanoes very fertile?
options: Volcanic ash and rock weather into mineral-rich soil
Volcanoes add water to the soil
Ash blocks all plant growth permanently
questions.expected: Volcanic ash and rock weather into mineral-rich soil
questions.memo: Weathered volcanic ash and lava release minerals like potassium and phosphorus, creating very fertile soils — which is why people farm near volcanoes despite the risk.

questions.question: Energy generated from the heat of volcanic/underground areas is called _______ energy.
questions.memo: Geothermal energy taps underground heat (steam) to generate electricity — used widely in Iceland, Kenya and New Zealand.

questions.question: A tall, steep-sided volcano built of alternating ash and lava layers is a _______ volcano.
questions.memo: Composite (stratovolcano) cones are steep and built of layers of ash and thick lava (e.g. Mount Fuji). Shield volcanoes are broad and gentle (runny lava, e.g. Hawaii).

questions.question: A broad, gently-sloping volcano formed by runny, fast-flowing lava is a _______ volcano.
questions.memo: Shield volcanoes (e.g. Mauna Loa) have gentle slopes because their thin, runny lava spreads far before cooling.

questions.question: True or false: an 'active' volcano is one that has erupted recently or is expected to erupt again.
questions.memo: Active = erupting or likely to erupt; dormant = 'sleeping' but could wake; extinct = not expected to erupt again.

questions.question: Hot, fast-moving clouds of gas, ash and rock that rush down a volcano's slopes are called _______.
questions.memo: Pyroclastic flows are among the deadliest volcanic hazards — superheated, fast and impossible to outrun.

questions.question: Why do many people continue to live near dangerous active volcanoes?
options: Fertile soils, geothermal energy, minerals, tourism and ancestral ties outweigh the risk for them
There is nowhere else on Earth to live
Governments force everyone to live there
questions.expected: Fertile soils, geothermal energy, minerals, tourism and ancestral ties outweigh the risk for them
questions.memo: People weigh real benefits (rich farmland, energy, jobs, home) against an occasional risk — a trade-off seen around many volcanoes.

questions.question: The Pacific 'Ring of Fire' is known for having many _______.
questions.memo: The Ring of Fire is a belt of plate boundaries around the Pacific with the world's highest concentration of volcanoes and earthquakes.

questions.question: Which volcanic hazard can affect air travel thousands of kilometres away?
options: Ash clouds that damage jet engines
questions.expected: Ash clouds that damage jet engines
questions.memo: Fine ash can drift far and is dangerous to aircraft engines, so eruptions can ground flights across whole regions.

questions.question: How can monitoring help reduce deaths from a volcanic eruption?
options: Scientists detect warning signs (gases, tremors, bulging) and order timely evacuations
Monitoring makes the soil more fertile
questions.expected: Scientists detect warning signs (gases, tremors, bulging) and order timely evacuations
questions.memo: Volcanoes usually give warning signs. Monitoring them allows authorities to evacuate people before an eruption — saving lives even if property is lost.

questions.question: True or false: a dormant volcano can never erupt again.
questions.memo: A dormant volcano is only 'sleeping' and can erupt again. Only an EXTINCT volcano is not expected to erupt.

questions.question: Magma rises towards the surface mainly because it is _______.
options: less dense than the surrounding rock
questions.expected: less dense than the surrounding rock
questions.memo: Hot, molten, gas-rich magma is less dense than the solid rock around it, so it is buoyant and forces its way upward.

questions.question: How are volcanoes and plate tectonics linked?
options: Most volcanoes form where plates pull apart or collide, allowing magma to reach the surface
Volcanoes have nothing to do with plates
Volcanoes only form on flat plains
questions.expected: Most volcanoes form where plates pull apart or collide, allowing magma to reach the surface
questions.memo: At divergent boundaries magma rises into the gap; at convergent boundaries a subducting plate melts and feeds volcanoes — both are products of plate tectonics.

GEO.G10.T3.POP.A1.title: Population distribution & density
GEO.G10.T3.POP.A1.description: Distribution vs density, calculating density, the physical and human factors behind where people live, and reading distribution from data.
GEO.G10.T3.POP.A1.recovery_strategy: DISTRIBUTION = the PATTERN of where people live. DENSITY = a NUMBER: people ÷ area (km²). High density is pulled by water, flat land, good climate, jobs and cities; deserts, mountains and dense forest are sparse.

questions.question: What does population DISTRIBUTION describe?
options: The pattern of where people live across an area
The number of people per km²
questions.expected: The pattern of where people live across an area
questions.memo: Distribution is the SPREAD or pattern — clustered, even or sparse. Density is a number (people per km²).

questions.question: Population density is calculated as _______.
questions.memo: Density = number of people ÷ area in km². It tells you how crowded a place is.
