questions.question: A district has 600 000 people living in an area of 3 000 km². What is its population density?
questions.memo: Density = 600 000 ÷ 3 000 = 200 people/km².

questions.question: Which is a PHYSICAL factor that attracts people to settle in an area?
options: Flat, fertile land with reliable water
questions.expected: Flat, fertile land with reliable water
questions.memo: Physical (natural) pulls: water, flat fertile land, mild climate, resources. Human pulls: jobs, services, transport, universities.

questions.question: Which type of area usually has a LOW population density?
questions.memo: Harsh environments — deserts (no water), high mountains (cold, steep), dense rainforest, frozen poles — repel settlement, giving low density.

questions.question: Sort each factor as PHYSICAL or HUMAN influence on where people live.
questions.memo: Physical = natural conditions (water, soil, climate, relief). Human = things people build or provide (jobs, services, transport).

questions.question:
The table shows two provinces. Which has the higher population density?

| Province | Population | Area (km²) |
|------|------|------|
| X | 4 000 000 | 20 000 |
| Y | 2 000 000 | 40 000 |
options: Province X (200/km²) is denser than Y (50/km²)
questions.expected: Province X (200/km²) is denser than Y (50/km²)
questions.memo: X: 4 000 000 ÷ 20 000 = 200/km². Y: 2 000 000 ÷ 40 000 = 50/km². X is four times denser even though both are large.

questions.question: True or false: two countries can have the same total population but very different population densities.
questions.memo: Density depends on area too. The same population spread over a small area is dense; over a large area it is sparse.

questions.question: An evenly-spread population and a clustered population can have the same density but differ in their _______.
questions.memo: Density is one number; distribution is the PATTERN. Same density can be spread evenly or bunched in clusters.

questions.question: Why are river valleys and coastlines often densely populated?
options: They offer water, flat fertile land, food and transport routes
People are forced to live there by law
questions.expected: They offer water, flat fertile land, food and transport routes
questions.memo: Water for drinking and farming, fertile flat land, fishing and easy trade by river/sea make valleys and coasts attractive — hence high density.

questions.question: A map shading people-per-km² in different colours by area is called a _______ map.
questions.memo: A choropleth map uses shades/colours to show how a value (like density) varies between areas — darker usually means higher.

questions.question: True or false: a high population density always means an area is overcrowded and cannot cope.
questions.memo: High density is not the same as overcrowding. A wealthy, well-serviced city can support a high density comfortably; 'overpopulation' depends on resources and services, not density alone.

questions.question: Which is an example of a sparsely populated area in South Africa?
questions.memo: The dry, hot Karoo of the Northern Cape has little water and farming, so very few people — low density. The big cities are densely populated.

questions.question: A town's population stays at 50 000 but its built-up area doubles. What happens to its population density?
options: Density falls because the same people spread over a larger area
questions.expected: Density falls because the same people spread over a larger area
questions.memo: Density = people ÷ area. If people stay the same but area doubles, density is halved.

questions.question: Most of the world's people live in which kind of zone?
options: Temperate areas with water, fertile land and mild climate
questions.expected: Temperate areas with water, fertile land and mild climate
questions.memo: Population concentrates where conditions support life and work — temperate, well-watered lowlands near coasts and rivers.

questions.question: Why might a mineral-rich desert town have a surprisingly high density despite a harsh climate?
options: A human factor (mining jobs) overrides the poor physical conditions
questions.expected: A human factor (mining jobs) overrides the poor physical conditions
questions.memo: Human pulls (jobs, money) can draw people even into harsh places — e.g. mining towns. Distribution reflects BOTH physical and human factors.

questions.question: True or false: population density is usually expressed as the number of people per square kilometre (people/km²).
questions.memo: Density is standardly given in people per km², which allows fair comparison between areas of different size.

questions.question: Which combination would give the HIGHEST population density?
options: A large population in a small area
A small population in a large area
A small population in a small area
A large population in a large area
questions.expected: A large population in a small area
questions.memo: Density rises when many people occupy little space. Many people ÷ small area = high density (e.g. an inner city).

questions.question: A planner sees a region with low density but rapid in-migration to one city. What does this reveal about distribution?
options: People are clustering unevenly — overall density is low but one node is growing fast
The whole region is evenly packed
Density and distribution are the same thing
questions.expected: People are clustering unevenly — overall density is low but one node is growing fast
questions.memo: Averages hide patterns: a low regional density can mask intense clustering in one growing city — that is why distribution (pattern) matters as well as density (number).

questions.question: A learner says 'high density' and 'large population' mean exactly the same thing. Why are they wrong?
options: A large population in a huge area can still have low density
Density and population can never differ
questions.expected: A large population in a huge area can still have low density
questions.memo: Population is a count; density also factors in area. A big country can hold many people yet be sparsely populated overall.

GEO.G10.T3.POP.A2.title: Population structure
GEO.G10.T3.POP.A2.description: Reading population pyramids, the shapes of expansive/constrictive/stationary pyramids, dependency ratio, and what structure implies for a country's future.
GEO.G10.T3.POP.A2.recovery_strategy: A pyramid stacks age groups (youngest at the bottom), males one side, females the other. WIDE base = many children = fast growth (expansive). Narrowing base = slowing (constrictive). Straight sides = stable (stationary).

questions.question: A population pyramid shows a country's population divided by _______.
questions.memo: A population pyramid is a back-to-back bar graph: age groups stacked vertically, one sex on each side.

questions.question: On a population pyramid, the youngest age group is shown _______.
questions.memo: Age 0–4 is at the base; the oldest groups are at the top. The base width shows how many children there are.

questions.question: A pyramid with a very WIDE base and narrow top indicates a population that is _______.
questions.memo: A wide base means many young children and high birth rates — an expansive, fast-growing population typical of many developing countries.

questions.question: Look at the three pyramid shapes. Which one shows an EXPANSIVE (fast-growing) population?
questions.memo: A (wide base) = expansive/growing. B (straight sides) = stationary/stable. C (narrow base) = constrictive/shrinking or ageing.

questions.question: A pyramid with fairly straight, vertical sides (similar numbers in each age group) shows a _______ population.
questions.memo: Straight sides mean birth and death rates are low and balanced — a stationary population with slow or zero growth (typical of many developed countries).

questions.question: The 'dependent' population usually includes which groups?
questions.memo: Dependants are too young or too old to work and rely on the working-age group (15–64). The dependency ratio compares dependants to workers.

questions.question: A country with a very wide pyramid base will need to plan especially for more _______.
questions.memo: Lots of children means high demand for schooling, child healthcare and, soon, jobs — key planning challenges for fast-growing populations.

questions.question:
The table gives one country's age structure. What does it suggest about growth?

| Age group | % of population |
|------|------|
| 0–14 | 42 |
| 15–64 | 54 |
| 65+ | 4 |
questions.memo: 42% under 15 and only 4% over 65 signals high birth rates and a young, expansive population.

questions.question: Which side of a population pyramid usually shows males?
options: The left side (females on the right) — but always check the labels
Always the right side regardless of labels
questions.expected: The left side (females on the right) — but always check the labels
questions.memo: By convention males are on the left and females on the right, but you must always read the axis labels to be sure.

questions.question: A pyramid with a NARROW base and a bulge in the older groups suggests a population that is _______.
options: ageing and may shrink in future
questions.expected: ageing and may shrink in future
questions.memo: Few children at the base plus many older people means low birth rates and an ageing population — a constrictive shape, often seen in wealthy ageing nations.

questions.question: True or false: a wide-based pyramid means a SHRINKING population.
questions.memo: A wide base means lots of children and FAST GROWTH, not shrinking. A narrow base would suggest shrinking.

questions.question: A high dependency ratio means _______.
options: many dependants are supported by relatively few workers
questions.expected: many dependants are supported by relatively few workers
questions.memo: A high dependency ratio strains the working population and the state, which must support many children and/or elderly with the taxes of fewer workers.

questions.question: Why might a country with an ageing pyramid worry about its future workforce and pensions?
options: Fewer young workers must support a growing number of retirees
Too many babies are being born
questions.expected: Fewer young workers must support a growing number of retirees
questions.memo: An ageing structure means a shrinking working-age base paying for more pensions and healthcare — a real planning challenge (e.g. Japan, Italy).

questions.question: A sudden 'notch' (much shorter bars) for one age band on a pyramid could be caused by _______.
options: a past war, famine or epidemic that reduced births or raised deaths
questions.expected: a past war, famine or epidemic that reduced births or raised deaths
questions.memo: Indentations record history: wars, famines or disease cut a cohort's numbers, leaving a lasting notch as that group ages up the pyramid.

questions.question: Which pyramid shape is most typical of a wealthy, developed country?
options: Narrow base with fairly even or top-heavy sides (low growth/ageing)
A perfect triangle of children only
questions.expected: Narrow base with fairly even or top-heavy sides (low growth/ageing)
questions.memo: Developed countries usually have low birth and death rates, so their pyramids are narrow-based and column-like or top-heavy.

questions.question: True or false: the SHAPE of a population pyramid can be used to predict a country's future population needs.
questions.memo: Shape forecasts demand: a wide base warns of future demand for schools and jobs; a top-heavy shape warns of future pension and care costs.

questions.question: On a pyramid, if each bar is roughly the same length up to old age, birth and death rates are most likely _______.
questions.memo: Even, column-like bars indicate a stationary population with low, balanced birth and death rates and little growth.

questions.question: A learner reads the longest bar at the BASE as 'the oldest group'. What is the mistake?
options: The base shows the YOUNGEST group; the oldest are at the top
The base shows the oldest group correctly
The longest bar is always the elderly
questions.expected: The base shows the YOUNGEST group; the oldest are at the top
questions.memo: Always read from the bottom (youngest, 0–4) up to the top (oldest). A long base = many young children, not elderly.

questions.question: Why is a large working-age 'bulge' (a 'youth bulge' moving into adulthood) sometimes called a demographic opportunity?
options: A big workforce can boost the economy if there are enough jobs and education
questions.expected: A big workforce can boost the economy if there are enough jobs and education
questions.memo: A large working-age share can drive growth (a 'demographic dividend') — BUT only if the economy creates enough jobs and skills; otherwise it raises unemployment.

questions.question: True or false: comparing two countries' pyramids can show which one is growing faster and which is ageing.
questions.memo: Side-by-side pyramids reveal differences at a glance: a wide-based one is growing fast; a top-heavy one is ageing.

GEO.G10.T3.POP.A3.title: Population growth
GEO.G10.T3.POP.A3.description: Birth and death rates, natural increase and growth rate, the demographic transition in plain terms, factors changing rates, and world case studies.
GEO.G10.T3.POP.A3.recovery_strategy: NATURAL INCREASE = birth rate − death rate (per 1 000), ÷10 for %. It does NOT include migration. As countries develop, death rates fall first, then birth rates fall later — so growth is fast in between, slow at the end.

questions.question: Birth rate and death rate are usually given as the number of births or deaths per _______ people per year.
questions.memo: Crude birth and death rates are 'per 1 000 of the population per year', which makes countries of different sizes comparable.

questions.question: Natural increase is calculated as _______.
questions.memo: Natural increase = birth rate − death rate. If births exceed deaths the population grows naturally.

questions.question: A country has a birth rate of 30 and a death rate of 10 (per 1 000). What is its natural increase rate?
questions.memo: Natural increase = 30 − 10 = 20 per 1 000 = 20 ÷ 10 = 2,0% per year.

questions.question: A learner adds the birth rate and death rate to find growth. Why is that wrong?
options: Natural increase is births MINUS deaths, not plus
questions.expected: Natural increase is births MINUS deaths, not plus
questions.memo: Deaths REDUCE a population, so you subtract: birth rate − death rate. Adding them would wildly overstate growth.

questions.question: True or false: total population change includes BOTH natural increase and migration.
questions.memo: Total change = natural increase (births − deaths) PLUS net migration (immigration − emigration). Natural increase alone ignores migration.

questions.question: As a country develops, which rate usually falls FIRST?
options: The death rate (better food, water and healthcare)
questions.expected: The death rate (better food, water and healthcare)
questions.memo: Improved health, food and clean water cut the death rate first. Birth rates fall later as education, family planning and urban life change family size.

questions.question: Population grows FASTEST when _______.
options: death rates have fallen but birth rates are still high
birth and death rates are both low
birth and death rates are both high
questions.expected: death rates have fallen but birth rates are still high
questions.memo: The widest gap between high births and falling deaths gives the fastest growth — the middle stage of the demographic transition.

questions.question: Which factor tends to LOWER birth rates in a country?
options: Better education of women and access to family planning
questions.expected: Better education of women and access to family planning
questions.memo: Education (especially of girls), women working, urban living, lower child mortality and family planning all push birth rates down.

questions.question:
The table shows one country over time. What is happening to its growth?

| Year | Birth rate | Death rate |
|------|------|------|
| 1980 | 42 | 18 |
| 2000 | 34 | 10 |
| 2020 | 24 | 8 |
options: Natural increase is slowing as the birth rate falls towards the death rate
Birth and death rates are rising
questions.expected: Natural increase is slowing as the birth rate falls towards the death rate
questions.memo: Gap shrinks: 1980 = 24, 2000 = 24, 2020 = 16 per 1 000. As birth rate drops towards the low death rate, natural increase slows.

questions.question: A birth rate LOWER than the death rate produces _______.
questions.memo: If deaths outnumber births, natural increase is negative — a natural decrease — and the population shrinks (unless migration offsets it).

questions.question: Order the stages of population change a developing country typically passes through.

items.text: High birth and high death rates — slow growth
Death rate falls, birth rate stays high — rapid growth
Birth rate falls too — growth slows
Low birth and low death rates — slow or no growth

questions.memo: This is the demographic transition: high–high → falling deaths → falling births → low–low. Growth is fastest in the middle.

questions.question: Many countries in Africa currently have _______ population growth.
options: relatively high (young populations, birth rates still above death rates)
questions.expected: relatively high (young populations, birth rates still above death rates)
questions.memo: Many African countries are in the rapid-growth stage: young populations and birth rates still well above death rates.

questions.question: Some wealthy countries now have very low or negative natural increase. A common response is to _______.
options: encourage immigration or higher birth rates to support the workforce
questions.expected: encourage immigration or higher birth rates to support the workforce
questions.memo: Ageing, low-growth countries may use immigration and family-friendly policies to keep enough workers supporting the economy and pensions.

questions.question: True or false: a falling growth RATE still means the population can keep getting bigger.
questions.memo: As long as births exceed deaths, the population grows — just more slowly. It only shrinks when growth becomes negative.

questions.question: Which is a likely consequence of very rapid population growth in a poor country?
options: Pressure on food, water, jobs, housing and services
questions.expected: Pressure on food, water, jobs, housing and services
questions.memo: Fast growth can outpace the economy and environment, straining food, water, housing, jobs, schools and clinics.

questions.question: The death rate of infants in their first year is the _______ rate, a key indicator of development.
questions.memo: Infant mortality rate (deaths under age 1 per 1 000 births) is a sensitive measure of healthcare and living standards; it falls as a country develops.

questions.question: Why does better healthcare often cause faster population growth at first, before growth slows later?
options: Deaths drop quickly while births stay high, widening the gap; births fall only later
Healthcare increases births immediately and forever
Healthcare has no effect on population
questions.expected: Deaths drop quickly while births stay high, widening the gap; births fall only later
questions.memo: Health gains cut the death rate fast; cultural change to smaller families takes longer, so growth surges first and eases afterwards.

questions.question: A country has a natural increase of 0 but its population still grows. The most likely reason is _______.
options: net immigration (more people moving in than out)
questions.expected: net immigration (more people moving in than out)
questions.memo: Total change = natural increase + net migration. With zero natural increase, growth must come from more immigration than emigration.

questions.question: True or false: the number of children an average woman has (the fertility rate) strongly affects how fast a population grows.
questions.memo: A high fertility rate drives fast growth; as fertility falls towards about two children per woman, growth slows towards replacement level.

questions.question: Two countries have the same birth rate, but country A grows faster. Which difference best explains this?
options: Country A has a lower death rate and/or net immigration
Country A has fewer people overall
Birth rate is the only thing that matters
questions.expected: Country A has a lower death rate and/or net immigration
questions.memo: Growth depends on births MINUS deaths PLUS migration. With equal births, a lower death rate or more immigration makes A grow faster.

GEO.G10.T3.POP.A4.title: Population movements
GEO.G10.T3.POP.A4.description: Migration concepts (emigration/immigration, internal/international, voluntary/forced), push and pull factors, rural-to-urban migration and urbanisation, and effects on source and destination.
GEO.G10.T3.POP.A4.recovery_strategy: EMIGRATE = Exit a country; IMMIGRATE = come In. PUSH factors drive people away (drought, war, no jobs); PULL factors attract them (jobs, safety, services). Most internal migration in developing countries is rural → urban.

questions.question: Migration means the movement of people to _______.
options: visit on holiday for a week
questions.memo: Migration is a permanent or long-term move of residence — not a short trip or holiday.

questions.question: A person who LEAVES their country to live elsewhere is an _______.
questions.memo: Emigrant = Exits a country. Immigrant = comes Into a country. The same person is an emigrant from home and an immigrant in the new country.

questions.question: A person who ARRIVES in a new country to settle is an _______.
questions.memo: Immigrant = comes In. (A refugee is a specific kind of forced immigrant fleeing danger.)

questions.question: Which is a PUSH factor (driving people to leave an area)?
options: Good schools in the new city
questions.memo: Push factors are negatives at the origin (drought, war, unemployment, poverty). Pull factors are positives at the destination (jobs, safety, services).

questions.question: Sort each factor as a PUSH (from origin) or PULL (to destination) factor.

items.text: Better job opportunities in the city
Safety and political stability in the destination

questions.memo: Push = bad things you flee FROM; pull = good things you move TO. Most migration results from a mix of both.

questions.question: Migration WITHIN the borders of one country is called _______ migration.
questions.memo: Internal migration stays inside a country (e.g. rural to urban); international migration crosses national borders.

questions.question: The most common type of internal migration in developing countries is _______.
questions.memo: People move from the countryside to cities seeking jobs and services — driving urbanisation.

questions.question: The growth in the proportion of people living in towns and cities is called _______.
questions.memo: Urbanisation is the rising share of a population living in urban areas, largely fed by rural-to-urban migration and city growth.

questions.question: A person forced to flee their country because of war or persecution is best described as a _______.
questions.memo: A refugee is forced to flee danger across a border. An economic migrant moves mainly by choice to find work.

questions.question: Which is an example of FORCED migration?
options: Fleeing a war or a major flood
questions.expected: Fleeing a war or a major flood
questions.memo: Forced migration leaves people no real choice (war, persecution, disaster). Voluntary migration is a chosen move, usually for work or study.

questions.question: What is a likely NEGATIVE effect of heavy out-migration on a rural SOURCE area?
options: Loss of young, working-age people and skills
questions.expected: Loss of young, working-age people and skills
questions.memo: When the young and able leave, rural areas lose labour and skills ('brain drain'), leaving behind the very young and old and weakening the local economy.

questions.question: What is a possible POSITIVE effect of migration for the source area?
options: Money sent home (remittances) supports families left behind
questions.expected: Money sent home (remittances) supports families left behind
questions.memo: Migrants often send remittances home, easing pressure on jobs at the source and funding food, schooling and small businesses.

questions.question: What is a likely CHALLENGE for a city receiving large numbers of migrants?
options: Pressure on housing, services and jobs, sometimes informal settlements
questions.expected: Pressure on housing, services and jobs, sometimes informal settlements
questions.memo: Rapid in-migration can outpace housing and services, leading to informal settlements, strained infrastructure and competition for jobs.

questions.question: A learner says 'you emigrate INTO a country'. What is the correction?
options: You emigrate OUT of a country and immigrate INTO one
Emigrate and immigrate mean the same
You can only emigrate at night
questions.expected: You emigrate OUT of a country and immigrate INTO one
questions.memo: Emigrate = exit; immigrate = come in. The learner mixed the two.

questions.question: Match each term to its meaning.
questions.memo: 1 Emigrant → C leaves a country. 2 Immigrant → A enters a country. 3 Refugee → D forced to flee danger. 4 Economic migrant → B moves mainly for work. (Prompt: 1=Emigrant, 2=Immigrant, 3=Refugee, 4=Economic migrant; A=enters a country, B=moves for work, C=leaves a country, D=flees danger.)

questions.question: True or false: most migrants are pushed AND pulled — several factors usually act together.
questions.memo: Decisions to move usually combine push factors (problems at home) and pull factors (opportunities elsewhere), not a single cause.

questions.question: Why can migration be a BENEFIT to a receiving country, despite the challenges?
options: Migrants fill labour shortages, bring skills and pay taxes
questions.expected: Migrants fill labour shortages, bring skills and pay taxes
questions.memo: Migrants often take needed jobs, add skills and youth, pay taxes and start businesses — real economic and cultural gains for the destination.

questions.question: A rural village is left mainly with the very young and the elderly after years of out-migration. What does this show?
options: Selective migration of working-age people has changed the village's age structure
Migration has no effect on age structure
questions.expected: Selective migration of working-age people has changed the village's age structure
questions.memo: Migration is often age-selective: the young and able leave for work, hollowing out the working-age group and skewing the age structure.

questions.question: In South Africa, the historical migrant-labour system mainly moved men to work in _______.
options: mines and cities, away from their rural homes
questions.expected: mines and cities, away from their rural homes
questions.memo: The migrant-labour system drew men from rural areas (and neighbouring countries) to mines and cities, splitting families — a lasting feature of SA's geography.

questions.question: A government wants to slow rural-to-urban migration. Which approach addresses the ROOT cause?
options: Improve rural jobs, schools and services so people have less reason to leave
Build a wall around the city
questions.expected: Improve rural jobs, schools and services so people have less reason to leave
questions.memo: Reducing the PUSH factors — better rural opportunities and services — tackles the cause, unlike simply trying to block people from moving.

GEO.G10.T3.POP.A5.title: HIV and AIDS
GEO.G10.T3.POP.A5.description: The difference between HIV and AIDS, effects on population structure and the economy, impact in Africa, and prevention, treatment and management.
GEO.G10.T3.POP.A5.recovery_strategy: HIV is the VIRUS; AIDS is the advanced STAGE if untreated. A heavy burden removes working-age adults, lowers life expectancy, leaves orphans and shrinks the pyramid's middle. ARVs, education and prevention reduce the impact.

questions.question: What does HIV stand for (in plain terms, what is it)?
options: A virus that weakens the body's immune system
A type of bacteria spread by water
A kind of cancer caused by smoking
questions.expected: A virus that weakens the body's immune system
questions.memo: HIV (Human Immunodeficiency Virus) attacks the immune system, making it harder for the body to fight other infections.

questions.question: What is the difference between HIV and AIDS?
options: HIV is the virus; AIDS is the advanced stage of illness it can cause
They are exactly the same thing
AIDS is the virus; HIV is the medicine
questions.expected: HIV is the virus; AIDS is the advanced stage of illness it can cause
questions.memo: HIV is the infection; AIDS (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome) is the late stage when the immune system is severely damaged. Treatment can prevent HIV from progressing to AIDS.

questions.question: True or false: a person living with HIV always has AIDS.
questions.memo: Many people live healthily with HIV for years, especially on treatment (ARVs). AIDS is only the advanced stage, which treatment can prevent.

questions.question: The medicines that control HIV and help prevent AIDS are called _______.
questions.memo: Antiretroviral drugs (ARVs) suppress the virus, keep people healthy and greatly reduce transmission. They control HIV but do not cure it.

questions.question: How does a severe HIV/AIDS epidemic affect a country's population pyramid?
options: It narrows the working-age middle as many adults die early
It has no effect on the pyramid
questions.expected: It narrows the working-age middle as many adults die early
questions.memo: Because it kills many young and middle-aged adults, the epidemic 'bites out' the middle of the pyramid, lowering life expectancy.

questions.question: Which region has been most heavily affected by HIV/AIDS?
questions.memo: Sub-Saharan Africa, including Southern Africa, has carried the world's heaviest HIV/AIDS burden, though treatment has greatly improved outcomes.

questions.question: A child who has lost one or both parents to AIDS is often referred to as an AIDS _______.
questions.memo: The epidemic has created many orphans, often cared for by grandparents or child-headed households — a major social impact.

questions.question: Sort each item as a way to PREVENT HIV spread or a SOCIAL/ECONOMIC IMPACT of the epidemic.

items.text: Testing and starting ARV treatment early
Higher healthcare costs and lower life expectancy

questions.memo: Prevention = actions that stop spread (condoms, education, testing, ARVs). Impacts = the effects on society and the economy (orphans, lost workers, costs).

questions.question: How does HIV/AIDS affect a country's economy?
options: It reduces the workforce and raises healthcare costs
questions.expected: It reduces the workforce and raises healthcare costs
questions.memo: Illness and early deaths among working-age adults cut productivity and household income while raising health and welfare spending.

questions.question:
The table shows life expectancy in one country. What does the dip and recovery most likely reflect?

| Year | Life expectancy (years) |
|------|------|
| 1990 | 62 |
| 2005 | 52 |
| 2020 | 64 |
options: A peak of HIV/AIDS deaths around 2005, then recovery as ARVs rolled out
A steady rise with no setbacks
A permanent fall in life expectancy
questions.expected: A peak of HIV/AIDS deaths around 2005, then recovery as ARVs rolled out
questions.memo: The mid-2000s dip reflects heavy AIDS mortality; the recovery by 2020 reflects widespread ARV treatment restoring life expectancy.

questions.question: Which is an effective PREVENTION strategy against HIV?
options: Education, condom use, testing and early treatment
Blaming and excluding people who are infected
questions.expected: Education, condom use, testing and early treatment
questions.memo: Combined prevention — education, condoms, regular testing, treatment-as-prevention and mother-to-child prevention — has driven new infections down.

questions.question: True or false: stigma and discrimination can make the epidemic worse by stopping people from testing and seeking treatment.
questions.memo: Fear of being judged keeps people from testing and treatment, allowing the virus to spread silently. Reducing stigma is part of effective management.

questions.question: ARV treatment that prevents a pregnant woman from passing HIV to her baby targets _______ transmission.
questions.memo: Prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) uses ARVs during pregnancy and birth to protect the baby — a major public-health success.

questions.question: Why does losing many young adults hit a country especially hard?
options: They are the main workers and parents, so the economy and families both suffer
Young adults do not contribute to society
Only retirees matter to the economy
questions.expected: They are the main workers and parents, so the economy and families both suffer
questions.memo: Young adults are the productive, child-raising core of society; their loss reduces output, breaks up families and increases dependency.

questions.question: True or false: with consistent ARV treatment, many people with HIV can live long, healthy lives and are far less likely to pass on the virus.
questions.memo: Effective treatment keeps people healthy and can suppress the virus so low that it is not transmitted ('undetectable = untransmittable').

questions.question: Grandparents raising grandchildren and 'child-headed households' are social effects linked to _______.
questions.memo: When parents die, care often shifts to elderly grandparents or to children themselves — reshaping households and increasing vulnerability.

questions.question: Why is a combined strategy (education + testing + treatment + reducing stigma) better than any single action against HIV/AIDS?
options: Each part supports the others, tackling spread, illness and barriers together
Only one action is ever needed
Combining strategies wastes money for no benefit
questions.expected: Each part supports the others, tackling spread, illness and barriers together
questions.memo: No single measure is enough: education changes behaviour, testing finds cases, ARVs treat and prevent, and reducing stigma keeps people engaged — together they work best.

questions.question: Which statement about HIV transmission is correct?
options: It is NOT spread by everyday contact like sharing food or hugging
It is spread by shaking hands
It is spread through the air like a cold
questions.expected: It is NOT spread by everyday contact like sharing food or hugging
questions.memo: HIV is not spread by casual everyday contact. Understanding this reduces stigma and fear while focusing prevention on real routes of transmission.

questions.question: A country expands free testing and ARV access. Over ten years, what trend would show this is working?
options: Falling AIDS deaths and rising life expectancy
A sudden fall in total population
questions.expected: Falling AIDS deaths and rising life expectancy
questions.memo: Success shows up as fewer AIDS deaths, recovering life expectancy and fewer new infections — exactly what wide ARV roll-out has achieved.

questions.question: True or false: HIV/AIDS is both a health issue and a development issue because it affects the workforce, families and the economy.
questions.memo: Its reach into labour, household income, orphan care and public spending makes HIV/AIDS a development challenge, not only a medical one.

GEO.G10.T4.WAT.A1.title: Water in the world
GEO.G10.T4.WAT.A1.description: The water cycle, the distribution of fresh and salt water, the value of water, and water as a shared, finite resource.
GEO.G10.T4.WAT.A1.recovery_strategy: About 97% of Earth's water is salt water; only ~3% is fresh, and most of that is frozen or underground — so usable fresh water is tiny. Water cycle: EVAPORATION → CONDENSATION → PRECIPITATION → runoff/infiltration → back to the sea.

questions.question: Roughly what share of the Earth's water is salt water in the oceans?
questions.memo: About 97% of all water is salty ocean water. Only ~3% is fresh, and most of that is locked in ice and groundwater.

questions.question: Most of the world's FRESH water is stored as _______.
options: ice in glaciers and ice caps
questions.expected: ice in glaciers and ice caps
questions.memo: The majority of fresh water is frozen in ice caps and glaciers; only a small fraction is easily-usable river, lake and shallow groundwater.

questions.question: The continuous movement of water between the sea, air and land is called the _______.
questions.memo: The water (hydrological) cycle recycles Earth's water through evaporation, condensation, precipitation and runoff — there is no 'new' water.

questions.question: Put the main stages of the water cycle in order, starting from the ocean.

items.text: Runoff and rivers carry water back to the sea

questions.memo: Evaporation → condensation → precipitation → runoff/infiltration → back to the sea, then it repeats endlessly.

questions.question: Look at the water-cycle diagram. Which label shows precipitation?
options: C — rain or snow falling to the ground
A — water rising as vapour from the sea
D — water soaking into the soil
questions.expected: C — rain or snow falling to the ground
questions.memo: A evaporation, B condensation, C precipitation (rain/snow), D infiltration. Precipitation is water FALLING from clouds.

questions.question: Water soaking down into the soil and rock is called _______.
questions.memo: Infiltration is water sinking into the ground to become soil moisture and groundwater. Runoff is water flowing over the surface.

questions.question: Water released into the air from plant leaves is called _______.
questions.memo: Transpiration is evaporation of water from plants. Together with evaporation it is sometimes called evapotranspiration.

questions.question: True or false: because the water cycle recycles water, the total amount of water on Earth stays almost the same.
questions.memo: Earth's water is finite and recycled, not created or destroyed. The same water has been cycling for billions of years.

questions.question: Why is fresh water described as a SCARCE resource even though Earth is called the 'blue planet'?
options: Almost all water is salty or frozen, leaving very little usable fresh water
There is no water on land at all
Fresh water is being created too fast
questions.expected: Almost all water is salty or frozen, leaving very little usable fresh water
questions.memo: The oceans look vast, but only ~3% is fresh and most of that is ice or deep groundwater — so easily-usable fresh water is a tiny, precious share.

questions.question: Which is a major USE of fresh water worldwide?
questions.memo: Agriculture is the biggest user of fresh water globally (irrigation), followed by industry and domestic use.

questions.question: Energy from the Sun drives the water cycle by causing _______.
questions.memo: Solar heating evaporates water from oceans and land, lifting it into the atmosphere to begin the cycle.

questions.question: An underground store of water held in rock and soil is called _______.
questions.memo: Groundwater fills spaces in soil and rock (aquifers) and is a vital fresh-water source, reached by wells and boreholes.

questions.question: A learner says 'condensation' is when rain falls to the ground. What is the correction?
options: Rain falling is PRECIPITATION; condensation is vapour forming clouds
Condensation is correct for falling rain
questions.expected: Rain falling is PRECIPITATION; condensation is vapour forming clouds
questions.memo: Condensation = vapour turning into cloud droplets. Precipitation = those droplets falling as rain, snow or hail.

questions.question: True or false: clean fresh water is essential for drinking, food production, health and most industries.
questions.memo: Water underpins life, farming, sanitation, health and industry — which is why its scarcity is such a serious global issue.

questions.question: Why are rivers and lakes a more readily-usable fresh-water source than ice caps?
options: They are liquid and accessible, while ice caps are frozen and remote
Ice caps are easy to pump to cities
questions.expected: They are liquid and accessible, while ice caps are frozen and remote
questions.memo: Although ice caps hold most fresh water, it is frozen and far from people. Rivers, lakes and shallow groundwater are the practical everyday sources.

questions.question: Water is called a 'shared' resource partly because rivers often _______.
questions.memo: Many rivers flow through several countries, so managing water fairly requires cooperation — a source of both partnership and conflict.

questions.question: Cutting down forests in a catchment can reduce infiltration and increase surface runoff. A likely result is _______.
options: more flooding and less groundwater recharge
no change to the water cycle
questions.expected: more flooding and less groundwater recharge
questions.memo: Without vegetation, rain runs off quickly instead of soaking in — raising flood peaks and lowering the recharge of groundwater. Human actions alter the water cycle.

questions.question: Which process returns water from the LAND and plants back to the atmosphere?
questions.memo: Evaporation (from soil and water bodies) and transpiration (from plants) move water from the land surface back into the air.

questions.question: True or false: as the world's population and economy grow, demand for fresh water is rising while the usable supply stays roughly fixed.
questions.memo: More people, farming and industry mean rising demand, but the usable fresh-water supply is limited — increasing water stress in many regions.

questions.question: Why is it accurate to say 'the water you drink today may have fallen as rain on dinosaurs'?
options: Earth's water is finite and endlessly recycled through the water cycle
Water is freshly made each year
questions.expected: Earth's water is finite and endlessly recycled through the water cycle
questions.memo: No new water is made; the same finite supply has cycled for billions of years — a vivid way to grasp why we must protect it.

GEO.G10.T4.WAT.A2.title: The world's oceans
GEO.G10.T4.WAT.A2.description: Oceans in the global system, warm and cold ocean currents and their effect on coastal climates, the Benguela and Agulhas currents, and the importance of oceans.
GEO.G10.T4.WAT.A2.recovery_strategy: Around SA: the BENGUELA (west coast) is COLD → dry, arid west coast. The AGULHAS (east coast) is WARM → moist, wetter east coast. Warm currents warm and wet a coast; cold currents cool and dry it.

questions.question: Large streams of moving water in the oceans are called ocean _______.
questions.memo: Ocean currents are continuous flows of water, driven by wind, temperature and salinity differences, that move heat around the planet.

questions.question: A WARM ocean current flowing past a coast tends to make that coast's climate _______.
questions.memo: Warm currents warm the air above them and add moisture, giving warmer, wetter coasts. Cold currents do the opposite.

questions.question: The cold ocean current along South Africa's WEST coast is the _______ current.
questions.memo: The cold Benguela current flows up the west coast, cooling and drying it — one reason the west coast is arid.

questions.question: The warm ocean current along South Africa's EAST coast is the _______ current.
questions.memo: The warm Agulhas current flows down the east coast, warming and moistening it — one reason the east coast is wetter and more lush.

questions.question: Why is South Africa's west coast much drier than its east coast?
options: The cold Benguela current dries the west, while the warm Agulhas moistens the east
The west coast has no ocean
The east coast is a desert
Both coasts have the same current
questions.expected: The cold Benguela current dries the west, while the warm Agulhas moistens the east
questions.memo: Cold currents reduce evaporation and rainfall (dry, arid west); warm currents boost moisture and rainfall (wet, green east).

questions.question: A learner says the Benguela current on the west coast is warm. What is the correction?
options: The Benguela is COLD; the warm current is the Agulhas on the east coast
There are no currents near SA
questions.expected: The Benguela is COLD; the warm current is the Agulhas on the east coast
questions.memo: West = cold Benguela (dry); East = warm Agulhas (wet). The learner swapped them.

questions.question: True or false: cold ocean currents can help create deserts along nearby coasts.
questions.memo: Cold currents cool the air, reducing evaporation and rainfall — contributing to coastal deserts like the Namib (Benguela) and Atacama (Humboldt).

questions.question: Match each current to its description.
questions.memo: 1 Benguela → B cold, west coast, dry. 2 Agulhas → A warm, east coast, wet. (Prompt: 1=Benguela, 2=Agulhas; A=warm east-coast current, B=cold west-coast current.)

questions.question: Cold ocean currents are often rich in nutrients, which supports _______.
questions.memo: Cold, nutrient-rich upwelling (like the Benguela) feeds plankton and fish, supporting important fishing industries on the west coast.

questions.question: Why are oceans important in the global climate system?
options: They store and move huge amounts of heat around the planet
They have no effect on climate
questions.expected: They store and move huge amounts of heat around the planet
questions.memo: Oceans absorb, store and redistribute solar heat via currents, moderating temperatures and shaping weather and climate worldwide.

questions.question:
The table shows two SA coastal towns at similar latitude. What does it suggest about the currents?

| Town | Coast | Avg rainfall (mm) |
|------|------|------|
| Port Nolloth | West | 60 |
| Durban | East | 1 000 |
options: The cold west-coast current gives low rainfall; the warm east-coast current gives high rainfall
Both coasts get the same rain
Currents have no effect on rainfall
questions.expected: The cold west-coast current gives low rainfall; the warm east-coast current gives high rainfall
questions.memo: The huge rainfall gap reflects the cold Benguela (dry west) versus the warm Agulhas (wet east).

questions.question: Oceans provide food, jobs and trade routes. This shows their _______ importance.
questions.memo: Fishing, shipping, tourism and offshore resources make oceans hugely important economically, as well as ecologically and climatically.

questions.question: What mainly drives surface ocean currents?
options: Prevailing winds, plus temperature and salinity differences
questions.expected: Prevailing winds, plus temperature and salinity differences
questions.memo: Steady winds push surface water; differences in temperature and salt content drive deeper circulation — together moving water around the globe.

questions.question: True or false: a warm current can make a coast warm enough to support lush vegetation even at a fairly high latitude.
questions.memo: Warm currents (like the Gulf Stream warming north-west Europe, or the Agulhas warming SA's east coast) raise coastal temperatures and rainfall.

questions.question: Why might fog often form along South Africa's cold west coast?
options: Warm air over the cold Benguela current cools to its dew point, forming fog
The west coast is very hot and dry with no moisture
There is never fog on the west coast
questions.expected: Warm air over the cold Benguela current cools to its dew point, forming fog
questions.memo: When moist air passes over the cold current it is chilled to its dew point, condensing into the coastal fog typical of the west coast and Namib.

questions.question: Overfishing and pollution threaten the oceans. This is a reason to _______.
options: manage and protect ocean resources sustainably
catch as many fish as possible now
questions.expected: manage and protect ocean resources sustainably
questions.memo: Oceans are a vital but vulnerable resource; sustainable management (quotas, marine protected areas, pollution control) keeps them productive for the future.

questions.question: How do ocean currents act like a 'global conveyor belt'?
options: They carry warm and cold water (and heat) between the tropics and the poles
They move only in tiny circles near beaches
They transport only fish, not heat
questions.expected: They carry warm and cold water (and heat) between the tropics and the poles
questions.memo: A worldwide system of surface and deep currents moves heat from the equator towards the poles and back, regulating global climate.

questions.question: South Africa's important west-coast fishing industry depends largely on the _______ current.
questions.memo: The cold Benguela's nutrient-rich upwelling supports plankton and fish, underpinning the west-coast fishing economy.

questions.question: True or false: warm currents generally bring fewer nutrients to the surface than cold upwelling currents.
questions.memo: Cold upwelling currents bring nutrients up from the deep, feeding rich fisheries; warm currents are usually nutrient-poor by comparison.

questions.question: Using the currents, explain why a traveller would expect green sugar-cane fields near Durban but arid scrub near the Namibian border.
options: Warm Agulhas brings rain to the east (sugar cane); cold Benguela keeps the west dry (scrub)
The east is a desert and the west is tropical
questions.expected: Warm Agulhas brings rain to the east (sugar cane); cold Benguela keeps the west dry (scrub)
questions.memo: The contrasting currents create contrasting climates and therefore contrasting vegetation along SA's two coasts.

GEO.G10.T4.WAT.A3.title: Water management in South Africa
GEO.G10.T4.WAT.A3.description: South Africa as a water-scarce country, our water sources, causes of shortages, and strategies to manage and conserve water.
GEO.G10.T4.WAT.A3.recovery_strategy: South Africa is WATER-SCARCE: rainfall is low (~half the world average) and uneven. We rely on dams, rivers, groundwater and inter-basin transfers. Manage demand by saving water, fixing leaks, drip irrigation, recycling and protecting catchments.

questions.question: South Africa is best described as a _______ country in terms of water.
questions.memo: South Africa is a water-scarce country: average rainfall (~450 mm) is about half the world average, and it is unevenly spread.

questions.question: Compared with the world average, South Africa's average rainfall is _______.
questions.memo: SA averages about 450 mm a year versus a world average near 860 mm — and much of the country is semi-arid.

questions.question: Large structures built across rivers to store water are called _______.
questions.memo: Dams store river water in reservoirs for use in dry periods — a key part of SA's water supply, along with rivers and groundwater.

questions.question: Moving water from a wetter river basin to a drier one through pipes/tunnels is called an _______ transfer.
questions.memo: Inter-basin transfer schemes (e.g. the Lesotho Highlands Water Project supplying Gauteng) move water from water-rich to water-poor regions.

questions.question: Which is a major CAUSE of water shortages in South Africa?
options: Low, uneven rainfall combined with rising demand and pollution
questions.expected: Low, uneven rainfall combined with rising demand and pollution
questions.memo: Shortages come from naturally low/uneven rainfall plus growing population and economy, pollution, leaks and droughts.

questions.question: Sort each action as one that SAVES water or one that WASTES water.

items.text: Hosing down the driveway with drinking water
Letting the tap run while brushing teeth
Planting thirsty lawns in a dry area

questions.memo: Saving: fix leaks, drip irrigation, rainwater harvesting, recycling. Wasting: hosing paving, running taps, water-hungry lawns in dry areas.

questions.question: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project is an example of _______.
options: an inter-basin transfer supplying water to Gauteng
questions.expected: an inter-basin transfer supplying water to Gauteng
questions.memo: It transfers water from the well-watered Lesotho highlands to the economic heartland of Gauteng — a major inter-basin transfer.

questions.question: Removing salt from seawater to make it drinkable is called _______.
questions.memo: Desalination turns seawater into fresh water. It helps coastal cities but is energy-intensive and expensive.

questions.question: Which is the BIGGEST user of water in South Africa?
questions.memo: Agriculture (mainly irrigation) uses roughly 60% of SA's water, followed by municipal/domestic and industrial/mining use.

questions.question: During a severe drought, a city brings in water restrictions. Why is this a sensible management step?
options: It lowers demand to match the reduced supply and protect remaining storage
It makes the dams fill faster
It has no effect on supply
questions.expected: It lowers demand to match the reduced supply and protect remaining storage
questions.memo: When supply drops, cutting demand (restrictions, tariffs, awareness) stretches the remaining water and avoids running dams dry — as in Cape Town's 'Day Zero' crisis.

questions.question: Recycling treated wastewater for irrigation or industry helps by _______.
options: reducing demand on fresh drinking-water sources
questions.expected: reducing demand on fresh drinking-water sources
questions.memo: Reusing treated water for non-drinking purposes frees up scarce fresh water and reduces pressure on dams and rivers.

questions.question: True or false: leaking municipal pipes can waste a large share of treated water before it reaches homes.
questions.memo: Aging, leaking infrastructure loses large volumes of treated water ('non-revenue water'); fixing leaks is one of the cheapest ways to save water.

questions.question: Why is protecting river catchments and wetlands important for water supply?
options: Healthy catchments and wetlands store and clean water, improving supply quality and reliability
Catchments have no link to rivers
questions.expected: Healthy catchments and wetlands store and clean water, improving supply quality and reliability
questions.memo: Catchments collect rainfall and wetlands act as natural sponges and filters — protecting them safeguards the quantity and quality of water downstream.

questions.question: Drip irrigation saves water mainly because it _______.
options: delivers water slowly straight to plant roots with little evaporation
sprays water high into the air
questions.expected: delivers water slowly straight to plant roots with little evaporation
questions.memo: Drip irrigation targets the roots and cuts evaporation and runoff, using far less water than flood or overhead spray methods.

questions.question:
The graph data show a dam over a drought. What management action does the trend call for?

| Month | Dam level (%) |
|------|------|
| Jan | 75 |
| Apr | 55 |
| Jul | 40 |
| Oct | 28 |
options: Introduce water restrictions as levels keep falling
Do nothing — the dam is fine
Open the dam to drain it faster
questions.expected: Introduce water restrictions as levels keep falling
questions.memo: Levels fall from 75% to 28% across the year — a clear downward trend that calls for restrictions and demand management before the dam runs critically low.

questions.question: Which combination of sources supplies most of South Africa's water?
options: Rivers and dams (surface water), plus some groundwater and transfers
questions.expected: Rivers and dams (surface water), plus some groundwater and transfers
questions.memo: SA depends mainly on surface water in rivers and dams, supplemented by groundwater, inter-basin transfers and a little desalination/reuse.

questions.question: Why does South Africa need to manage water at NATIONAL level, not just town by town?
options: Rivers and transfers link regions, so water must be shared and planned across the country
Each town's water is totally separate
Water cannot be moved between areas
questions.expected: Rivers and transfers link regions, so water must be shared and planned across the country
questions.memo: Because catchments and transfer schemes cross municipal and provincial lines, fair, reliable supply needs coordinated national planning.

questions.question: True or false: educating the public to use water wisely is part of water management, not separate from it.
questions.memo: Demand management — public awareness, tariffs and behaviour change — is a core, low-cost part of managing a scarce resource.

questions.question: Polluting a river upstream affects users downstream. This shows that water management must consider _______.
options: the whole catchment, because everyone shares the same water
questions.expected: the whole catchment, because everyone shares the same water
questions.memo: Water connects all users in a catchment, so pollution or overuse upstream harms those downstream — management must be catchment-wide.

questions.question: Cape Town's 'Day Zero' drought (2017–2018) is best used as an example of _______.
options: how demand management and conservation can avert a water crisis
an area with too much rainfall
questions.expected: how demand management and conservation can avert a water crisis
questions.memo: Sharp restrictions, awareness and new sources helped Cape Town avoid taps running dry — a real case study in managing scarcity.

GEO.G10.T4.WAT.A4.title: Floods
GEO.G10.T4.WAT.A4.description: Causes of floods, natural vs human contributing factors, effects on people and the environment, and ways to reduce risk and respond.
GEO.G10.T4.WAT.A4.recovery_strategy: CAUSES of floods: heavy/long rain, snowmelt, dam failure — worsened by HUMAN actions (clearing vegetation, paving, building on floodplains, blocked drains). EFFECTS: lost lives, damaged homes/crops, disease, erosion. Reduce risk with drainage, wetlands, barriers, warnings and zoning.

questions.question: A flood happens when _______.
options: water covers land that is normally dry
questions.expected: water covers land that is normally dry
questions.memo: A flood is an overflow of water onto land that is usually dry, often when a river exceeds its banks.

questions.question: Which is a NATURAL cause of flooding?
questions.memo: Natural causes: heavy/long rain, rapid snowmelt, storm surges, dam-wall failure. Human actions can make these worse but are not the natural trigger.

questions.question: Sort each as a NATURAL cause or a HUMAN factor that worsens flooding.
questions.memo: Natural triggers (rain, snowmelt, surge) can be made far worse by human actions (deforestation, paving, building on floodplains, blocked drains).

questions.question: Why does paving over soil with concrete increase flood risk?
options: Water cannot soak in, so more runs off quickly into rivers
It has no effect on flooding
questions.expected: Water cannot soak in, so more runs off quickly into rivers
questions.memo: Hard surfaces stop infiltration, so rain rushes off into drains and rivers all at once, raising flood peaks — a key reason cities flood.

questions.question: Low, flat land beside a river that naturally floods is called a _______.
questions.memo: A floodplain is the flat land bordering a river that floods when the river overflows. Building there puts people directly in harm's way.

questions.question: Which is an EFFECT (not a cause) of a flood?
questions.memo: Effects are the consequences: damaged homes and crops, lost lives, displaced people, disease, eroded soil. The others are causes.

questions.question: A learner lists 'heavy rain' as an EFFECT of a flood. What is the correction?
options: Heavy rain is a CAUSE of flooding, not an effect
Heavy rain is correctly an effect
Heavy rain has nothing to do with floods
questions.expected: Heavy rain is a CAUSE of flooding, not an effect
questions.memo: Causes come first (heavy rain → river overflows); effects follow (damage, disease). The learner mixed cause and effect.

questions.question: Which is a serious HEALTH effect often following floods?
options: Spread of water-borne diseases from contaminated water
questions.expected: Spread of water-borne diseases from contaminated water
questions.memo: Floodwater mixes with sewage and waste, contaminating supplies and spreading diseases like cholera and diarrhoea — a major after-effect.

questions.question: Which measure helps REDUCE flood risk?
options: Building good drainage and protecting wetlands
questions.expected: Building good drainage and protecting wetlands
questions.memo: Drainage, wetlands (natural sponges), flood barriers, reforestation, dams and zoning all reduce flood risk; removing natural buffers increases it.

questions.question: Wetlands help reduce flooding because they _______.
options: soak up and slowly release floodwater
questions.expected: soak up and slowly release floodwater
questions.memo: Wetlands act like sponges, storing floodwater and releasing it slowly — which is why protecting them is a natural flood defence.

questions.question: A flood early-warning system mainly helps by _______.
options: giving people time to evacuate and protect property
questions.expected: giving people time to evacuate and protect property
questions.memo: Warnings based on rainfall and river monitoring give crucial time to move people and belongings to safety, cutting deaths and losses.

questions.question: True or false: building on a floodplain can increase BOTH the flood risk and the damage when a flood happens.
questions.memo: It puts people and property directly in the flood's path and replaces absorbent ground with hard surfaces — raising both risk and damage.

questions.question: Why do informal settlements often suffer badly in floods?
options: They are often on vulnerable land like floodplains with poor drainage and weak housing
They are always on high, safe ground
They have the strongest flood defences
questions.expected: They are often on vulnerable land like floodplains with poor drainage and weak housing
questions.memo: Limited land choices push some settlements onto risky floodplains or steep slopes with poor drainage and fragile homes, increasing their vulnerability.

questions.question: Order the sensible steps in responding to an approaching flood.

items.text: An early warning is issued to communities
Rescue and clean-up begin after the water recedes

questions.memo: Monitor → warn → evacuate → respond and recover. Acting early in this chain saves the most lives.

questions.question: Planting trees and keeping vegetation in a catchment reduces flooding because plants _______.
options: help rain soak in and slow runoff
questions.expected: help rain soak in and slow runoff
questions.memo: Vegetation intercepts rain and helps it infiltrate, slowing and reducing runoff into rivers — the opposite of deforestation, which worsens floods.

questions.question: True or false: a flash flood is dangerous mainly because it rises very quickly with little warning.
questions.memo: Flash floods surge within minutes to hours after intense rain, often catching people unprepared — which makes them especially deadly.

questions.question: Which is an ENVIRONMENTAL effect of severe flooding?
options: Soil erosion and damage to habitats
questions.expected: Soil erosion and damage to habitats
questions.memo: Fast floodwater strips topsoil, destroys habitats and washes pollution into rivers — though gentle floods can also deposit fertile silt.

questions.question: Why is zoning land (not allowing housing on floodplains) an effective long-term flood strategy?
options: It keeps people and property out of the highest-risk areas
It increases building in danger zones
questions.expected: It keeps people and property out of the highest-risk areas
questions.memo: Land-use zoning prevents new development in flood-prone areas, reducing future risk and damage — a cheaper, lasting solution than repeated rescue.

questions.question: Two towns get the same heavy rain, but one floods far worse. Which difference best explains this?
options: The worse-hit town has more paving, cleared land and building on the floodplain
The worse-hit town has more wetlands and trees
Rainfall is the only factor that ever matters
The towns are identical in every way
questions.expected: The worse-hit town has more paving, cleared land and building on the floodplain
questions.memo: Human land-use choices change flood outcomes: more hard surfaces and floodplain building, fewer natural sponges, mean a worse flood from the same rain.

questions.question: Why are floods considered both a natural hazard AND partly a human-made problem?
options: Natural events trigger them, but human land use often increases their frequency and damage
They are entirely natural with no human role
They are entirely caused by humans with no natural trigger
They are neither natural nor human
questions.expected: Natural events trigger them, but human land use often increases their frequency and damage
questions.memo: Heavy rain is natural, but deforestation, paving and floodplain settlement turn manageable events into disasters — so prevention is partly in human hands.

GEO.G11.MAP.A1.title: Topographic map techniques (cross-sections, gradient, intervisibility)
GEO.G11.MAP.A1.description: Given-number 1:50 000 map skills: contours to landforms, cross-sections, vertical exaggeration, gradient, intervisibility and area.
GEO.G11.MAP.A1.recovery_strategy: Vertical exaggeration = vertical scale ÷ horizontal scale. Gradient = VI ÷ HD (both metres) as 1:n. Intervisibility: draw the cross-section — if land rises into the line of sight, the points cannot see each other.

questions.question: A cross-section (profile) drawn from a topographic map shows _______.
options: the shape of the land surface along a chosen line
questions.expected: the shape of the land surface along a chosen line
questions.memo: A cross-section is a side view of the land's ups and downs along a line between two points, built from the contour heights it crosses.

questions.question: Vertical exaggeration is calculated as _______.
questions.memo: VE = vertical scale ÷ horizontal scale. It tells you how many times the heights have been stretched to make the profile readable.

questions.question: Why is vertical exaggeration used when drawing a cross-section?
options: To make small height differences visible on the profile
questions.expected: To make small height differences visible on the profile
questions.memo: Heights are tiny compared with horizontal distances, so the vertical scale is stretched to show relief clearly. It does NOT change the real landscape.

questions.question: Closely-spaced contours on the profile line mean the cross-section will show _______.
questions.memo: Closely-spaced contours = rapid height change = steep slope. Widely-spaced contours = gentle slope.

questions.question: Intervisibility means working out whether _______.
options: two points can see each other across the land
two towns are the same size
questions.expected: two points can see each other across the land
questions.memo: Intervisibility asks: is the line of sight between two points blocked by higher ground in between? A cross-section answers it.

questions.question: Point A (200 m) and point B (200 m) are separated by a hill rising to 350 m. Are A and B intervisible?
options: No — the 350 m hill blocks the line of sight
Yes — they are the same height
questions.expected: No — the 350 m hill blocks the line of sight
questions.memo: Although A and B are equal in height, the higher hill (350 m) between them rises into the line of sight, so they cannot see each other.

questions.question: The vertical interval between two points is 100 m and the horizontal distance is 2 000 m. The average gradient is _______.
A cross-section uses a vertical scale of 1 cm = 20 m and a horizontal scale of 1:50 000 (1 cm = 500 m). What is the vertical exaggeration?
questions.memo: Vertical scale 1 cm = 20 m → 1:2 000. VE = horizontal scale ÷ vertical = 50 000 ÷ 2 000 = 25 times. (Equivalently 500 m ÷ 20 m = 25.)

questions.question: On a 1:50 000 map, contour lines are usually drawn at a vertical interval of _______.
questions.memo: South African 1:50 000 maps use a 20 m contour interval — each line up is 20 m higher.

questions.question: Contours that form a V pointing UPSTREAM (towards higher ground) usually indicate a _______.
questions.memo: Where a contour crosses a valley it bends into a V pointing upstream (uphill). This is the classic sign of a river valley on a contour map.

questions.question: Order the steps to draw a cross-section between two points.

items.text: Draw the section line and mark each contour it crosses
Note the height where each contour meets the line
Plot those heights on a graph with a vertical scale
Join the plotted points to show the land's shape

questions.memo: Mark the contours along the line, read their heights, plot them against a vertical scale, then join the points to reveal the profile.

questions.question: Two points are 6 cm apart on a 1:50 000 map. The real distance is _______.
questions.memo: 6 cm × 0,5 km = 3 km on a 1:50 000 map.

questions.question: A higher vertical exaggeration makes a cross-section's slopes appear _______ than they really are.
questions.memo: Stretching the vertical scale makes hills look steeper and more dramatic than the true, gentler reality — useful for showing relief but not the real angle.

questions.question: A rectangular farm is 5 cm by 4 cm on a 1:50 000 map. Its real area is _______.
questions.memo: Convert first: 5 cm = 2,5 km, 4 cm = 2 km. Area = 2,5 × 2 = 5 km².

questions.question: On a contour map, concentric closed contours with the highest value in the centre show a _______.
questions.memo: Closed loops increasing inward = a hill. If the values DEcrease inward (often with hachure ticks), it is a depression.

questions.question: A learner calculates VE as horizontal scale ÷ vertical scale and gets 0,04. What did they do wrong?
options: They inverted the formula; VE = vertical ÷ horizontal scale
questions.expected: They inverted the formula; VE = vertical ÷ horizontal scale
questions.memo: VE = vertical scale ÷ horizontal scale. Inverting it gives a tiny fraction; the real VE should be a number greater than 1 (e.g. 25).

questions.question: Why does a road that climbs gently up a hillside cross many contour lines at a shallow angle rather than going straight up?
options: A gentle gradient is achieved by traversing the slope, crossing contours gradually
Roads must always cross contours at right angles
It makes the road longer for no reason
Contours force roads to be straight
questions.expected: A gentle gradient is achieved by traversing the slope, crossing contours gradually
questions.memo: Going straight up crosses contours quickly = steep. Zig-zagging across the slope spreads the climb over a longer distance = gentler, safer gradient.

questions.question: True or false: vertical exaggeration changes the appearance of a cross-section but not the real height of the land.
questions.memo: VE is only a drawing tool to make relief visible; the actual heights and the real gradient of the land are unchanged.

questions.question: Point A is at 480 m and point B is at 120 m, 4 500 m apart. The average gradient is _______.
An observer on a 600 m hilltop looks towards a town at 250 m. A ridge at 500 m stands halfway between. Is the town visible?
options: No — the line of sight from 600 m down to 250 m dips below the 500 m ridge
Yes — the observer is higher than the ridge
questions.expected: No — the line of sight from 600 m down to 250 m dips below the 500 m ridge
questions.memo: The sight line drops steadily from 600 m to 250 m; at the halfway ridge it is around 425 m, BELOW the 500 m ridge — so the ridge blocks the view. Draw the section to check.

GEO.G11.MAP.A2.title: Aerial photos, orthophotos & GIS data
GEO.G11.MAP.A2.description: Oblique vs vertical photos, tone/texture/shadow interpretation, orthophoto features, and GIS data ideas (resolution, data types, raster vs vector).
GEO.G11.MAP.A2.recovery_strategy: Vertical photo = straight down (map-like, tops only); oblique = angled (sides visible, 3-D feel). Use TONE, TEXTURE and SHADOW to identify features. Spatial resolution = pixel ground size; spectral resolution = number of wavelength bands.

questions.question: A vertical aerial photograph is taken _______.
options: at an angle from the side
questions.memo: A vertical photo looks straight down (like a map view — you see the tops of features). An oblique photo is taken at an angle.

questions.question: An oblique aerial photograph is useful because it _______.
options: shows the sides of features and gives a 3-D impression
shows only the ground directly below
questions.expected: shows the sides of features and gives a 3-D impression
questions.memo: An oblique (angled) photo reveals the sides and heights of buildings and landforms, giving a more lifelike 3-D view — but with uneven scale.

questions.question: On an aerial photo, which three clues help identify features?
questions.memo: TONE (light/dark), TEXTURE (smooth/rough) and SHADOW (shape and height) are the key clues for interpreting features on a photo.

questions.question: A smooth, dark area with a regular edge on a photo is most likely _______.
options: a water body such as a dam
questions.expected: a water body such as a dam
questions.memo: Water usually appears dark and smooth (low texture) with a clear edge. Forests look dark but rough; built-up areas look light with a blocky texture.

questions.question: Shadows on an aerial photo are useful because they help show a feature's _______.
questions.memo: The length and shape of a shadow reveal how tall and what shape a feature is — helping tell a tall building from a low one.

questions.question: Why can you measure true distances on an orthophoto map but not on a raw aerial photo?
options: The orthophoto has been corrected to a uniform, true scale
questions.expected: The orthophoto has been corrected to a uniform, true scale
questions.memo: Orthophotos are geometrically corrected so scale is constant everywhere; raw photos have tilt and relief distortion, so measurements would be inaccurate.

questions.question: Spatial resolution of a satellite image refers to _______.
options: the ground area covered by one pixel
the time the image was taken
questions.expected: the ground area covered by one pixel
questions.memo: Spatial resolution = the size on the ground of one pixel. Smaller pixels (e.g. 1 m) = higher spatial resolution = finer detail.

questions.question: Spectral resolution refers to _______.
options: the number and width of wavelength bands a sensor records
questions.expected: the number and width of wavelength bands a sensor records
questions.memo: Spectral resolution is about WAVELENGTHS — how many bands (e.g. visible, infrared) the sensor captures. It is different from spatial (pixel-size) resolution.

questions.question: Match each GIS data type to an example.
questions.memo: 1 Point → C a single trig beacon. 2 Line → A a road or river. 3 Area (polygon) → D a farm boundary. 4 Attribute → B a table of facts about each feature. (Prompt: 1=Point, 2=Line, 3=Area, 4=Attribute; A=a road, B=a facts table, C=a trig beacon, D=a farm boundary.)

questions.question: Sort each as VECTOR or RASTER data.

items.text: A river drawn as a line

questions.memo: Vector = points, lines, polygons. Raster = grids of cells/pixels (images, scans, elevation grids).

questions.question: To orient an aerial photo with a topographic map, you line up _______.
options: common features such as roads, rivers and railway lines on both
questions.expected: common features such as roads, rivers and railway lines on both
questions.memo: Matching obvious shared features (roads, rivers, dams) on the photo and the map lets you align them so you can compare and locate features.

questions.question: A rough, patterned area with regular straight lines on a photo most likely shows _______.
questions.memo: Ploughed/planted fields show a regular, geometric texture (straight rows and field boundaries) that natural features rarely have.

questions.question: True or false: a vertical aerial photo shows the tops of features, while an oblique photo also shows their sides.
questions.memo: Looking straight down (vertical) you see only tops; looking at an angle (oblique) you also see the sides and get a sense of height.

questions.question: Capturing data from a paper map onto layers of tracing paper is a simple way to build a _______.
questions.memo: A 'paper GIS' uses separate tracing-paper layers (roads, rivers, land use) that can be overlaid — showing the layering idea behind a digital GIS.

questions.question: Which image would have the HIGHEST spatial resolution (finest detail)?
options: One where each pixel covers 0,5 m on the ground
One where each pixel covers 30 m
One where each pixel covers 250 m
One where each pixel covers 1 km
questions.expected: One where each pixel covers 0,5 m on the ground
questions.memo: Smaller ground area per pixel = higher spatial resolution. A 0,5 m pixel shows far more detail than a 1 km pixel.

questions.question: True or false: tone, texture and shadow can be used together to tell a tall building from a low one on a photograph.
questions.memo: A tall building casts a longer shadow and may show its lit and shaded sides; combining the clues distinguishes it from a low structure.

questions.question: Why might a planner prefer vector data for road networks and raster data for satellite imagery?
options: Roads are best as precise lines (vector); imagery is naturally a grid of pixels (raster)
There is no reason to choose
questions.expected: Roads are best as precise lines (vector); imagery is naturally a grid of pixels (raster)
questions.memo: Vector suits sharp features with clear shapes (roads, boundaries); raster suits continuous imagery and surfaces (photos, elevation). Each fits its data type.

questions.question: Light-toned, blocky areas crossed by a grid of straight lines on a photo usually indicate _______.
questions.memo: Towns show light tones (roofs, roads) in a blocky, grid-like texture from streets and buildings — distinct from smooth water or rough forest.

questions.question: A learner says spatial and spectral resolution are the same thing. Correct them.
options: Spatial = pixel ground size; spectral = number of wavelength bands — different things
questions.expected: Spatial = pixel ground size; spectral = number of wavelength bands — different things
questions.memo: Spatial resolution is about DETAIL (pixel size); spectral resolution is about COLOUR/WAVELENGTH bands. A sensor can be high in one and low in the other.

questions.question: Why is comparing an orthophoto map with a topographic map of the same area useful?
options: The photo shows real detail while the map adds names, heights and symbols — together they give a fuller picture
The two always show different places
The orthophoto replaces the need for any map
Maps and photos cannot be compared
questions.expected: The photo shows real detail while the map adds names, heights and symbols — together they give a fuller picture
questions.memo: An orthophoto gives true-scale visual detail; the topographic map adds contours, names and symbols. Used side by side, each fills the other's gaps.

GEO.G11.T1.ATM.A1.title: The Earth's energy balance
