GEO.G11.T1.ATM.A1.description: Unequal heating by latitude and season, the role of axial tilt and revolution, and the transfer of energy by winds and ocean currents.
GEO.G11.T1.ATM.A1.recovery_strategy: Equator = concentrated sunlight (energy SURPLUS); poles = slanted, spread-out sunlight (DEFICIT). Winds and currents move heat from surplus to deficit. Seasons come from the 23,5° AXIAL TILT, not distance to the Sun.

questions.question: Why does the equator receive more solar energy per square metre than the poles?
options: The Sun's rays strike the equator more directly (concentrated), but hit the poles at a low angle (spread out)
The equator is much closer to the Sun
The poles are in permanent darkness
The Sun only shines on the equator
questions.expected: The Sun's rays strike the equator more directly (concentrated), but hit the poles at a low angle (spread out)
questions.memo: Near-vertical rays at the equator concentrate energy on a small area; slanted rays at the poles spread the same energy over a larger area, so it is cooler.

questions.question: Areas that receive more incoming energy than they lose have an energy _______.
questions.memo: The tropics have an energy SURPLUS (gain more than they lose); the poles have a DEFICIT. The atmosphere and oceans move heat between them.

questions.question: What causes the seasons?
options: The tilt of the Earth's axis as it revolves around the Sun
The Earth moving closer to and further from the Sun
questions.expected: The tilt of the Earth's axis as it revolves around the Sun
questions.memo: Earth's 23,5° axial tilt means each hemisphere leans towards the Sun (summer) or away (winter) at different times of the year — that is the seasons.

questions.question: The Earth's axis is tilted at about _______ from the vertical.
questions.memo: The 23,5° tilt is what gives us seasons, varying day length and the tropics/polar circles.

questions.question: How is surplus heat moved from the tropics towards the poles?
options: By winds (air circulation) and ocean currents
By the rotation of the Moon
It is not moved at all
questions.expected: By winds (air circulation) and ocean currents
questions.memo: Global winds and ocean currents transfer heat polewards, balancing the surplus at the equator and the deficit at the poles.

questions.question: True or false: the southern hemisphere has summer when it is tilted TOWARDS the Sun (around December).
questions.memo: When the southern hemisphere leans towards the Sun (around December) it gets more direct energy and longer days — southern summer.

questions.question: A learner says 'it's summer because Earth is closest to the Sun'. Why is this wrong?
options: Seasons come from axial TILT, not distance; when one hemisphere has summer the other has winter
Earth never moves closer to the Sun
The Sun gets hotter in summer
Distance and tilt are the same thing
questions.expected: Seasons come from axial TILT, not distance; when one hemisphere has summer the other has winter
questions.memo: If distance caused seasons, the whole Earth would have summer together. Instead, opposite hemispheres have opposite seasons — proof it is tilt, not distance.

questions.question: Look at the diagram of insolation hitting a curved Earth. Which label shows where rays are most spread out (lowest concentration)?
options: D — in the upper atmosphere only
questions.memo: At the poles (C) the curved surface tilts the rays to a low angle, spreading energy over a large area — the least concentrated insolation.

questions.question: Days and nights are roughly equal everywhere on Earth at the _______.
questions.memo: At the two equinoxes (around 21 March and 23 September) the Sun is overhead at the equator and day and night are about equal worldwide.

questions.question: Without the transfer of heat by winds and currents, the tropics and poles would become _______.
options: ever hotter and ever colder respectively
questions.expected: ever hotter and ever colder respectively
questions.memo: Heat transfer prevents runaway extremes: it cools the surplus tropics and warms the deficit poles, keeping the planet's climate balanced.

questions.question: The Sun is directly overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn around _______ (southern summer).
questions.memo: At the December solstice the overhead Sun reaches the Tropic of Capricorn (23,5°S), giving the southern hemisphere its longest day.

questions.question: Why are polar regions colder even when they have 24 hours of daylight in summer?
options: The Sun stays low, so its energy is spread thinly and much is reflected by ice
The Sun is switched off there
questions.expected: The Sun stays low, so its energy is spread thinly and much is reflected by ice
questions.memo: Even all-day sun is weak at a low angle, and bright ice reflects much of it (high albedo) — so the poles stay cold despite long daylight.

questions.question: The total incoming solar energy roughly equals the total energy the Earth radiates back to space. This overall stability is called the _______.
questions.memo: Over the whole planet, energy in ≈ energy out — the energy balance that keeps global temperature roughly stable (until greenhouse gases tip it).

questions.question: True or false: ocean currents play a part in moving heat around the globe, not just winds.
questions.memo: Warm and cold ocean currents carry vast amounts of heat between latitudes, working alongside winds to balance the planet's energy.

questions.question:
The table shows midday Sun angle and temperature at three latitudes. What link does it show?

| Latitude | Midday Sun angle | Temp (°C) |
|------|------|------|
| 0° (equator) | 90° | 31 |
| 35° | 55° | 20 |
| 70° | 20° | 2 |
options: Lower Sun angle (higher latitude) means lower temperature
Sun angle has no link to temperature
questions.expected: Lower Sun angle (higher latitude) means lower temperature
questions.memo: As latitude rises the Sun angle falls and energy spreads out, so temperature drops — exactly the insolation-angle effect.

questions.question: Earth's movement once around the Sun each year is called its _______.
questions.memo: REVOLUTION = the yearly orbit around the Sun (gives seasons with the tilt). ROTATION = the daily spin on its axis (gives day and night).

questions.question: Why does the angle of the Sun change with the seasons at a place like Cape Town?
options: The tilted Earth leans the hemisphere towards or away from the Sun through the year
The Sun physically moves north and south
Cape Town moves up and down
questions.expected: The tilted Earth leans the hemisphere towards or away from the Sun through the year
questions.memo: As Earth revolves with its fixed tilt, a place leans towards the Sun (high summer Sun) then away (low winter Sun) — changing the midday Sun angle.

questions.question: Energy SURPLUS regions are found mainly _______.
questions.memo: The tropics gain more energy than they lose (surplus); high latitudes lose more than they gain (deficit). Transfer evens this out.

questions.question: True or false: the unequal heating of the Earth is the basic driver of global winds and ocean currents.
questions.memo: Differences in heating create pressure and temperature differences, which set air and water in motion — the engine behind global circulation.

questions.question: How does the energy balance connect to global air circulation (the next topic)?
options: Unequal heating creates pressure differences that drive the global wind cells
It has no connection to winds
questions.expected: Unequal heating creates pressure differences that drive the global wind cells
questions.memo: The surplus/deficit pattern creates low pressure where air is heated and high pressure where it cools — and that pressure difference drives the Hadley, Ferrel and polar cells.

GEO.G11.T1.ATM.A2.title: Global air circulation
GEO.G11.T1.ATM.A2.description: Pressure belts, the tri-cellular model (Hadley, Ferrel, polar), temperature–pressure–wind links, Coriolis force and geostrophic flow, global wind belts and regional/local winds.
GEO.G11.T1.ATM.A2.recovery_strategy: Hot air RISES → LOW pressure (equator); cool air SINKS → HIGH pressure (~30° and poles). Cells equator→pole: HADLEY → FERREL → POLAR. Coriolis bends winds (right in N, left in S), making the trade winds and westerlies.

questions.question: At the equator, intense heating makes air rise, creating a belt of _______.
questions.memo: Rising warm air leaves low pressure at the surface (the equatorial low). Sinking cool air creates high pressure.

questions.question: At about 30° north and south, sinking air creates belts of _______.
questions.memo: Air that rose at the equator sinks at ~30°, forming the subtropical high-pressure belts — home to the world's great deserts.

questions.question: The three circulation cells, from the equator to the pole, are the _______.
questions.memo: From equator to pole: HADLEY (0–30°), FERREL (30–60°), POLAR (60–90°). They make up the tri-cellular model of circulation.

questions.question: Look at the global circulation diagram. Which label shows the Hadley cell?
options: A — the cell between the equator and about 30°
C — the cell between 60° and the pole
questions.expected: A — the cell between the equator and about 30°
questions.memo: A Hadley (0–30°), B Ferrel (30–60°), C polar (60–90°). The Hadley cell carries equatorial rising air poleward, sinking at ~30°.

questions.question: Wind blows from _______ pressure to _______ pressure.
questions.memo: Air moves down the pressure gradient, from high to low pressure. The bigger the difference, the stronger the wind.

questions.question: The force that deflects moving air (right in the northern hemisphere, left in the southern) is the _______ force.
questions.memo: The Coriolis force, caused by Earth's rotation, bends winds and currents — right in the north, left in the south — shaping the global wind belts.

questions.question: The steady winds blowing from the subtropical highs towards the equator are the _______.
questions.memo: The trade winds (tropical easterlies) blow from ~30° towards the equatorial low. The westerlies blow from ~30° towards 60°.

questions.question: Why is the subtropical high-pressure belt (~30°) associated with deserts?
options: Sinking, drying air there suppresses cloud and rainfall
Rising air there causes constant rain
It is too cold for deserts
Deserts form only at the poles
questions.expected: Sinking, drying air there suppresses cloud and rainfall
questions.memo: Descending air in the subtropical highs warms and dries, preventing clouds — which is why the Sahara, Kalahari and Australian deserts lie near 30°.

questions.question: A geostrophic wind blows _______.
options: parallel to the isobars, where pressure-gradient and Coriolis forces balance
straight from high to low across the isobars
questions.expected: parallel to the isobars, where pressure-gradient and Coriolis forces balance
questions.memo: High up, away from friction, the pressure-gradient force and the Coriolis force balance, so the wind flows parallel to the isobars — a geostrophic wind.

questions.question: Order these from the equator towards the pole.
questions.memo: Pressure belts alternate low–high–low–high from equator to pole: equatorial low, subtropical high, subpolar low, polar high.

questions.question: The relationship between temperature and pressure is that warm air tends to create _______ pressure.
questions.memo: Warm air rises and expands, lowering surface pressure (low). Cold air sinks and is denser, raising pressure (high).

questions.question: A seasonal wind that reverses direction between summer and winter, bringing a wet and a dry season, is a _______.
questions.memo: Monsoons reverse with the seasons (e.g. South Asia): wet onshore winds in summer, dry offshore winds in winter — driven by land/sea heating differences.

questions.question: A warm, dry wind that descends the leeward side of a mountain range (called a berg wind in South Africa) is a _______ wind.
questions.memo: A Föhn (berg) wind warms and dries as it descends a mountain's lee side, often raising coastal temperatures sharply.

questions.question: True or false: in the southern hemisphere the Coriolis force deflects moving air to the LEFT.
questions.memo: Coriolis deflection is to the LEFT in the southern hemisphere and to the right in the northern hemisphere.

questions.question: The mid-latitude winds blowing from the subtropical highs towards 60° are the _______.
questions.memo: The westerlies blow from ~30° towards ~60° (from the west). They drive the mid-latitude cyclones that bring the Western Cape its winter rain.

questions.question: Match each global wind/belt to its location.
questions.memo: 1 Trade winds → B between ~30° and the equator. 2 Westerlies → C between ~30° and 60°. 3 Polar easterlies → A between 60° and the poles. (Prompt: 1=Trade winds, 2=Westerlies, 3=Polar easterlies; A=60°–poles, B=30°–equator, C=30°–60°.)

questions.question: Closely-spaced isobars indicate a steep pressure gradient, which produces _______ winds.
questions.memo: A steep pressure gradient (isobars close together) drives strong winds; a gentle gradient (isobars far apart) gives light winds.

questions.question: Why does global air circulation exist at all?
options: It redistributes heat from the over-heated equator to the cooler poles
It is caused by the Moon
questions.expected: It redistributes heat from the over-heated equator to the cooler poles
questions.memo: Circulation is the atmosphere's response to unequal heating: it moves surplus tropical heat polewards, balancing the planet's energy.

questions.question: The rising air of the equatorial low produces a climate that is generally _______.
questions.memo: Rising, cooling, moist air at the equator gives heavy convectional rain — the hot, wet climate of equatorial rainforests.

questions.question: A learner says 'rising warm air creates high pressure'. Correct them.
options: Rising warm air creates LOW pressure; sinking cool air creates high pressure
Rising air creates no pressure change
questions.expected: Rising warm air creates LOW pressure; sinking cool air creates high pressure
questions.memo: Warm air rises and removes weight from the surface = LOW pressure. Cool air sinks and presses down = HIGH pressure. The learner reversed it.

GEO.G11.T1.ATM.A3.title: Africa's weather and climate
GEO.G11.T1.ATM.A3.description: Africa's climate regions, subsidence and convergence, the oceans' role, El Niño/La Niña, and reading African synoptic maps.
GEO.G11.T1.ATM.A3.recovery_strategy: CONVERGENCE (air meeting and rising) → rain (equatorial belt). SUBSIDENCE (sinking air ~30°) → deserts (Sahara, Kalahari). El Niño often brings DRIER/drought to southern Africa; La Niña often brings WETTER conditions.

questions.question: Heavy rainfall in the equatorial belt of Africa is mainly due to air _______.
questions.memo: Where trade winds converge near the equator, air rises, cools and brings heavy convectional rain — the wet equatorial climate.

questions.question: The Sahara and Kalahari deserts lie near 30° where air is _______.
questions.memo: Sinking air in the subtropical highs warms and dries, suppressing rain — creating Africa's great deserts at ~30°N and 30°S.

questions.question: A learner says 'sinking air at 30° causes heavy rain'. Why is this wrong?
options: Sinking air warms and dries, suppressing rain — it causes deserts, not rain
Rain only falls from sinking air
questions.expected: Sinking air warms and dries, suppressing rain — it causes deserts, not rain
questions.memo: Rising air cools and rains; SINKING air warms and dries. The subtropical highs at 30° are dry desert belts.

questions.question: Africa's climate regions are arranged roughly _______ the equator.
options: symmetrically (in mirror-image belts) north and south of
questions.expected: symmetrically (in mirror-image belts) north and south of
questions.memo: Africa's climate belts (equatorial, savanna, desert, Mediterranean) repeat in near mirror image north and south of the equator, following the pressure belts.

questions.question: How do the oceans help control Africa's climate?
options: Warm and cold currents change coastal temperature and rainfall
Oceans have no effect on climate
questions.expected: Warm and cold currents change coastal temperature and rainfall
questions.memo: Warm currents (e.g. Agulhas) warm and moisten coasts; cold currents (e.g. Benguela) cool and dry them — shaping Africa's coastal climates.

questions.question: El Niño is associated with which effect on much of southern Africa?
options: Drier conditions and increased drought risk
questions.expected: Drier conditions and increased drought risk
questions.memo: During El Niño, changed Pacific ocean–atmosphere patterns often bring below-normal rainfall and drought to southern Africa.

questions.question: La Niña tends to bring southern Africa _______.
questions.memo: La Niña is broadly the opposite of El Niño: it often brings wetter, above-average rainfall (and flood risk) to southern Africa.

questions.question: A learner swaps the effects, saying 'El Niño brings floods and La Niña brings drought to southern Africa'. Correct it.
options: It is reversed: El Niño tends to bring drought, La Niña tends to bring wetter conditions
questions.expected: It is reversed: El Niño tends to bring drought, La Niña tends to bring wetter conditions
questions.memo: For southern Africa: El Niño → drier/drought; La Niña → wetter. The learner has them the wrong way round.

questions.question: The hot, wet climate with rain all year and dense rainforest is found in Africa's _______ region.
questions.memo: The equatorial region (e.g. Congo Basin) has high temperatures and heavy rain all year, supporting tropical rainforest.

questions.question: The savanna (tropical wet-and-dry) regions of Africa are known for _______.
options: a distinct wet summer and dry winter, with grassland
rain every day of the year
questions.expected: a distinct wet summer and dry winter, with grassland
questions.memo: Savanna climates have a marked wet season (summer) and dry season (winter), supporting tall grasses and scattered trees — much of Africa's interior.

questions.question: The Western Cape's winter-rainfall, dry-summer climate is described as _______.
questions.memo: A Mediterranean climate has warm dry summers and mild wet winters — the south-western Cape, watered by winter cold fronts.

questions.question:
The table shows rainfall for two African places. Which climate does B fit?

| Place | Jan rain (mm) | Jul rain (mm) | Total (mm) |
|------|------|------|------|
| A (equatorial) | 210 | 180 | 2 200 |
| B | 2 | 5 | 35 |
questions.memo: Place B's tiny year-round totals (35 mm) signal a desert climate, in contrast to wet equatorial Place A.

questions.question: The zone near the equator where the trade winds converge and rainfall is high is the _______.
questions.memo: The ITCZ is the belt of converging trade winds and rising air near the equator; it shifts seasonally and brings Africa's tropical rains.

questions.question: True or false: as the overhead Sun and the ITCZ shift north and south through the year, they move Africa's rain belts with them.
questions.memo: The seasonal migration of the ITCZ explains why savanna areas get summer rain — the rain belt follows the overhead Sun.

questions.question: A cold ocean current along a coast (like the Benguela) tends to make that coast _______.
questions.memo: Cold currents cool the air, reducing evaporation and rainfall — producing arid coasts such as the Namib alongside the Benguela.

questions.question: Match each African climate region to a key feature.
questions.memo: 1 Equatorial → C wet all year, rainforest. 2 Savanna → D wet summer, dry winter. 3 Desert → A very dry, ~30°. 4 Mediterranean → B wet winter, dry summer. (Prompt: 1=Equatorial, 2=Savanna, 3=Desert, 4=Mediterranean; A=very dry near 30°, B=wet winter dry summer, C=wet all year, D=wet summer dry winter.)

questions.question: Why does El Niño matter so much for southern African farmers?
options: Drought risk threatens crops, livestock and food security
It has no effect on farming
It only affects fishing in Peru
questions.expected: Drought risk threatens crops, livestock and food security
questions.memo: El Niño droughts can devastate rain-fed agriculture, raising food prices and threatening food security across the region — so forecasts guide planning.

questions.question: On a synoptic map over southern Africa in summer, a low-pressure cell over the interior is linked to _______.
questions.memo: A summer interior low draws in moist air that rises and produces afternoon convectional thunderstorms over much of the highveld.

questions.question: True or false: convergence of air leads to rising air and rain, while subsidence leads to sinking air and dry conditions.
questions.memo: Converging air must rise (→ rain); subsiding air sinks and dries (→ drought/desert). This pair explains much of Africa's rainfall pattern.

questions.question: Why does Africa straddling the equator give it such a wide range of climates?
options: It spans many pressure belts and latitudes, from equatorial to Mediterranean and desert
It has only one climate everywhere
Climate depends only on the day of the week
questions.expected: It spans many pressure belts and latitudes, from equatorial to Mediterranean and desert
questions.memo: Stretching across both tropics and into the subtropics, Africa passes through equatorial, savanna, desert and Mediterranean belts — a full range of climates.

GEO.G11.T1.ATM.A4.title: Droughts and desertification
GEO.G11.T1.ATM.A4.description: Areas at risk, causes of droughts and desertification, effects and differing vulnerability, and management strategies.
GEO.G11.T1.ATM.A4.recovery_strategy: DROUGHT = a temporary spell of below-normal rainfall. DESERTIFICATION = land permanently degrading to desert, often from human pressure (overgrazing, deforestation) ON TOP of dry climate. Manage with sustainable land use, reforestation and water harvesting.

questions.question: A drought is best defined as _______.
options: a prolonged period of below-normal rainfall
questions.expected: a prolonged period of below-normal rainfall
questions.memo: Drought is a temporary but extended shortage of rainfall relative to what an area normally receives, causing water stress.

questions.question: Desertification is _______.
options: the process of fertile land degrading into desert-like conditions
questions.expected: the process of fertile land degrading into desert-like conditions
questions.memo: Desertification is long-term land degradation in dry areas, where productive land becomes barren and desert-like — often partly human-caused.

questions.question: What is the key difference between a drought and desertification?
options: Drought is temporary; desertification is long-term land degradation
Drought is permanent; desertification is temporary
questions.expected: Drought is temporary; desertification is long-term land degradation
questions.memo: A drought ends when the rains return; desertification is a lasting loss of land productivity that is hard to reverse.

questions.question: Which is a HUMAN cause of desertification?
questions.memo: Overgrazing, deforestation, over-cultivation and poor irrigation strip protective vegetation and degrade soil, driving desertification.

questions.question: Sort each cause as mainly NATURAL or mainly HUMAN.

items.text: A long spell of below-normal rainfall
A shift in pressure belts reducing rain

questions.memo: Natural drivers (low rain, heat, pressure shifts) combine with human pressures (overgrazing, deforestation, over-cultivation) to cause desertification.

questions.question: The semi-arid belt along the southern edge of the Sahara, severely affected by desertification, is the _______.
questions.memo: The Sahel is a classic desertification case study — recurrent drought plus population and grazing pressure have degraded the land.

questions.question: Which is an EFFECT of severe drought on people?
options: Crop failure, water shortages and food insecurity
questions.expected: Crop failure, water shortages and food insecurity
questions.memo: Drought destroys crops and livestock, dries water sources and raises food prices — leading to hunger, hardship and sometimes migration.

questions.question: Why are poorer, rural communities often MORE vulnerable to drought than wealthy ones?
options: They depend directly on rain-fed farming and have fewer reserves and alternatives
They always live in wetter areas
They have more irrigation and savings
Wealth makes no difference to vulnerability
questions.expected: They depend directly on rain-fed farming and have fewer reserves and alternatives
questions.memo: Reliance on rain-fed subsistence farming, limited savings, weak infrastructure and few alternative incomes make poor rural communities most exposed — vulnerability is social, not just physical.

questions.question: Which strategy helps combat desertification?
options: Reforestation, controlled grazing and water harvesting
Increasing herd sizes on fragile land
questions.expected: Reforestation, controlled grazing and water harvesting
questions.memo: Restoring vegetation, rotating and limiting grazing, harvesting rainwater, building check dams and using shelterbelts all help hold soil and moisture.

questions.question: Planting lines of trees across the path of the wind to hold soil and moisture creates a _______.
questions.memo: Shelterbelts reduce wind speed, cut soil erosion and evaporation, and protect crops — a key anti-desertification measure (e.g. Africa's 'Great Green Wall').

questions.question: True or false: removing vegetation makes soil more likely to be blown or washed away, worsening desertification.
questions.memo: Plants protect and bind the soil; once stripped, the bare soil erodes by wind and water, accelerating land degradation.

questions.question: Which is an ENVIRONMENTAL effect of desertification?
options: Loss of biodiversity and fertile soil
questions.expected: Loss of biodiversity and fertile soil
questions.memo: Desertification destroys habitats and topsoil, reduces plant and animal life and lowers the land's ability to recover — a downward spiral.

questions.question:
The table shows a region's rainfall. Which years were drought years (well below the 500 mm average)?

| Year | Rainfall (mm) |
|------|------|
| 2018 | 510 |
| 2019 | 260 |
| 2020 | 240 |
| 2021 | 520 |
questions.memo: 2019 (260) and 2020 (240) are far below the 500 mm average — drought years; 2018 and 2021 are near normal.

questions.question: How can climate change worsen droughts in dry regions?
options: Higher temperatures increase evaporation and can reduce or shift rainfall
It has no effect on drought
questions.expected: Higher temperatures increase evaporation and can reduce or shift rainfall
questions.memo: Warming raises evaporation and can make rainfall less reliable, intensifying and lengthening droughts in already-dry regions.

questions.question: Overgrazing leads to desertification because livestock _______.
options: eat and trample vegetation faster than it can recover, exposing the soil
questions.expected: eat and trample vegetation faster than it can recover, exposing the soil
questions.memo: Too many animals strip and compact the land; without plant cover the soil bakes, erodes and loses fertility — classic desertification.

questions.question: True or false: areas with low and unreliable rainfall are most at risk of both drought and desertification.
questions.memo: Semi-arid margins (like the Sahel and parts of the Karoo) have fragile, low-rainfall environments most easily tipped into drought and degradation.

questions.question: Why is community involvement important in fighting desertification?
options: Local people must adopt sustainable grazing and farming for solutions to last
It is impossible to involve communities
questions.expected: Local people must adopt sustainable grazing and farming for solutions to last
questions.memo: Because land use is local, lasting change needs local buy-in — managing herds, restoring soil and protecting trees — supported by government and education.

questions.question: Rainwater harvesting helps dry areas by _______.
options: capturing and storing rain for use during dry spells
questions.expected: capturing and storing rain for use during dry spells
questions.memo: Tanks, check dams and contour trenches capture scarce rain so it can be used later and recharge the soil — building resilience to drought.

questions.question: A learner says a single dry season equals desertification. Why is this wrong?
options: Desertification is long-term degradation; one dry season is just a short drought
A dry season is wetter than normal
questions.expected: Desertification is long-term degradation; one dry season is just a short drought
questions.memo: Desertification builds up over years of pressure and dryness; a single dry season is a temporary drought, not permanent land degradation.

questions.question: Why is desertification described as both a physical and a human problem?
options: Dry climate sets the stage, but human land-use pressure often triggers and worsens it
It is purely caused by rainfall with no human role
It is purely human with no climate role
It has neither physical nor human causes
questions.expected: Dry climate sets the stage, but human land-use pressure often triggers and worsens it
questions.memo: A naturally dry, fragile climate plus overgrazing, deforestation and over-cultivation together cause desertification — so management must tackle both.

GEO.G11.T2.GEO.A1.title: Topography of horizontally layered rocks
GEO.G11.T2.GEO.A1.description: Landforms on flat-lying rock (mesa, butte, conical hill, basaltic plateau, canyon, Karoo), scarp retreat, and human use.
GEO.G11.T2.GEO.A1.recovery_strategy: A hard cap rock protects soft rock below. As scarp retreat eats the edges, a wide flat-topped MESA shrinks to a smaller flat-topped BUTTE, then a CONICAL HILL once the cap is gone. Mesa > butte > conical hill.

questions.question: A wide, flat-topped hill with steep sides, capped by hard rock, is a _______.
questions.memo: A mesa is a broad flat-topped hill protected by a resistant cap rock, with steep sides — wider than it is tall.

questions.question: A smaller, narrower flat-topped hill (taller than it is wide) is a _______.
questions.memo: A butte is what remains after a mesa is eroded further — narrower than a mesa but still flat-topped while the cap rock survives.

questions.question: Order these flat-topped landforms by stage of erosion, from least to most eroded.
questions.memo: Erosion shrinks a plateau → mesa → butte → conical hill as the protective cap rock is gradually worn away.

questions.question: Look at the diagram of flat-lying rock landforms. Which label shows the butte?
options: C — the cone with no flat top
questions.memo: A mesa (wide), B butte (narrow flat top), C conical hill (cap rock gone). The butte is the slimmer flat-topped remnant.

questions.question: What protects the flat top of a mesa or butte from being worn down quickly?
options: A layer of hard, resistant cap rock
questions.expected: A layer of hard, resistant cap rock
questions.memo: A resistant cap rock (often dolerite/basalt over softer Karoo rock) shields the softer layers below, keeping the top flat as the sides retreat.

questions.question: The backward erosion of a steep slope, keeping its shape while moving inland, is called _______.
questions.memo: Scarp retreat (back-wasting) is the parallel retreat of a cliff/scarp as weathering and erosion eat into it, leaving mesas and buttes as remnants.

questions.question: Much of South Africa's Karoo has this flat-topped scenery because the rocks lie _______.
options: roughly horizontally, capped by hard dolerite
questions.expected: roughly horizontally, capped by hard dolerite
questions.memo: Horizontal Karoo sediments capped by resistant dolerite produce the region's typical mesas, buttes and conical hills.

questions.question: A deep, steep-sided valley cut by a river into flat-lying rock is a _______.
questions.memo: Canyons (e.g. the Blyde River Canyon) form where rivers cut down through horizontal resistant rock, leaving steep walls.

questions.question: A large, flat, elevated area of horizontal rock is a _______.
questions.memo: A plateau is an extensive raised flatland; erosion of its edges produces mesas and buttes.

questions.question: Once the hard cap rock is finally removed, a butte erodes into a _______.
questions.memo: With no cap rock left to protect a flat top, the soft rock weathers into a rounded conical hill — the final stage.

questions.question: True or false: a mesa is wider than a butte, and a butte is wider than a conical hill.
questions.memo: Size order: mesa > butte > conical hill, reflecting progressive erosion of the same kind of landform.

questions.question: How do people typically USE flat-topped plateau and mesa landscapes?
options: Grazing livestock and some farming on the flat tops and plains
Building ski resorts in the tropics
questions.expected: Grazing livestock and some farming on the flat tops and plains
questions.memo: The flat surfaces suit grazing (sheep farming in the Karoo) and some cultivation; steep scarps are used less but offer scenic and tourism value.

questions.question: A basaltic plateau forms where _______.
options: repeated lava flows build up flat-lying layers of basalt
questions.expected: repeated lava flows build up flat-lying layers of basalt
questions.memo: Successive runny lava flows spread out and harden into horizontal basalt layers, creating extensive flat-topped basaltic plateaus (e.g. the Lesotho highlands).

questions.question: Why do steep scarp slopes on these landforms retreat while the tops stay flat?
options: The hard cap rock resists erosion on top while softer rock is undercut at the sides
The tops are made of sand
The sides are harder than the top
questions.expected: The hard cap rock resists erosion on top while softer rock is undercut at the sides
questions.memo: Weathering attacks the exposed softer rock on the steep sides; as it is undercut, the cap rock breaks off and the scarp retreats — keeping a flat top.

questions.question: True or false: canyons show that rivers can cut deeply into horizontal resistant rock over long time spans.
questions.memo: Given enough time, downcutting rivers carve deep canyons through hard horizontal rock, leaving near-vertical walls.

questions.question: On a contour map, a mesa would appear as _______.
options: closely-spaced contours around a flat top with few contours on the summit
questions.expected: closely-spaced contours around a flat top with few contours on the summit
questions.memo: Steep sides = tightly-packed contours forming a ring; the flat top has widely-spaced or no inner contours — the contour signature of a mesa.

questions.question: Why are mesas and buttes called 'relict' (remnant) landforms?
options: They are leftover pieces of a once-larger plateau that erosion has reduced
questions.expected: They are leftover pieces of a once-larger plateau that erosion has reduced
questions.memo: Mesas and buttes are surviving fragments of a former extensive plateau, isolated as scarp retreat removed the rock between them.

questions.question: Which sequence shows DECREASING resistance to erosion (most to least protected top)?
questions.memo: As the protective cap is progressively lost, the landform shrinks plateau → mesa → butte → conical hill.

questions.question: True or false: the same hard cap rock that forms a mesa's flat top is what makes the top resistant to weathering.
questions.memo: The resistant cap rock both creates and preserves the flat top; once it goes, the flat top is lost.

questions.question: A geologist finds several aligned buttes of the same cap rock height across a plain. What does this suggest?
options: They are erosion remnants of one former continuous rock layer/plateau
Each butte formed separately as a volcano
They were dropped by a glacier
questions.expected: They are erosion remnants of one former continuous rock layer/plateau
questions.memo: Matching cap-rock heights show the buttes were once joined as a single layer; erosion isolated them, leaving 'islands' of the old surface.

GEO.G11.T2.GEO.A2.title: Topography of inclined/tilted strata
GEO.G11.T2.GEO.A2.description: Landforms on tilted rock (scarp and dip slopes, cuesta, homoclinal ridge, hogsback, cuesta basin/dome) and human use.
GEO.G11.T2.GEO.A2.recovery_strategy: On tilted strata the GENTLE side following the rock dip is the DIP SLOPE; the STEEP cut-across side is the SCARP SLOPE. Steeper dip = different landform: gentle = CUESTA; moderate = HOMOCLINAL RIDGE; near-vertical = HOGSBACK.

questions.question: On a cuesta, the gentle slope that follows the angle of the tilted rock layers is the _______.
questions.memo: The DIP SLOPE follows the rock's dip (gentle); the SCARP SLOPE cuts across the layers (steep). A cuesta has one of each.

questions.question: The steep slope of a cuesta, cutting across the rock layers, is the _______.
questions.memo: The scarp (escarpment) slope is the steep face cutting across the strata; the dip slope is the gentle back following the dip.

questions.question: A ridge with one gentle dip slope and one steep scarp slope, formed on gently-tilted rock, is a _______.
questions.memo: A cuesta is an asymmetrical ridge on gently dipping rock: gentle dip slope + steep scarp slope.

questions.question: Look at the diagram of a cuesta. Which label shows the steep scarp slope?
options: A — the steep side cutting across the layers
B — the gentle side following the dip
questions.expected: A — the steep side cutting across the layers
questions.memo: A scarp slope (steep, across the strata); B dip slope (gentle, along the dip). A cuesta is asymmetrical.

questions.question: As the angle of dip of the rock increases, a cuesta gives way to a _______, then a hogsback.
questions.memo: Gentle dip = cuesta; moderate dip = homoclinal ridge (both slopes fairly steep); near-vertical dip = hogsback (two steep, near-equal slopes).

questions.question: A sharp, symmetrical ridge formed where rock layers are tilted almost vertically is a _______.
questions.memo: A hogsback has two steep, roughly equal slopes because the resistant rock is nearly vertical (e.g. the Hogsback area, Eastern Cape).

questions.question: Match each landform to its angle of dip.
questions.memo: 1 Cuesta → C gentle dip. 2 Homoclinal ridge → B moderate dip. 3 Hogsback → A near-vertical dip. (Prompt: 1=Cuesta, 2=Homoclinal ridge, 3=Hogsback; A=near-vertical dip, B=moderate dip, C=gentle dip.)

questions.question: A circular or basin-shaped arrangement of cuestas, with scarps facing inward, is a _______.
questions.memo: Where strata dip inward around a downwarp, cuestas form a ring with scarps facing IN — a cuesta basin. A dome has scarps facing OUT.

questions.question: In a cuesta DOME, the scarp slopes of the encircling cuestas face _______.
questions.memo: Around an up-warped dome the strata dip outward, so the steep scarps face away from the centre — the mirror image of a basin.

questions.question: True or false: on a cuesta the dip slope and scarp slope have the same steepness.
questions.memo: A cuesta is ASYMMETRICAL — gentle dip slope, steep scarp slope. Only a hogsback has two near-equal steep slopes.

questions.question: A learner says the dip slope is the steeper side of a cuesta. Correct them.
options: The dip slope is the GENTLE side; the scarp slope is the steep side
questions.expected: The dip slope is the GENTLE side; the scarp slope is the steep side
questions.memo: Dip slope = gentle (follows the dip); scarp slope = steep (cuts across). The learner swapped them.

questions.question: Why do these ridges form on tilted strata of ALTERNATING hard and soft rock?
options: Soft layers erode faster, leaving the resistant layers standing up as ridges
All layers erode at the same rate
Hard rock erodes faster than soft
questions.expected: Soft layers erode faster, leaving the resistant layers standing up as ridges
questions.memo: Differential erosion: soft beds wear into valleys, resistant beds remain as cuesta/ridge crests — the steeper the dip, the more symmetrical the ridge.

questions.question: On a contour map, a cuesta shows _______.
options: closely-spaced contours on the scarp side and widely-spaced contours on the dip side
questions.expected: closely-spaced contours on the scarp side and widely-spaced contours on the dip side
questions.memo: The steep scarp = tight contours; the gentle dip slope = widely-spaced contours. The asymmetry is the contour clue to a cuesta.

questions.question: How might people USE a cuesta landscape?
options: Farming the gentler dip slopes and valleys; ridges may give defensive sites or routes
It cannot be used at all
questions.expected: Farming the gentler dip slopes and valleys; ridges may give defensive sites or routes
questions.memo: Gentle dip slopes and valley floors suit farming and settlement; steep scarps are barriers but offer viewpoints, defence and routeways through gaps.

questions.question: The escarpment that separates South Africa's interior plateau from the coastal plains is an example of landscape shaped by _______.
options: scarp slopes and back-wasting on a large scale
questions.expected: scarp slopes and back-wasting on a large scale
questions.memo: The Great Escarpment is a major scarp; back-wasting (scarp retreat) has shaped this dramatic edge of the plateau over millions of years.

questions.question: True or false: the steeper the dip of the rock, the more symmetrical (equal-sided) the resulting ridge becomes.
questions.memo: Gentle dip = very asymmetrical cuesta; steep/near-vertical dip = symmetrical hogsback. Dip angle controls the shape.

questions.question: A homoclinal ridge differs from a cuesta mainly because _______.
options: its rock dips more steeply, making both slopes steeper
questions.expected: its rock dips more steeply, making both slopes steeper
questions.memo: A homoclinal ridge forms on more steeply dipping rock than a cuesta, so its dip slope is also fairly steep — midway towards a hogsback.

questions.question: Which feature would you NOT expect on horizontal rock, only on tilted rock?
options: A cuesta with a dip and scarp slope
questions.expected: A cuesta with a dip and scarp slope
questions.memo: Cuestas (and hogsbacks) need TILTED strata. Mesas, buttes and plateaus form on HORIZONTAL rock.

questions.question: True or false: a cuesta basin and a cuesta dome both have rings of cuestas, but their scarp slopes face opposite directions.
questions.memo: Basin: strata dip inward, scarps face IN. Dome: strata dip outward, scarps face OUT. Same ridges, opposite orientation.

questions.question: A surveyor maps a long ridge with a gentle eastern slope and a steep western cliff. What landform and dip direction is this?
options: A cuesta whose rock dips gently to the east (dip slope east, scarp west)
questions.expected: A cuesta whose rock dips gently to the east (dip slope east, scarp west)
questions.memo: Gentle slope = dip slope (rock dips that way, here east); steep slope = scarp (west). The asymmetry identifies a cuesta and its dip direction.

GEO.G11.T2.GEO.A3.title: Topography of massive igneous rocks
GEO.G11.T2.GEO.A3.description: Intrusive igneous bodies (batholith, laccolith, lopolith, dyke, sill) and the development of granite domes and tors.
GEO.G11.T2.GEO.A3.recovery_strategy: Intrusions: BATHOLITH = huge deep mass; LACCOLITH = dome that pushes layers up; LOPOLITH = saucer/basin shape; DYKE = cuts ACROSS layers (often vertical); SILL = runs ALONG layers (horizontal). Tors = blocks left when jointed granite weathers and loose material is removed.

questions.question: Igneous rock that cools and hardens BELOW the surface forms an _______ rock.
questions.memo: Intrusive (plutonic) rock cools slowly underground (e.g. granite). Extrusive rock cools on the surface (e.g. basalt lava).

questions.question: A very large, deep mass of intrusive igneous rock (often granite) is a _______.
questions.memo: A batholith is a huge body of igneous rock formed deep underground; it may be exposed at the surface after long erosion.

questions.question: An intrusion that cuts ACROSS the existing rock layers (often vertical) is a _______.
questions.memo: A dyke is a discordant intrusion cutting across the bedding; a sill is concordant, running parallel to the layers.

questions.question: An intrusion that runs ALONG (parallel to) the rock layers is a _______.
questions.memo: A sill squeezes between and parallel to existing layers (concordant). The Drakensberg has resistant dolerite sills.

questions.question: Look at the diagram of igneous intrusions. Which label shows the sill?
options: B — the sheet running parallel to the rock layers
A — the sheet cutting vertically across the layers
questions.expected: B — the sheet running parallel to the rock layers
questions.memo: A dyke (cuts across), B sill (parallel to layers), C batholith (huge deep mass). The sill follows the bedding.

questions.question: A dome-shaped intrusion that pushes the overlying rock layers UPWARD is a _______.
questions.memo: A laccolith is a blister-shaped intrusion with a flat floor and domed top that arches the layers above it upward.

questions.question: A large saucer- or basin-shaped intrusion that sags DOWNWARD in the middle is a _______.
questions.memo: A lopolith is a basin-shaped intrusion (e.g. South Africa's Bushveld Igneous Complex, a major source of platinum).

questions.question: Match each intrusion to its shape.
questions.memo: 1 Dyke → C cuts vertically across layers. 2 Sill → A runs parallel to layers. 3 Laccolith → D dome pushing layers up. 4 Lopolith → B saucer/basin shape. (Prompt: 1=Dyke, 2=Sill, 3=Laccolith, 4=Lopolith; A=parallel sheet, B=basin shape, C=vertical cross-cutting sheet, D=domed up.)

questions.question: A rounded hill of bare, exfoliating granite, often a former batholith now exposed, is a granite _______.
questions.memo: Granite domes (bornhardts), like Spitzkoppe or Paarl Rock, are smooth, rounded masses of resistant granite exposed and shaped by exfoliation.

questions.question: A cluster of large, rounded granite blocks stacked on a hilltop is a _______.
questions.memo: Tors are piles of rounded granite blocks left after weathering along joints loosens the rock and finer material is removed.

questions.question: Tors form mainly because granite weathers along its _______.
questions.memo: Weathering attacks the network of joints in granite; widely-jointed corners round off into blocks, while closely-jointed rock weathers away — leaving a tor.

questions.question: A learner says a sill cuts vertically across the rock layers. Correct them.
options: A sill runs PARALLEL to the layers; a DYKE cuts across them
Sills and dykes are the same
A sill is a surface lava flow
questions.expected: A sill runs PARALLEL to the layers; a DYKE cuts across them
questions.memo: Sill = concordant (parallel); dyke = discordant (cross-cutting). The learner described a dyke.

questions.question: Why do intrusions like dykes and sills often appear at the surface as ridges?
options: The hard igneous rock resists erosion better than the softer rock around it
Intrusions are made of soft sand
They are pushed up by rivers
questions.expected: The hard igneous rock resists erosion better than the softer rock around it
questions.memo: Resistant intruded rock stands out as a wall-like ridge once the softer surrounding rock erodes away — differential erosion in action.

questions.question: Sort each as an INTRUSIVE igneous body or an EXTRUSIVE/other feature.

items.text: Volcanic ash layer at the surface

questions.memo: Intrusive bodies cool underground (batholith, dyke, sill, laccolith); lava flows and ash are extrusive (surface) features.

questions.question: South Africa's Bushveld Igneous Complex, the world's largest source of platinum, is a giant _______.
questions.memo: The Bushveld Complex is a vast saucer-shaped lopolith holding enormous platinum, chromium and other mineral riches.

questions.question: True or false: intrusive igneous rocks cool slowly underground, giving them large, visible crystals.
questions.memo: Slow underground cooling allows large crystals to grow (e.g. coarse-grained granite); fast surface cooling gives fine-grained rock like basalt.

questions.question: Why are granite domes and tors only visible at the surface today?
options: Erosion has stripped away the overlying rock that once buried the intrusion
They float up from the mantle
questions.expected: Erosion has stripped away the overlying rock that once buried the intrusion
questions.memo: These granite bodies formed deep underground; only after millions of years of erosion removing the cover rock are they exposed.

questions.question: The peeling-off of curved sheets of rock from a granite dome is called _______.
questions.memo: Exfoliation (onion-skin weathering) peels curved shells off the granite as pressure is released and temperature changes — rounding the dome.

questions.question: True or false: a dyke is discordant (cuts across layers) while a sill is concordant (parallel to layers).
questions.memo: Discordant = cross-cutting (dyke); concordant = parallel (sill). This is the key distinction between the two sheet intrusions.

questions.question: A long, narrow, near-vertical wall of resistant rock runs straight across a landscape of softer rock. What is it most likely to be?
options: An exposed dyke standing up after the softer rock eroded
questions.expected: An exposed dyke standing up after the softer rock eroded
questions.memo: A straight, wall-like ridge of hard rock cutting across the country is the surface expression of an eroded dyke.

GEO.G11.T2.GEO.A4.title: Slopes
GEO.G11.T2.GEO.A4.description: South Africa's topography overview, slope types, slope elements (crest, cliff, talus, pediment) and their characteristics, slope development and slope retreat.
GEO.G11.T2.GEO.A4.recovery_strategy: Top to bottom: CREST (rounded top) → CLIFF / FREE FACE (steep bare rock) → TALUS / SCREE (loose broken rock below the cliff) → PEDIMENT (gentle rock surface at the base). Slope retreat = the slope moves back keeping its shape.

questions.question: The rounded, uppermost part of a hillslope is the _______.
questions.memo: The crest is the convex, rounded top of the slope where weathering begins; below it comes the cliff, then talus, then pediment.

questions.question: The steep, bare rock face of a slope is the cliff or _______.
questions.memo: The free face (cliff/scarp) is the steep exposed rock from which fragments break off to form the talus below.

questions.question: The pile of loose, broken rock fragments that collects at the base of a cliff is the _______.
questions.memo: Talus (scree) is the apron of rock debris that falls from the free face and accumulates below it.

questions.question: The gently-sloping rock surface at the very bottom of the slope is the _______.
questions.memo: The pediment is the gentle, concave rock surface at the slope foot, often thinly covered with debris being moved away.

questions.question: Order the slope elements from TOP to BOTTOM.
questions.memo: From the top down: crest → cliff (free face) → talus → pediment.

questions.question: Look at the slope diagram. Which label shows the talus (scree)?
options: C — the loose rock pile below the cliff
B — the steep bare rock face
D — the gentle surface at the base
questions.expected: C — the loose rock pile below the cliff
questions.memo: A crest, B free face/cliff, C talus (loose debris), D pediment. The talus sits between the cliff and the pediment.

questions.question: A learner says the talus is the steep, vertical rock face. Correct them.
options: The talus is the LOOSE rock pile; the steep face is the cliff/free face
questions.expected: The talus is the LOOSE rock pile; the steep face is the cliff/free face
questions.memo: Talus = the broken debris that has FALLEN from the cliff. The cliff itself is the free face.

questions.question: Slope RETREAT (back-wasting) means a slope _______.
options: moves backward (inland) while keeping its overall shape
turns into a flat plain instantly
questions.expected: moves backward (inland) while keeping its overall shape
questions.memo: In parallel slope retreat the whole profile shifts back as the cliff is eroded, leaving an extending pediment — keeping its shape.

questions.question: Slope DECLINE means a slope _______ over time.
questions.memo: In slope decline the angle reduces over time as the slope is worn down and smoothed — contrasted with parallel retreat, which keeps the angle.

questions.question: Most of South Africa's interior is a high, fairly flat _______ edged by the Great Escarpment.
questions.memo: South Africa's topography is dominated by a high interior plateau, separated from the lower coastal plains by the Great Escarpment.

questions.question: On which slope element does loose material move mainly by rockfall directly from above?
questions.memo: Fragments break off the steep free face and fall to form the talus below; the gentler pediment moves material by water and creep.

questions.question: Match each slope element to its description.
questions.memo: 1 Crest → C rounded top. 2 Free face → D steep bare rock. 3 Talus → A loose debris pile. 4 Pediment → B gentle base surface. (Prompt: 1=Crest, 2=Free face, 3=Talus, 4=Pediment; A=loose debris, B=gentle base, C=rounded top, D=steep bare rock.)

questions.question: True or false: the talus slope is generally less steep than the free face above it.
questions.memo: Talus settles at its 'angle of rest' (around 30–35°), gentler than the near-vertical free face that supplies it.

questions.question: As a free face retreats by back-wasting, the _______ at its base grows wider.
questions.memo: Each step of cliff retreat extends the gentle pediment inland; over time large pediments (and pediplains) develop.

questions.question: Why is the crest usually rounded and convex?
options: Weathering and soil creep smooth and round the upper slope
questions.expected: Weathering and soil creep smooth and round the upper slope
questions.memo: On the crest, weathering loosens material and slow soil creep rounds it into a convex form — distinct from the sharp free face below.

questions.question: Closely-spaced contours on a topographic map correspond to which slope element?
questions.memo: Steep cliffs = very tight (or merged) contours; the gentle pediment and crest show more widely-spaced contours.

questions.question: True or false: in arid climates, slopes tend to retreat parallel (keeping their angle), forming wide pediments.
questions.memo: In dry climates parallel retreat (back-wasting) dominates, producing extensive pediments and flat-topped remnants like mesas.

questions.question: Which slope element would be the SAFEST and easiest to build a road or settlement on?
options: The very top of a cliff
questions.memo: The gentle, stable pediment is far safer for roads and settlement than the steep cliff or the loose, mobile talus.

questions.question: Why is building on or below a steep talus slope risky?
options: Loose rock can fall or slide, and the slope can fail during heavy rain
Talus is the most stable ground
There is no risk at all
questions.expected: Loose rock can fall or slide, and the slope can fail during heavy rain
questions.memo: Talus is loose and near its angle of rest; rockfall and debris slides (especially when wet) make it hazardous to build on or below.

questions.question: A profile shows a rounded top, a vertical bare-rock band, a 32° debris slope, then a gentle rock foot. Identify the four elements in order.
questions.memo: Rounded top = crest; vertical bare rock = free face; ~32° debris = talus; gentle rock foot = pediment. Top to bottom order.

GEO.G11.T2.GEO.A5.title: Mass movements & human responses
GEO.G11.T2.GEO.A5.description: The concept of mass movement, types (creep, solifluction, landslides, rockfalls, mudflows, slumps), impacts, and prevention strategies with SA case studies.
GEO.G11.T2.GEO.A5.recovery_strategy: Mass movement = downhill movement of rock/soil under GRAVITY. Speed varies: CREEP is very slow; ROCKFALLS/LANDSLIDES are sudden and fast. Water often triggers them. Reduce risk with drainage, terracing, retaining walls, planting and avoiding unstable slopes.

questions.question: Mass movement is the downhill movement of rock and soil mainly under the force of _______.
questions.memo: Gravity pulls weathered material downslope. Water often acts as a trigger by adding weight and reducing friction.

questions.question: The very SLOW, almost invisible downhill movement of soil is called _______.
questions.memo: Soil creep moves only millimetres a year but bends fences, tilts poles and curves tree trunks over time.

questions.question: The sudden, fast collapse of rock and soil down a steep slope is a _______.
questions.memo: Landslides move large amounts of material rapidly downhill, often triggered by heavy rain, earthquakes or undercutting.

questions.question: A flow of water-saturated soil and debris down a slope is a _______.
questions.memo: Mudflows occur when soil becomes saturated and flows like a thick liquid — fast and very destructive, common after intense rain.

questions.question: A slump is a mass movement in which material moves _______.
options: downward and outward along a curved surface, rotating as it goes
questions.expected: downward and outward along a curved surface, rotating as it goes
questions.memo: A slump rotates along a concave (curved) slip surface, leaving a tilted block and a crescent-shaped scar at the top.

questions.question: The slow downslope flow of water-saturated soil over frozen ground (in cold climates) is _______.
questions.memo: Solifluction is the slow flow of saturated soil, typically over a frozen or impermeable layer in cold/periglacial regions.

questions.question: Sort each mass movement as FAST or SLOW.

items.text: Slow downhill creep of hillside soil

questions.memo: Fast: rockfall, landslide, mudflow. Slow: soil creep, solifluction. Speed is a key way to classify mass movements.

questions.question: Which factor most commonly TRIGGERS landslides and mudflows?
options: Heavy or prolonged rainfall saturating the slope
questions.expected: Heavy or prolonged rainfall saturating the slope
questions.memo: Water adds weight and reduces friction between particles, so heavy rain is the most common trigger; earthquakes and slope undercutting also trigger movement.

questions.question: How can a mass movement IMPACT people?
options: Destroying homes, roads and lives, and blocking rivers
questions.expected: Destroying homes, roads and lives, and blocking rivers
questions.memo: Mass movements bury and destroy buildings and infrastructure, cause injury and death, and can dam rivers — a serious hazard on steep, populated slopes.

questions.question: Building retaining walls and improving drainage on a slope helps by _______.
options: holding material in place and removing excess water
questions.expected: holding material in place and removing excess water
questions.memo: Retaining walls support the slope and drains remove the water that triggers failure — two key engineering responses to mass-movement risk.

questions.question: Planting vegetation on a slope reduces mass-movement risk because roots _______.
options: bind the soil and take up water
questions.expected: bind the soil and take up water
questions.memo: Roots anchor the soil and absorb water, increasing stability — which is why removing vegetation makes slopes far more prone to failure.

questions.question: A learner says soil creep happens in seconds like a rockfall. Correct them.
options: Soil creep is extremely slow (millimetres a year); rockfalls are sudden
Soil creep is faster than a rockfall
questions.expected: Soil creep is extremely slow (millimetres a year); rockfalls are sudden
questions.memo: Creep is barely perceptible and acts over years; rockfalls happen in seconds. They sit at opposite ends of the speed scale.

questions.question: Tilted fences, leaning poles and curved tree trunks on a hillside are evidence of _______.
questions.memo: These slow, cumulative signs reveal soil creep — material has crept downhill over years, bending fixed objects.

questions.question: Why does steepening a slope (e.g. cutting a road into it) increase mass-movement risk?
options: It removes support from the base, making the slope above unstable
questions.expected: It removes support from the base, making the slope above unstable
questions.memo: Undercutting the toe of a slope removes the material that held it up, so gravity can pull the over-steepened slope down — a common cause of road-cut failures.

questions.question: Match each mass movement to its key feature.
questions.memo: 1 Soil creep → C very slow soil movement. 2 Rockfall → A blocks falling from a cliff. 3 Mudflow → D saturated soil flowing. 4 Slump → B rotation on a curved surface. (Prompt: 1=Soil creep, 2=Rockfall, 3=Mudflow, 4=Slump; A=falling cliff blocks, B=rotational slip, C=very slow soil movement, D=saturated flow.)

questions.question: True or false: heavy rainfall makes most types of mass movement MORE likely.
questions.memo: Water adds weight and lubricates particles, so saturated slopes are far more likely to creep, slide or flow.

questions.question: Why are informal settlements on steep slopes especially vulnerable to mass movements?
options: Slopes may be unstable, with cut platforms, poor drainage and fragile housing
They are always on flat, safe land
questions.expected: Slopes may be unstable, with cut platforms, poor drainage and fragile housing
questions.memo: Limited land pushes some settlements onto steep, unstable slopes; cutting platforms, poor drainage and weak structures raise the risk of deadly slides.

questions.question: Terracing a hillslope for farming helps reduce mass movement by _______.
options: breaking a long steep slope into shorter, flatter steps
questions.expected: breaking a long steep slope into shorter, flatter steps
questions.memo: Terraces reduce the effective slope angle and slow runoff, cutting erosion and the chance of the slope failing.

questions.question: True or false: avoiding building on or below known unstable slopes is one of the simplest ways to reduce mass-movement disasters.
questions.memo: Land-use zoning that keeps people away from high-risk slopes prevents loss of life and is cheaper than repeated rescue and rebuilding.

questions.question: After heavy rain, a saturated hillside above a township slides as a fast wall of mud. Which type is this, and one response?
options: A mudflow; respond with drainage, slope stabilisation and warning/evacuation systems
Soil creep; respond by ignoring it
A rockfall on flat ground; no response needed
Solifluction in the tropics; build on it
questions.expected: A mudflow; respond with drainage, slope stabilisation and warning/evacuation systems
questions.memo: Saturated, fast-flowing soil is a mudflow. Responses include improving drainage, stabilising and vegetating the slope, zoning and early-warning/evacuation.

GEO.G11.T3.DEV.A1.title: The concept of development
GEO.G11.T3.DEV.A1.description: Development terminology, the meaning of development (economic/social/sustainable/spatial), and indicators (GNP, GDP, HDI, Gini, life expectancy, infant mortality).
GEO.G11.T3.DEV.A1.recovery_strategy: Development is more than money: health, education, equality, sustainability. HDI combines income, education and life expectancy (higher = more developed). The GINI coefficient measures inequality (higher = MORE unequal). Infant mortality FALLS as development rises.

questions.question: What does 'development' mean in geography?
options: Improvement in people's quality of life — economic, social and environmental
Only the amount of money a country has
questions.expected: Improvement in people's quality of life — economic, social and environmental
questions.memo: Development is broad: rising incomes AND better health, education, equality and a sustainable environment — not wealth alone.

questions.question: MEDC stands for a More Economically _______ Country.
questions.memo: MEDC = More Economically Developed Country (richer, industrialised); LEDC = Less Economically Developed Country.

questions.question: GDP stands for Gross Domestic _______.
questions.memo: GDP (Gross Domestic Product) is the total value of goods and services produced in a country in a year — a core economic indicator.

questions.question: The Human Development Index (HDI) combines income, education and _______.
questions.memo: HDI blends GNI per capita, years of schooling and life expectancy into one 0–1 score — a fuller measure than money alone.

questions.question: A HIGHER HDI value (closer to 1) means a country is _______.
questions.memo: HDI runs from 0 to 1; the closer to 1, the higher the level of human development.

questions.question: The Gini coefficient measures a country's _______.
questions.memo: The Gini coefficient measures how evenly income is shared: 0 = perfect equality, 1 = maximum inequality. South Africa has one of the highest.

questions.question: A HIGHER Gini coefficient means _______.
questions.memo: Higher Gini = income is more unequally distributed (a small group holds much of the wealth). The learner must not read it as 'more equal'.

questions.question: As a country develops, its infant mortality rate usually _______.
questions.memo: Better healthcare, nutrition and clean water cut infant deaths, so a LOW infant mortality rate signals higher development.

questions.question: Match each indicator to what it measures.
questions.memo: 1 GDP → C total value produced. 2 HDI → A income, education and life expectancy combined. 3 Gini → D income inequality. 4 Infant mortality → B baby deaths per 1 000 births. (Prompt: 1=GDP, 2=HDI, 3=Gini, 4=Infant mortality; A=income+education+life expectancy, B=baby deaths, C=value produced, D=inequality.)

questions.question: Why is GDP per capita alone a limited measure of development?
options: It is an average that hides inequality and ignores health, education and environment
It only applies to small countries
questions.expected: It is an average that hides inequality and ignores health, education and environment
questions.memo: An average can be high while many remain poor; it says nothing about how wealth is shared or about health, schooling and sustainability — hence HDI and Gini.

questions.question: Social indicators of development include _______.
options: literacy rate and access to healthcare
questions.expected: literacy rate and access to healthcare
questions.memo: Social indicators measure wellbeing: literacy, schooling, healthcare access, clean water and sanitation — alongside economic indicators.

questions.question:
The table compares two countries. Which is MORE developed overall?

| Country | GDP/capita ($) | HDI | Infant mortality |
|------|------|------|------|
| X | 42 000 | 0,90 | 4 |
| Y | 3 000 | 0,52 | 48 |
options: Country X — higher GDP and HDI, lower infant mortality
questions.expected: Country X — higher GDP and HDI, lower infant mortality
questions.memo: X leads on every measure: higher income, higher HDI and far fewer infant deaths — clearly more developed.

questions.question: 'Sustainable development' means meeting today's needs _______.
options: without preventing future generations from meeting theirs
by using up all resources now
questions.expected: without preventing future generations from meeting theirs
questions.memo: Sustainable development balances economic, social and environmental needs so growth does not rob the future.

questions.question: True or false: a country can have a high average income yet still rank lower on HDI because of poor health and education.
questions.memo: Income is only one of HDI's three parts; weak schooling or low life expectancy can pull a wealthy country's HDI down.

questions.question: Life expectancy is a development indicator because it reflects _______.
questions.memo: How long people live captures the quality of healthcare, diet, water and safety — so it rises with development.

questions.question: Differences in development can be seen at which scales?
questions.memo: Inequality exists between continents and countries AND within them — between provinces, cities and even neighbourhoods.

questions.question: A learner reads a higher Gini coefficient as 'more equal'. Correct them.
options: A higher Gini means MORE inequality, not more equality
questions.expected: A higher Gini means MORE inequality, not more equality
questions.memo: Gini rises towards 1 as income becomes more UNEQUAL. Lower Gini = more equal. The learner reversed it.

questions.question: True or false: 'developed' and 'developing' are simplified labels and there is actually a wide range between countries.
questions.memo: Development is a spectrum, not two boxes; many countries are 'emerging' or somewhere in between — the labels are a rough shorthand.

questions.question: Why might two indicators (e.g. GDP and HDI) be used TOGETHER rather than one alone?
options: Each shows a different aspect, so together they give a fuller, more reliable picture
They always give the same number
One indicator is enough for everything
questions.expected: Each shows a different aspect, so together they give a fuller, more reliable picture
questions.memo: Economic and social indicators capture different things; combining them reduces the risk of a misleading single-measure judgement.

questions.question: South Africa has a high GDP for the continent but also one of the world's highest Gini coefficients. What does this show?
options: The country produces wealth, but it is very unequally shared among its people
It is the poorest country in Africa
questions.expected: The country produces wealth, but it is very unequally shared among its people
questions.memo: A solid GDP alongside extreme inequality shows that national wealth does not reach everyone — a central development challenge for South Africa.

GEO.G11.T3.DEV.A2.title: Frameworks for development
GEO.G11.T3.DEV.A2.description: Factors affecting development and their interlinks, development models (Rostow, core-periphery, sustainability), and community-based development.
GEO.G11.T3.DEV.A2.recovery_strategy: Development factors interlink (poor education → low skills → weak economy → less money for schools). Rostow = stages of growth (criticised as 'one path'). CORE-PERIPHERY: a wealthy CORE draws resources, money and people from a poorer PERIPHERY.

questions.question: Which is a factor that can affect a country's development?
options: Access to resources, education and trade
The number of letters in its name
questions.expected: Access to resources, education and trade
questions.memo: Development depends on many interlinked factors: resources, energy, education, history, trade, population and the environment.

questions.question: Development factors are described as 'inter-related' because they _______.
options: influence one another (e.g. education affects the economy)
questions.expected: influence one another (e.g. education affects the economy)
questions.memo: The factors form a web: weak education lowers skills, which weakens the economy, which limits money for schools — a cycle.

questions.question: Rostow's model describes development as passing through a series of _______.
questions.memo: Rostow's free-market model sees countries moving through stages from traditional society to high mass consumption.

questions.question: A common CRITICISM of Rostow's model is that it _______.
options: assumes all countries follow the same single path to development
has too many stages to count
questions.expected: assumes all countries follow the same single path to development
questions.memo: Critics say Rostow is too linear and Western-centred, ignoring history, colonialism, trade barriers and different paths countries can take.

questions.question: In the core-periphery model, the CORE is the _______ region.
questions.memo: The CORE is the rich, developed centre (jobs, industry, services); the PERIPHERY is the poorer surrounding region that supplies it.

questions.question: In the core-periphery model, the periphery tends to LOSE its _______ to the core.
questions.memo: Resources, capital and the most skilled workers flow from the periphery to the core, widening the gap between them.

questions.question: A learner says the periphery exploits the core. Correct them.
options: It is the other way round — the wealthy core draws resources and people from the poorer periphery
There is no core or periphery
questions.expected: It is the other way round — the wealthy core draws resources and people from the poorer periphery
questions.memo: The dominant CORE benefits at the periphery's expense, not the reverse. The learner has the relationship backwards.

questions.question: A sustainability model of development balances which three elements?
questions.memo: Sustainable development rests on three pillars — economy, society and environment — kept in balance so growth lasts.

questions.question: Sort each as a factor that tends to HELP or HINDER development.
questions.memo: Education, resources, energy and stability drive development; trade imbalances, environmental damage and runaway population growth hold it back.

questions.question: Community-based development means development that is _______.
options: planned and driven with and by local communities to meet their own needs
imposed from far away with no local input
questions.expected: planned and driven with and by local communities to meet their own needs
questions.memo: Community-based (bottom-up) development involves local people in identifying needs and running projects — more likely to be appropriate and lasting.

questions.question: A 'top-down' development project is one that is _______.
options: planned by government or large organisations, often large-scale
questions.expected: planned by government or large organisations, often large-scale
questions.memo: Top-down projects (e.g. a big dam) are decided by central authorities; bottom-up projects start with the community. Each has strengths and weaknesses.

questions.question: Why can a 'cycle of poverty' be hard to break?
options: Low income → poor education/health → low skills → low income, repeating
Education has no link to income
questions.expected: Low income → poor education/health → low skills → low income, repeating
questions.memo: The interlinked factors reinforce each other in a loop, so breaking out usually needs intervention in several areas at once (education, health, jobs).

questions.question: True or false: appropriate technology (small-scale, affordable, locally repairable) often suits community development better than large imported machines.
questions.memo: Appropriate technology fits local skills, materials and budgets, so it is more likely to be used and maintained than costly imported equipment.

questions.question: The core-periphery model can be applied at which scale(s)?
questions.memo: Core-periphery works at many scales: rich vs poor countries globally, and a dominant city/region vs poorer areas within one country.

questions.question: Within South Africa, Gauteng acts as an economic _______ that attracts people and investment from poorer provinces.
questions.memo: Gauteng is a national core: its concentration of jobs and industry pulls migrants and capital from peripheral provinces like the Eastern Cape and Limpopo.

questions.question: Match each model/approach to its key idea.
questions.memo: 1 Rostow → B stages of economic growth. 2 Core-periphery → C rich core draws from poor periphery. 3 Sustainability → A balance economy, society and environment. (Prompt: 1=Rostow, 2=Core-periphery, 3=Sustainability; A=balance three pillars, B=growth stages, C=core draws from periphery.)

questions.question: True or false: free-market models assume that economic growth will gradually spread wealth and lift living standards.
questions.memo: Free-market/Rostow-type thinking expects growth to 'trickle down' — a view critics challenge, arguing it can leave many behind.

questions.question: An advantage of bottom-up (community) development over top-down projects is that it _______.
options: better fits local needs and gains community ownership
is always cheaper to plan nationally
questions.expected: better fits local needs and gains community ownership
questions.memo: Because communities shape and run them, bottom-up projects suit real local needs and are more likely to be maintained — though they can be small in scale.

questions.question: Why might a single large top-down dam project both help AND harm development?
options: It can supply water and power but may displace people and damage the environment
It has no effects at all
questions.expected: It can supply water and power but may displace people and damage the environment
questions.memo: Big projects bring benefits (water, electricity, jobs) but also costs (displacement, ecological damage, debt) — development involves trade-offs.

questions.question: Why do geographers use development MODELS at all?
options: They simplify complex reality to help explain and compare patterns of development
They give the exact future of every country
They replace the need for any data
questions.expected: They simplify complex reality to help explain and compare patterns of development
questions.memo: Models are simplified tools to spot patterns and compare places; they are useful but always imperfect, which is why each has criticisms.

GEO.G11.T3.DEV.A3.title: Trade and development
GEO.G11.T3.DEV.A3.description: World trade and terms of trade, trading relationships (free trade, barriers, subsidies, fair trade), globalisation, and export-led development.
GEO.G11.T3.DEV.A3.recovery_strategy: Many developing countries export cheap RAW materials and import expensive MANUFACTURED goods — poor terms of trade that keep them dependent. FREE TRADE = no barriers; TRADE BARRIERS = tariffs/quotas; FAIR TRADE = better prices/conditions for producers.

questions.question: International trade is the buying and selling of goods and services _______.
questions.memo: International trade exchanges goods and services across national borders, linking the world's economies.

questions.question: Raw materials such as ores, crops and timber are also called _______.
questions.memo: Commodities are basic raw materials traded in bulk; many developing countries depend on exporting them.

questions.question: Why do poor 'terms of trade' disadvantage many developing countries?
options: They export cheap raw materials but import expensive manufactured goods
They export expensive goods and import cheap ones
They do not trade at all
Raw materials are always more valuable than manufactures
questions.expected: They export cheap raw materials but import expensive manufactured goods
questions.memo: Selling low-value raw materials and buying high-value finished products means money flows out faster than in — keeping countries dependent and poorer.

questions.question: Free trade means trade with _______.
questions.memo: Free trade removes tariffs and quotas so goods move freely. Protectionism does the opposite to shield local industry.

questions.question: A tax placed on imported goods is a _______.
