questions.memo: A tariff is an import tax (a trade barrier) that makes foreign goods more expensive to protect local producers. A quota limits the QUANTITY allowed in.

questions.question: A government payment to help local producers compete is a _______.
questions.memo: Subsidies lower local producers' costs so they can sell cheaper — but they can disadvantage foreign producers who get no such help.

questions.question: Fair trade aims to ensure that producers in developing countries receive _______.
options: fairer prices and better working conditions
questions.expected: fairer prices and better working conditions
questions.memo: Fair trade guarantees producers a fairer, more stable price and supports decent conditions and community investment — helping development.

questions.question: A learner says fair trade means 'no rules at all'. Correct them.
options: Fair trade has STANDARDS ensuring fair prices and conditions; 'no rules' describes free trade
Fair trade only helps rich countries
questions.expected: Fair trade has STANDARDS ensuring fair prices and conditions; 'no rules' describes free trade
questions.memo: Fair trade is about ethical STANDARDS protecting producers, not the absence of rules. The learner confused it with free trade.

questions.question: Globalisation refers to the growing _______ of the world's economies and cultures.
questions.memo: Globalisation links economies, cultures and people worldwide through trade, technology, transport and communication.

questions.question: Sort each as a likely BENEFIT or DRAWBACK of globalisation for a developing country.

items.text: Local firms outcompeted by big multinationals

questions.memo: Globalisation can bring markets, investment, jobs and technology, but also competition that harms local firms, price shocks and labour exploitation.

questions.question: Export-led development is a strategy of growing the economy by _______.
options: producing goods to sell to other countries
only farming for the home market
questions.expected: producing goods to sell to other countries
questions.memo: Export-led growth (used by the 'Asian Tigers') builds industries aimed at foreign markets to earn income and create jobs — with risks if those markets weaken.

questions.question: A risk of relying heavily on exporting ONE commodity is that _______.
options: a fall in its world price can badly damage the whole economy
questions.expected: a fall in its world price can badly damage the whole economy
questions.memo: Dependence on a single commodity leaves a country exposed to price swings; diversifying exports spreads the risk.

questions.question: Adding value by PROCESSING raw materials before export helps a country because _______.
options: processed goods sell for more, keeping more income and creating jobs
raw materials are always worth more
questions.expected: processed goods sell for more, keeping more income and creating jobs
questions.memo: Beneficiation (e.g. refining ore into metal, roasting beans into coffee) captures more value and employment at home rather than exporting raw and importing finished goods.

questions.question: True or false: trade barriers in rich countries can make it harder for developing countries to sell their goods.
questions.memo: Tariffs, quotas and subsidies in wealthy markets can block or undercut developing-country exports, worsening trade imbalances.

questions.question:
The table shows a country's trade. What does it reveal?

| Exports | Value | Imports | Value |
|------|------|------|------|
| Raw cocoa | low per tonne | Chocolate | high per tonne |
| Iron ore | low per tonne | Machinery | high per tonne |
options: It exports low-value raw materials and imports high-value manufactured goods (poor terms of trade)
It is getting rich from trade
Trade has no effect on it
questions.expected: It exports low-value raw materials and imports high-value manufactured goods (poor terms of trade)
questions.memo: Selling cheap raw cocoa/ore and buying costly chocolate/machinery is the classic unequal pattern that disadvantages developing economies.

questions.question: A trade bloc (like SADC or the EU) is a group of countries that _______.
options: agree to reduce trade barriers between themselves
questions.expected: agree to reduce trade barriers between themselves
questions.memo: Trade blocs lower tariffs among members to boost trade; South Africa belongs to SADC and SACU.

questions.question: True or false: choosing fair-trade products can directly support better incomes for farmers in developing countries.
questions.memo: When consumers buy fair-trade goods, more of the price reaches producers, supporting fairer incomes and community projects.

questions.question: Why might multinational companies locate factories in developing countries?
options: Lower labour costs and access to resources and new markets
Because there are no workers there
questions.expected: Lower labour costs and access to resources and new markets
questions.memo: Cheaper labour, resources and growing markets attract multinationals — bringing jobs and investment but raising concerns about wages and conditions.

questions.question: How can trade, used well, support development?
options: Earning income, creating jobs and funding services and infrastructure
By exporting only at a loss
questions.expected: Earning income, creating jobs and funding services and infrastructure
questions.memo: Trade that earns good income and adds value can fund schools, health and infrastructure — provided terms of trade are fair and exports are diversified.

questions.question: Why is 'export-led development' described as needing to be 'critically examined'?
options: It can drive growth but also create dependence on volatile foreign markets and low-wage work
It always succeeds without any risk
It is identical to subsistence farming
questions.expected: It can drive growth but also create dependence on volatile foreign markets and low-wage work
questions.memo: Export-led strategies lifted some economies fast but can leave countries vulnerable to global demand swings and reliant on low-paid labour — benefits and risks both.

GEO.G11.T3.DEV.A4.title: Development issues and challenges
GEO.G11.T3.DEV.A4.description: The role of women in development, development's effect on the environment, and the roles of the state and business in South African development.
GEO.G11.T3.DEV.A4.recovery_strategy: Empowering women (education, jobs, rights, healthcare) lowers birth rates and lifts whole communities. Development can harm the environment, so it must be balanced. The state and business can lead development together via public-private partnerships.

questions.question: Educating and empowering women tends to _______ a country's development.
questions.memo: When women are educated and able to work and make decisions, birth rates fall, family health and income improve and the whole economy benefits.

questions.question: Gender issues in development include differences in women's access to _______.
options: education, resources, land and decision-making power
questions.expected: education, resources, land and decision-making power
questions.memo: Gender inequality shows in unequal access to schooling, land, credit, jobs and political power — holding back women and development.

questions.question: Why does educating girls often lower a country's birth rate?
options: Educated women tend to marry later, have fewer children and use family planning
Education has no link to birth rates
questions.expected: Educated women tend to marry later, have fewer children and use family planning
questions.memo: Schooling expands women's choices and opportunities, typically lowering fertility and improving child health — a powerful development lever.

questions.question: Rapid, unmanaged economic development can harm the environment through _______.
questions.memo: Industry, mining and urban growth can pollute air and water, clear forests and use up resources — which is why development must be made sustainable.

questions.question: A learner says economic growth and the environment never conflict. Correct them.
options: Growth often harms the environment, so the two can conflict and must be balanced
questions.expected: Growth often harms the environment, so the two can conflict and must be balanced
questions.memo: Unchecked growth can damage the environment; sustainable development seeks a balance rather than assuming no conflict exists.

questions.question: In a public-private partnership (PPP), development is delivered by _______.
options: government and private business working together
questions.expected: government and private business working together
questions.memo: PPPs combine public oversight and funding with private-sector skills and investment to deliver infrastructure and services.

questions.question: Under 'central control by the state', who mainly directs development?
options: The government plans and controls the economy strongly
questions.expected: The government plans and controls the economy strongly
questions.memo: Strong state control means government leads planning and key industries; 'weak state control' leaves more to the free market and private business.

questions.question: Sort each as mainly a ROLE OF THE STATE or a ROLE OF BUSINESS in development.

items.text: Building public roads, schools and clinics
Investing capital to create factories and jobs
Producing and selling goods for profit

questions.memo: The state provides infrastructure, laws and services; business invests, produces and innovates. Together (via PPPs) they drive development.

questions.question: Giving women access to land and credit supports development because it _______.
options: lets them farm, start businesses and earn income for their families
questions.expected: lets them farm, start businesses and earn income for their families
questions.memo: With land and finance, women can be productive farmers and entrepreneurs, raising household income, food security and community wellbeing.

questions.question: True or false: development that ignores the environment may bring short-term gains but long-term costs.
questions.memo: Damaging soil, water and air for quick growth can undermine farming, health and future prosperity — short-term gain, long-term loss.

questions.question: Women are often described as 'central to development' partly because they _______.
options: do much of the farming, caregiving and household management in many societies
questions.expected: do much of the farming, caregiving and household management in many societies
questions.memo: Women produce much of the food and run households, so investing in them multiplies benefits for children, families and economies.

questions.question: An ADVANTAGE of strong state control of development is that it can _______.
options: direct resources to priorities like infrastructure and reducing inequality
questions.expected: direct resources to priorities like infrastructure and reducing inequality
questions.memo: A strong state can plan and fund national priorities and target poverty — though it risks inefficiency or corruption if poorly run.

questions.question: A DISADVANTAGE of very weak state control can be that _______.
options: the market may neglect the poor and essential services
questions.expected: the market may neglect the poor and essential services
questions.memo: Left entirely to the market, profit-driven business may underserve poor areas and public goods like rural clinics — a reason for some state involvement.

questions.question: Why are PPPs (public-private partnerships) attractive for big development projects?
options: They combine public funding/oversight with private investment and efficiency
questions.expected: They combine public funding/oversight with private investment and efficiency
questions.memo: PPPs share risk and strengths — the state provides oversight and access, business provides capital and know-how — useful for infrastructure delivery.

questions.question: True or false: tackling gender inequality is now seen as essential to achieving wider development goals.
questions.memo: Global development frameworks treat gender equality as both a goal in itself and a driver of progress in health, education and the economy.

questions.question: Match each actor to its development contribution.
questions.memo: 1 State → B laws, infrastructure and services. 2 Business → C investment, jobs and innovation. 3 PPP → A combining public and private strengths. (Prompt: 1=State, 2=Business, 3=PPP; A=public+private together, B=laws/infrastructure/services, C=investment/jobs/innovation.)

questions.question: How can development be made more environmentally sustainable?
options: Using cleaner technology, renewable energy and managing resources wisely
questions.expected: Using cleaner technology, renewable energy and managing resources wisely
questions.memo: Cleaner production, renewables, recycling, pollution control and protected areas let economies grow while limiting environmental harm.

questions.question: Why is the role of the state in South African development a matter of debate?
options: There are trade-offs between strong state direction, market freedom and partnerships
There is only one correct answer everyone agrees on
questions.expected: There are trade-offs between strong state direction, market freedom and partnerships
questions.memo: Different mixes of state control, market freedom and PPPs have different strengths and risks — so the right balance is genuinely debated.

questions.question: True or false: a development project can succeed economically yet fail socially if it ignores local communities and equality.
questions.memo: Profit alone is not 'development' if benefits bypass communities or deepen inequality — social and environmental outcomes matter too.

questions.question: Why is empowering women often called a development 'multiplier'?
options: Gains in women's education and income spread to children, families and communities
It has a one-time, tiny effect
questions.expected: Gains in women's education and income spread to children, families and communities
questions.memo: Investing in women ripples outward — better-fed, better-schooled children and stronger local economies — so the returns multiply across society.

GEO.G11.T3.DEV.A5.title: The role of development aid
GEO.G11.T3.DEV.A5.description: Development aid and co-operation, types of aid (technical, conditional, humanitarian), and the positive and negative impacts of aid.
GEO.G11.T3.DEV.A5.recovery_strategy: TECHNICAL aid = skills/expertise; CONDITIONAL aid = strings attached; HUMANITARIAN aid = emergency relief. Aid can help (infrastructure, emergencies) BUT may create dependency, debt or serve the donor's interests — weigh both sides.

questions.question: Development aid is _______.
options: help (money, goods or skills) given to support a country's development
questions.expected: help (money, goods or skills) given to support a country's development
questions.memo: Aid is assistance — financial, material or technical — given by governments or organisations to support development or relief.

questions.question: Emergency relief after a disaster (food, water, medicine, shelter) is _______ aid.
questions.memo: Humanitarian aid is short-term emergency help to save lives after disasters such as floods, droughts or conflict.

questions.question: Aid given as skills, training and expertise is _______ aid.
questions.memo: Technical aid provides know-how — engineers, teachers, training — to build a country's own long-term capacity.

questions.question: Aid that comes with conditions the receiver must meet is _______ aid.
questions.memo: Conditional (tied) aid requires the receiver to do certain things — e.g. buy from the donor or adopt set policies — which can limit its benefit.

questions.question: A learner calls emergency disaster relief 'conditional aid'. Correct them.
options: Emergency relief is HUMANITARIAN aid; conditional aid has strings attached
It is not aid at all
questions.expected: Emergency relief is HUMANITARIAN aid; conditional aid has strings attached
questions.memo: Saving lives after a disaster is humanitarian aid. Conditional aid is defined by its attached requirements, not by emergencies.

questions.question: Match each aid type to an example.
questions.memo: 1 Humanitarian → C food and shelter after a flood. 2 Technical → A engineers training local staff. 3 Conditional → B a loan requiring set policy changes. (Prompt: 1=Humanitarian, 2=Technical, 3=Conditional; A=engineers training staff, B=loan with policy conditions, C=flood relief.)

questions.question: A POSITIVE impact of well-managed aid is that it can _______.
options: fund infrastructure, healthcare and education and save lives in emergencies
questions.expected: fund infrastructure, healthcare and education and save lives in emergencies
questions.memo: Effective aid builds roads, schools and clinics, supplies expertise and provides life-saving relief — real development gains when well used.

questions.question: A NEGATIVE impact of aid can be that it _______.
options: creates dependency or debt and may serve the donor's interests
questions.expected: creates dependency or debt and may serve the donor's interests
questions.memo: Poorly designed aid can foster dependence, add to debt, undercut local producers or mainly benefit the donor — which is why it is critically examined.

questions.question: Sort each as a POTENTIAL BENEFIT or POTENTIAL PROBLEM of aid.

items.text: New schools, clinics and water supplies
Aid tied to buying the donor's products
Skills and training that build local capacity
Rising debt from aid given as loans

questions.memo: Aid can relieve disasters, build services and skills (benefits) but also cause dependency, tied spending and debt (problems) — it must be judged case by case.

questions.question: Development co-operation differs from one-off charity because it focuses on _______.
options: long-term partnership and building a country's own capacity
questions.expected: long-term partnership and building a country's own capacity
questions.memo: Co-operation works WITH partner countries over time to build lasting capacity, rather than just handing over short-term relief.

questions.question: Why can long-term food aid sometimes HARM local farmers?
options: Free imported food can undercut local prices, discouraging local production
It raises local food prices too high
It has no effect on farming
questions.expected: Free imported food can undercut local prices, discouraging local production
questions.memo: If free or cheap food floods a market for too long, local farmers cannot compete and may stop producing — a hidden cost of poorly-timed aid.

questions.question: Aid that builds local skills (technical aid) is valued because it _______.
options: helps a country become self-reliant over time
questions.expected: helps a country become self-reliant over time
questions.memo: Teaching skills and transferring technology leaves lasting capacity, reducing the need for future aid — 'teach to fish' rather than 'give a fish'.

questions.question: True or false: emergency humanitarian aid is mainly short-term, while development aid aims at long-term improvement.
questions.memo: Humanitarian aid responds to immediate crises; development aid invests in lasting infrastructure, services and capacity.

questions.question: Aid given by one government directly to another is called _______ aid.
questions.memo: Bilateral aid flows country-to-country; multilateral aid is channelled through international bodies like the UN or World Bank.

questions.question: Why might a donor attach CONDITIONS to aid?
options: To pursue its own economic or political interests, or to require certain reforms
Only to help the receiver with no self-interest
To give the money away randomly
questions.expected: To pursue its own economic or political interests, or to require certain reforms
questions.memo: Conditions may push reforms OR serve the donor (e.g. buying donor goods). Tied aid is a key reason aid must be examined critically.

questions.question: True or false: aid can be a positive force, a negative one, or both — so it should be judged case by case.
questions.memo: There is no single verdict on aid; outcomes depend on the type, design, conditions and how well it is managed.

questions.question: NGOs (non-governmental organisations) often deliver aid by _______.
questions.memo: NGOs (e.g. charities) deliver aid and development work directly at community level, often reaching people governments cannot.

questions.question: How can aid be made MORE effective?
options: Target real local needs, involve communities, build capacity and reduce harmful conditions
Give it with no plan and the most conditions possible
questions.expected: Target real local needs, involve communities, build capacity and reduce harmful conditions
questions.memo: Aid works best when it fits local needs, builds lasting skills, involves communities and avoids tying that mainly benefits the donor.

questions.question: A country becomes reliant on yearly aid to pay for basic services. This illustrates the risk of _______.
questions.memo: Aid dependency is when a country cannot fund essentials without continued aid — a key argument for capacity-building over endless hand-outs.

questions.question: Why might the SAME aid project be judged a success by some and a failure by others?
options: People weigh its benefits (relief, infrastructure) against its costs (dependency, debt, conditions) differently
Aid always has only one outcome
Aid has no effects to judge
questions.expected: People weigh its benefits (relief, infrastructure) against its costs (dependency, debt, conditions) differently
questions.memo: Because aid brings both gains and drawbacks, judgements depend on which effects matter most to whom — hence the need for balanced case studies.

GEO.G11.T4.RES.A1.title: Using resources
GEO.G11.T4.RES.A1.description: Resources and economic development, exploitation and depletion, and sustainability.
GEO.G11.T4.RES.A1.recovery_strategy: RENEWABLE resources replenish (sun, wind, water, forests if managed); NON-RENEWABLE run out (coal, oil, minerals). Sustainable use = meeting today's needs WITHOUT preventing future generations from meeting theirs — use wisely, not not at all.

questions.question: A renewable resource is one that _______.
options: can replenish itself naturally over a short time
can never be replaced once used
questions.expected: can replenish itself naturally over a short time
questions.memo: Renewable resources (sun, wind, water, forests, fish) replenish if not over-used; non-renewables (coal, oil, minerals) take millions of years to form.

questions.question: Which is a NON-renewable resource?
questions.memo: Coal, oil, gas and minerals are finite and non-renewable. Sun, wind and water are renewable.

questions.question: Sort each resource as RENEWABLE or NON-RENEWABLE.
questions.memo: Renewable: sun, wind, managed forests. Non-renewable: coal, oil, minerals (gold). Managed forests count as renewable only if replanted faster than used.

questions.question: A learner calls coal a renewable resource. Correct them.
options: Coal is NON-renewable — it forms over millions of years and runs out
Coal is a type of sunlight
questions.expected: Coal is NON-renewable — it forms over millions of years and runs out
questions.memo: Coal forms over geological time and cannot be replaced on a human timescale — it is non-renewable.

questions.question: Resources are linked to economic development because they _______.
options: provide raw materials, energy and income for industry and growth
questions.expected: provide raw materials, energy and income for industry and growth
questions.memo: Resources fuel industry, generate export income and create jobs — a major driver of economic development when used well.

questions.question: The over-use of a resource faster than it can be replaced is called _______.
questions.memo: Depletion is exhausting a resource through over-exploitation; sustainable use avoids this by keeping use within renewal limits.

questions.question: Sustainable use of resources means _______.
options: meeting present needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs
using everything as fast as possible
only the rich may use resources
questions.expected: meeting present needs without harming future generations' ability to meet theirs
questions.memo: Sustainability balances use and conservation so resources remain available for the future — not unlimited use, and not zero use.

questions.question: A learner thinks sustainability means using NO resources at all. Correct them.
options: It means using resources WISELY within their renewal limits, not abstaining entirely
It means using everything at once
questions.expected: It means using resources WISELY within their renewal limits, not abstaining entirely
questions.memo: Sustainable use is careful, balanced use — not total abstinence. We can use resources as long as we do not exhaust them.

questions.question: Recycling supports sustainability mainly by _______.
options: reducing the need to extract new raw materials
questions.expected: reducing the need to extract new raw materials
questions.memo: Recycling reuses materials, cutting demand for new extraction and reducing waste and energy use — a key sustainability tool.

questions.question: Even a renewable resource like a forest can be depleted if it is _______.
options: harvested faster than it can regrow
questions.expected: harvested faster than it can regrow
questions.memo: Renewables are only sustainable within limits: over-cutting forests or over-fishing exhausts them just like a non-renewable.

questions.question: True or false: a country rich in resources can still fail to develop if it manages them poorly (the 'resource curse').
questions.memo: The 'resource curse' describes resource-rich countries that stay poor due to corruption, conflict, over-dependence or environmental damage — management matters.

questions.question: Which is an example of EXPLOITATION of a resource?
questions.memo: Exploitation means extracting and using a resource (mining, logging, drilling) — beneficial economically but needing careful management.

questions.question: Why is reducing consumption ('reduce, reuse, recycle' — reduce first) the most powerful step?
options: Using less in the first place saves the most resources and energy
questions.expected: Using less in the first place saves the most resources and energy
questions.memo: Cutting demand at source avoids extraction, processing and waste altogether — more effective than dealing with waste after the fact.

questions.question: Match each term to its meaning.
questions.memo: 1 Renewable → C replenishes naturally. 2 Non-renewable → A finite, runs out. 3 Sustainable use → B use within renewal limits. (Prompt: 1=Renewable, 2=Non-renewable, 3=Sustainable use; A=finite/runs out, B=use within limits, C=replenishes naturally.)

questions.question: True or false: as resources become scarcer, their price usually rises, encouraging conservation and alternatives.
questions.memo: Scarcity raises prices, which can spur efficiency, recycling and a switch to alternatives — though it can also raise costs for the poor.

questions.question: Which action moves a society towards SUSTAINABLE resource use?
options: Shifting to renewable energy and recycling materials
Burning resources as fast as possible
questions.expected: Shifting to renewable energy and recycling materials
questions.memo: Renewables, efficiency, recycling and conservation reduce pressure on finite resources and lower environmental harm.

questions.question: Why is water sometimes called a renewable resource that can still become scarce?
options: It is recycled naturally, but pollution and over-use can outstrip clean supply locally
There is unlimited clean water everywhere
questions.expected: It is recycled naturally, but pollution and over-use can outstrip clean supply locally
questions.memo: The water cycle renews water, yet local demand, pollution and uneven distribution can still cause real scarcity — renewable does not mean unlimited.

questions.question: True or false: over-dependence on a single non-renewable resource is risky because it will eventually run out or fall in price.
questions.memo: Relying on one finite, price-volatile resource is risky; diversifying the economy builds resilience for when it runs low or prices crash.

questions.question: How does sustainable resource use link economic, social and environmental goals?
options: It keeps resources available for jobs and income (economic), wellbeing (social) and a healthy planet (environmental)
questions.expected: It keeps resources available for jobs and income (economic), wellbeing (social) and a healthy planet (environmental)
questions.memo: Sustainable use protects the resource base that the economy, society and environment all depend on — the three pillars of sustainability.

questions.question: A fishing community catches fish only at the rate the population can replace each year. Why is this sustainable?
options: The fish stock can renew itself, so it lasts indefinitely
The fish will run out quickly
questions.expected: The fish stock can renew itself, so it lasts indefinitely
questions.memo: Catching within the renewal rate keeps the stock stable for the future — the essence of sustainable use of a renewable resource.

GEO.G11.T4.RES.A2.title: Soil and soil erosion
GEO.G11.T4.RES.A2.description: Soil formation, soil as a resource, causes of erosion, evidence in SA, effects, and prevention/control strategies.
GEO.G11.T4.RES.A2.recovery_strategy: Soil forms slowly from weathered rock + organic matter — precious and slow to replace. Erosion is sped by overgrazing, ploughing, deforestation and bare soil. Types: SHEET (thin layer), RILL (small channels), GULLY/DONGA (deep). Control with contour ploughing, terracing, cover crops, managed grazing.

questions.question: Soil is formed mainly from _______ plus decayed organic matter.
questions.memo: Soil develops over long periods from weathered rock (the parent material) mixed with humus (decayed plants and animals).

questions.question: Soil is described as a precious resource because it _______.
options: forms very slowly and is essential for growing food
questions.expected: forms very slowly and is essential for growing food
questions.memo: It can take hundreds of years to form a few centimetres of fertile topsoil, yet it underpins almost all food production — so it must be protected.

questions.question: Soil erosion is the _______ of soil by water and wind.
questions.memo: Erosion strips away soil, especially fertile topsoil, by water and wind — faster when the soil is bare and unprotected.

questions.question: Which is a HUMAN cause of soil erosion?
questions.memo: Overgrazing, over-cultivation, deforestation and ploughing up and down slopes expose and loosen soil, greatly speeding erosion.

questions.question: Erosion that removes a thin, even layer of topsoil across a slope is _______ erosion.
questions.memo: Sheet erosion peels off a thin surface layer fairly evenly; it is hard to notice until much fertile topsoil is lost.

questions.question: Deep channels cut into the land by running water (called dongas in South Africa) are _______ erosion.
questions.memo: Gully (donga) erosion carves deep, steep-sided channels — the most dramatic and damaging visible form of water erosion.

questions.question: Order the water-erosion types from LEAST to MOST severe.
questions.memo: Erosion often worsens in stages: sheet → rill (small channels) → gully (deep dongas) as water concentrates and cuts deeper.

questions.question: Sort each as a CAUSE or a CONTROL of soil erosion.

items.text: Ploughing up and down a steep slope

questions.memo: Causes expose/loosen soil (overgrazing, slope ploughing, bare ground); controls protect it (contour ploughing, terracing, cover crops, windbreaks).

questions.question: Look at the diagram of erosion features. Which label shows gully (donga) erosion?
options: A — the thin even surface loss
questions.memo: A sheet (thin layer), B rill (small channels), C gully/donga (deep channel). The donga is the deep, dramatic cut.

questions.question: Ploughing ACROSS a slope (along the contours) rather than up and down it helps because it _______.
options: slows water runoff and traps soil
questions.expected: slows water runoff and traps soil
questions.memo: Contour ploughing creates ridges across the slope that slow runoff and hold soil and water — a simple, effective control.

questions.question: Why does removing vegetation make soil erosion worse?
options: Bare soil has no roots to bind it or leaves to shield it from rain and wind
Plants have no effect on soil
questions.expected: Bare soil has no roots to bind it or leaves to shield it from rain and wind
questions.memo: Plant cover protects soil: leaves break the rain's impact and roots hold the soil. Strip it away and rain and wind carry the soil off.

questions.question: An EFFECT of severe soil erosion on farming is _______.
options: loss of fertile topsoil and lower crop yields
more water in rivers being cleaner
questions.expected: loss of fertile topsoil and lower crop yields
questions.memo: Erosion strips the nutrient-rich topsoil, reducing fertility and yields, and can ruin land for farming — threatening food security.

questions.question: Eroded soil washed into rivers and dams causes _______.
options: siltation, reducing water storage and quality
questions.expected: siltation, reducing water storage and quality
questions.memo: Sediment from erosion silts up rivers and dams, cutting their capacity, harming aquatic life and raising water-treatment costs.

questions.question: Planting rows of trees as windbreaks reduces erosion by _______.
options: slowing the wind near the ground so it cannot lift the soil
questions.expected: slowing the wind near the ground so it cannot lift the soil
questions.memo: Windbreaks (shelterbelts) cut wind speed, preventing the wind from picking up and blowing away dry topsoil.

questions.question: True or false: soil that takes centuries to form can be lost in a few seasons of poor land management.
questions.memo: Erosion can strip in a few years what took centuries to build — a key reason soil conservation is urgent.

questions.question: Crop rotation and leaving crop residues on fields help soil by _______.
options: maintaining fertility and protecting the surface
questions.expected: maintaining fertility and protecting the surface
questions.memo: Rotating crops restores nutrients and residues cover and feed the soil, keeping it fertile and shielded from erosion.

questions.question: Why is gully (donga) erosion especially hard to fix?
options: Deep channels concentrate fast water and keep cutting back, needing major rehabilitation
They are only a thin surface loss
questions.expected: Deep channels concentrate fast water and keep cutting back, needing major rehabilitation
questions.memo: Once a donga forms, concentrated runoff deepens and extends it (headward erosion); fixing it needs check dams, replanting and reshaping — costly work.

questions.question: True or false: managing the number of grazing animals on the land helps prevent overgrazing and erosion.
questions.memo: Keeping stock within the land's carrying capacity and rotating grazing lets vegetation recover, protecting the soil.

questions.question: A farmer ploughs straight up and down a steep slope and leaves it bare over winter. Predict the result and a fix.
options: Heavy erosion is likely; fix with contour ploughing, cover crops and terracing
The soil will improve on its own
questions.expected: Heavy erosion is likely; fix with contour ploughing, cover crops and terracing
questions.memo: Up-and-down furrows channel water downhill and bare soil is unprotected — a recipe for erosion. Contour ploughing, cover crops and terraces would prevent it.

questions.question: Why is soil conservation a national priority for a country like South Africa?
options: Limited fertile soil and water make protecting topsoil vital for long-term food security
Food can be made without soil
questions.expected: Limited fertile soil and water make protecting topsoil vital for long-term food security
questions.memo: With scarce arable land and water, losing topsoil threatens food production and rural livelihoods — so conservation is a national concern.

GEO.G11.T4.RES.A3.title: Conventional energy sources
GEO.G11.T4.RES.A3.description: Thermal/hydro/nuclear in SA, coal-based generation and its impacts, nuclear case study, and SA's conventional energy potential.
GEO.G11.T4.RES.A3.recovery_strategy: South Africa relies heavily on COAL-fired thermal power (cheap, abundant, but high CO₂, air pollution, acid rain, ash). Nuclear (Koeberg) gives steady low-carbon power but raises waste/safety concerns. Conventional sources are reliable but non-renewable and polluting.

questions.question: Most of South Africa's electricity is generated from _______.
questions.memo: Coal-fired thermal power stations (mostly in Mpumalanga) supply the large majority of South Africa's electricity.

questions.question: In a coal-fired (thermal) power station, coal is burned to _______.
options: heat water into steam that turns turbines to generate electricity
questions.expected: heat water into steam that turns turbines to generate electricity
questions.memo: Burning coal boils water to high-pressure steam, which spins turbines connected to generators — the basic thermal process.

questions.question: A learner says most SA electricity comes from nuclear power. Correct them.
options: Most comes from COAL; nuclear (Koeberg) supplies only a small share
questions.expected: Most comes from COAL; nuclear (Koeberg) supplies only a small share
questions.memo: Coal dominates SA's electricity; Koeberg is the only nuclear station and supplies a modest portion, mainly to the Western Cape.

questions.question: Which is an environmental impact of burning coal for electricity?
options: Air pollution, CO₂ emissions and acid rain
questions.expected: Air pollution, CO₂ emissions and acid rain
questions.memo: Coal burning releases CO₂ (warming), sulphur and nitrogen oxides (acid rain), particulates (smog) and ash — major environmental costs.

questions.question: Acid rain is caused mainly by _______ released when coal is burned.
questions.memo: Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides combine with water in the air to form acids that fall as acid rain, harming forests, soils and water.

questions.question: Hydro-electric power generates electricity using the energy of _______.
questions.memo: Hydropower uses moving water (often from a dam) to spin turbines — a renewable conventional source, though SA has limited suitable rivers.

questions.question: Nuclear power stations generate electricity by _______.
options: splitting atoms (fission) to release heat that makes steam
questions.expected: splitting atoms (fission) to release heat that makes steam
questions.memo: Nuclear fission releases large amounts of heat with no CO₂ at the point of generation; the heat raises steam to drive turbines.

questions.question: South Africa's only nuclear power station is _______.
questions.memo: Koeberg, near Cape Town, is South Africa's only nuclear station. Medupi and Kusile are large coal stations; Gariep is a hydro dam.

questions.question: Sort each as an ADVANTAGE or DISADVANTAGE of nuclear power.

items.text: Small amount of fuel for lots of energy

questions.memo: Nuclear: low-carbon, reliable, energy-dense (advantages) but waste, accident risk and high cost (disadvantages).

questions.question: Why is South Africa heavily dependent on coal despite its pollution?
options: It has large, cheap coal reserves and existing coal power infrastructure
It has no coal at all
questions.expected: It has large, cheap coal reserves and existing coal power infrastructure
questions.memo: Abundant, low-cost coal and decades of investment in coal stations make it the backbone of SA's grid — hard and costly to replace quickly.

questions.question: The solid waste left after burning coal is _______.
questions.memo: Coal burning leaves large volumes of ash that must be stored in dumps, posing dust and water-pollution problems.

questions.question: True or false: coal, oil and natural gas are all non-renewable 'fossil fuels'.
questions.memo: Fossil fuels formed from ancient organisms over millions of years; they are finite (non-renewable) and release CO₂ when burned.

questions.question: Coal mining itself (before burning) can damage the environment through _______.
options: land disturbance, dust and acid mine drainage
questions.expected: land disturbance, dust and acid mine drainage
questions.memo: Mining scars the land, creates dust and can produce acid mine drainage that pollutes rivers and groundwater — impacts adding to those of burning.

questions.question: An advantage of conventional (coal/nuclear) power over many renewables is that it _______.
options: provides steady, reliable base-load power day and night
questions.expected: provides steady, reliable base-load power day and night
questions.memo: Coal and nuclear run continuously, supplying dependable base-load power, whereas solar and wind vary with weather and time of day.

questions.question:
The table shows SA's electricity mix. What does it indicate?

| Source | Share (%) |
|------|------|
| Coal | 80 |
| Nuclear | 5 |
| Hydro/pumped | 5 |
| Renewables | 10 |
options: The grid is dominated by coal, with a small but growing renewable share
questions.expected: The grid is dominated by coal, with a small but growing renewable share
questions.memo: Coal at ~80% dominates; nuclear, hydro and renewables make up the rest — the renewable share is rising but still small.

questions.question: Why is heavy reliance on coal a long-term concern for South Africa?
options: Coal is finite and polluting, and global pressure to cut carbon is rising
Coal lasts forever and is clean
questions.expected: Coal is finite and polluting, and global pressure to cut carbon is rising
questions.memo: Finite reserves, health and climate impacts, and a global shift away from carbon mean SA must gradually diversify its energy mix.

questions.question: True or false: nuclear power produces very little CO₂ while generating, but creates long-lived radioactive waste.
questions.memo: Nuclear's big advantage is low operating carbon; its big challenge is safely storing radioactive waste for thousands of years.

questions.question: Hydro-electric power is considered cleaner than coal because it _______.
options: produces electricity without burning fuel or emitting CO₂
questions.expected: produces electricity without burning fuel or emitting CO₂
questions.memo: Hydropower uses moving water and emits virtually no CO₂ in operation — though dams can have their own social and ecological impacts.

questions.question: Why does South Africa have limited large-scale hydro-electric potential?
options: It is a dry country with few large, reliable, fast-flowing rivers
It has too many huge rivers
It has no rivers at all
questions.expected: It is a dry country with few large, reliable, fast-flowing rivers
questions.memo: Low, variable rainfall and few big rivers limit hydro potential, so SA imports some hydropower (e.g. from Cahora Bassa) and relies on coal.

questions.question: Weighing it up, why is conventional energy described as reliable but problematic?
options: Coal and nuclear give steady power but bring pollution, waste, finite fuel or accident risks
They are perfect with no drawbacks
They have no role in SA
questions.expected: Coal and nuclear give steady power but bring pollution, waste, finite fuel or accident risks
questions.memo: Conventional sources deliver dependable base-load power, but their environmental, health, waste and depletion costs are pushing a shift towards renewables.

GEO.G11.T4.RES.A4.title: Non-conventional energy sources
GEO.G11.T4.RES.A4.description: Solar and wind energy in SA and the world, the future of renewables in SA, and their effects on the economy and environment.
GEO.G11.T4.RES.A4.recovery_strategy: SA has excellent SOLAR (sunny interior) and WIND (coastal) potential. Renewables are clean and inexhaustible BUT can be intermittent (no sun at night, variable wind), need storage, and have upfront costs. They cut emissions and create new industries and jobs.

questions.question: Non-conventional (renewable) energy includes _______.
questions.memo: Non-conventional sources are renewables like solar, wind, hydro, biomass, geothermal and tidal — inexhaustible and low-carbon.

questions.question: Solar panels (photovoltaic cells) generate electricity directly from _______.
questions.memo: Photovoltaic (PV) cells convert sunlight straight into electricity; solar can also heat water (solar thermal).

questions.question: South Africa has strong potential for SOLAR energy mainly because _______.
options: its interior has many hours of strong sunshine
questions.expected: its interior has many hours of strong sunshine
questions.memo: The sunny, dry interior (e.g. Northern Cape) has some of the world's best solar resources, ideal for solar farms.

questions.question: Wind farms are best located where there is _______.
options: strong, steady wind, often along coasts or ridges
questions.expected: strong, steady wind, often along coasts or ridges
questions.memo: Reliable strong wind — common along the Western and Eastern Cape coasts — turns turbine blades to generate electricity.

questions.question: A learner says South Africa has poor solar resources. Correct them.
options: SA actually has EXCELLENT solar resources, among the best in the world
questions.expected: SA actually has EXCELLENT solar resources, among the best in the world
questions.memo: South Africa's high solar radiation makes it ideal for solar power — the opposite of the learner's claim.

questions.question: A key ADVANTAGE of solar and wind energy is that they _______.
options: are clean, renewable and produce no CO₂ while generating
questions.expected: are clean, renewable and produce no CO₂ while generating
questions.memo: Once built, solar and wind generate electricity without burning fuel or emitting CO₂ — cutting pollution and climate impact.

questions.question: A key DISADVANTAGE of solar and wind power is that they are _______.
options: intermittent (vary with weather and time of day)
questions.expected: intermittent (vary with weather and time of day)
questions.memo: Solar stops at night and wind varies, so output is intermittent; this is why storage (batteries) and backup are important.

questions.question: A learner says solar power works equally well at night. Correct them.
options: Solar needs sunlight, so it does not generate at night without stored energy
questions.expected: Solar needs sunlight, so it does not generate at night without stored energy
questions.memo: No sun means no solar generation; night-time supply needs batteries or other backup — a real limitation to plan for.

questions.question: Sort each as an ADVANTAGE or DISADVANTAGE of renewable energy.

items.text: No fuel cost and no CO₂ when generating
Needs large areas of land or sea

questions.memo: Advantages: clean, free fuel, inexhaustible, new jobs. Disadvantages: intermittent, high setup cost, land/visual impact.

questions.question: Why might wider use of renewables BENEFIT South Africa's economy?
options: It creates new industries and jobs and reduces reliance on imported fuel and coal
questions.expected: It creates new industries and jobs and reduces reliance on imported fuel and coal
questions.memo: A renewables sector brings manufacturing, installation and maintenance jobs, energy security and export potential, while cutting emissions.

questions.question: Storing renewable electricity for when the sun isn't shining or the wind isn't blowing usually needs _______.
questions.memo: Energy storage (batteries, pumped-hydro) saves surplus renewable power for later, smoothing out intermittency.

questions.question: True or false: renewable energy sources will not run out in the way coal and oil eventually will.
questions.memo: Sun and wind are effectively inexhaustible, unlike finite fossil fuels — a core advantage of renewables.

questions.question: A possible ENVIRONMENTAL drawback of large wind or solar farms is _______.
options: land use, visual impact and effects on birds/habitats
questions.expected: land use, visual impact and effects on birds/habitats
questions.memo: Renewables are low-carbon but large farms use land, change landscapes and can affect wildlife — impacts to manage through good siting.

questions.question: Biomass energy comes from _______.
options: burning or processing plant and animal material
questions.expected: burning or processing plant and animal material
questions.memo: Biomass (wood, crop waste, biogas from manure) is a renewable source if the material is regrown — widely used for rural cooking and heating.

questions.question: Why does the upfront COST of renewables matter for a developing country?
options: Building solar/wind farms needs large initial investment, even though running costs are low
They have high fuel costs forever
questions.expected: Building solar/wind farms needs large initial investment, even though running costs are low
questions.memo: High capital cost can be a barrier, even though there are no fuel costs afterwards — financing and partnerships help overcome it.

questions.question: True or false: combining different renewables (e.g. solar by day, wind at night) plus storage can make supply more reliable.
questions.memo: Mixing complementary sources and adding storage smooths out the gaps, making an intermittent supply more dependable.

questions.question: Rooftop solar at homes and businesses helps the national grid by _______.
options: reducing demand on power stations, especially during the day
questions.expected: reducing demand on power stations, especially during the day
questions.memo: Distributed rooftop solar cuts daytime demand on the central grid and can feed surplus back in — easing pressure and load-shedding.

questions.question: The future of non-conventional energy in South Africa is likely to involve _______.
options: a growing share of solar and wind in the energy mix
questions.expected: a growing share of solar and wind in the energy mix
questions.memo: SA's plans and projects point to steadily expanding solar and wind to diversify supply, cut emissions and create jobs.

questions.question: True or false: shifting towards renewables can improve South Africa's energy security by reducing reliance on a single fuel.
questions.memo: A diverse mix of solar, wind and others reduces dependence on coal and the risks of any one source failing or becoming costly.

questions.question: Weighing it up, why are renewables described as the future despite their drawbacks?
options: They are clean, inexhaustible and increasingly cheap, and intermittency can be managed with storage and a mix
They can never be made reliable
questions.expected: They are clean, inexhaustible and increasingly cheap, and intermittency can be managed with storage and a mix
questions.memo: Falling costs, zero fuel, low emissions and improving storage outweigh the manageable challenge of intermittency — pointing to a renewable future.

GEO.G11.T4.RES.A5.title: Energy management in South Africa
GEO.G11.T4.RES.A5.description: SA's changing energy needs and energy management towards greener economies — the roles of government, business and individuals.
GEO.G11.T4.RES.A5.recovery_strategy: Managing energy is a SHARED responsibility: governments (policy, renewables, grid), businesses (efficient processes, cleaner tech) and individuals (saving electricity, efficient appliances). Energy EFFICIENCY = getting the same result using LESS energy.

questions.question: Energy management means using energy _______.
options: efficiently and sustainably to meet needs while reducing waste and harm
questions.expected: efficiently and sustainably to meet needs while reducing waste and harm
questions.memo: Energy management balances reliable supply with efficiency, conservation and a shift to cleaner sources.

questions.question: Energy EFFICIENCY means _______.
options: getting the same result using less energy
using more energy for the same task
questions.expected: getting the same result using less energy
questions.memo: Efficiency = the same service (light, heat, transport) for less energy — e.g. LED bulbs that give the same light using far less power.

questions.question: A learner thinks energy efficiency means switching everything off and going without. Correct them.
options: Efficiency means the SAME service for LESS energy, not doing without
questions.expected: Efficiency means the SAME service for LESS energy, not doing without
questions.memo: Efficiency keeps the benefit (light, heating) while cutting the energy needed — different from simply going without.

questions.question: Which is an INDIVIDUAL action that saves energy?
options: Switching off lights and using energy-efficient appliances
Using the oldest, least efficient devices
questions.expected: Switching off lights and using energy-efficient appliances
questions.memo: Households save energy by switching off unused devices, using LED bulbs and efficient appliances, insulating, and using solar water heaters.

questions.question: Sort each energy-management action by who is mainly responsible.

items.text: Upgrading factory machines to use less power
Switching off lights and unplugging chargers
Investing in a national power grid
Using a solar geyser at home

questions.memo: Government sets policy and infrastructure; business makes operations efficient and cleaner; individuals save energy at home. All three are needed.

questions.question: A learner says only the government is responsible for energy management. Correct them.
options: It is a SHARED responsibility of government, business AND individuals
questions.expected: It is a SHARED responsibility of government, business AND individuals
questions.memo: Energy management works best when all three act: policy and grid (government), efficient operations (business) and daily saving (individuals).

questions.question: South Africa's energy needs have been CHANGING because of _______.
options: a growing population and economy plus a shift towards cleaner energy
a shrinking population needing no power
questions.expected: a growing population and economy plus a shift towards cleaner energy
questions.memo: Rising demand from more people and economic growth, alongside pressure to cut carbon, is reshaping SA's energy planning.

questions.question: A 'greener economy' aims to grow while _______.
options: reducing pollution and using resources more sustainably
questions.expected: reducing pollution and using resources more sustainably
questions.memo: A green economy delivers growth and jobs while cutting emissions, saving energy and using renewable resources — a sustainable path.

questions.question: How can businesses contribute to energy management?
options: Using efficient machines, cleaner technology and on-site renewables
Wasting as much power as possible
questions.expected: Using efficient machines, cleaner technology and on-site renewables
questions.memo: Industry uses a lot of energy, so efficiency upgrades, cleaner processes and rooftop solar cut both costs and emissions significantly.

questions.question: 'Load-shedding' (planned power cuts) happens when _______.
options: electricity demand exceeds the available supply
there is too much spare electricity
questions.expected: electricity demand exceeds the available supply
questions.memo: When demand outstrips supply, utilities cut power in rotation to protect the grid — a strong reason for both new capacity and demand management.

questions.question: Reducing demand at peak times (e.g. evening) helps the grid by _______.
options: lowering the maximum load power stations must meet
questions.expected: lowering the maximum load power stations must meet
questions.memo: Shifting or cutting peak-time use flattens the demand curve, easing strain on power stations and reducing the need for load-shedding.

questions.question: True or false: energy management includes BOTH increasing clean supply and reducing wasteful demand.
questions.memo: Two sides of the same coin: build cleaner supply (renewables) AND cut waste through efficiency and conservation.

questions.question: A solar water heater (geyser) saves a household energy because it _______.
options: uses free sunlight instead of electricity to heat water
uses more electricity than a normal geyser
questions.expected: uses free sunlight instead of electricity to heat water
questions.memo: Water heating is a big household electricity user; solar geysers cut that demand sharply using free solar energy.

questions.question: Government can encourage energy saving by _______.
options: incentives, efficiency standards and public-awareness campaigns
questions.expected: incentives, efficiency standards and public-awareness campaigns
questions.memo: Policy tools — rebates for solar, minimum efficiency standards, labelling and education — steer households and business towards saving energy.

questions.question: Why is reducing energy demand sometimes called the 'cheapest power station'?
options: Saving energy avoids the need to build costly new capacity
Saving energy costs more than a new station
questions.expected: Saving energy avoids the need to build costly new capacity
questions.memo: Every unit saved is a unit you don't have to generate — efficiency is usually far cheaper and faster than building new power stations.

questions.question: True or false: switching to more renewable energy supports both energy security and a greener economy.
questions.memo: Renewables diversify supply (security) and cut emissions and create green jobs (greener economy) — serving both goals at once.

questions.question: A sustainable lifestyle in energy terms means _______.
options: using energy carefully and choosing efficient, cleaner options
using as much energy as possible
questions.expected: using energy carefully and choosing efficient, cleaner options
questions.memo: Sustainable living means mindful energy use — efficient appliances, less waste, public transport and renewable choices where possible.

questions.question: Match each actor to a typical energy-management action.
questions.memo: 1 Government → B set policy and build the grid. 2 Business → C make operations efficient and cleaner. 3 Individual → A save power and use efficient appliances. (Prompt: 1=Government, 2=Business, 3=Individual; A=save power at home, B=policy and grid, C=efficient operations.)

questions.question: Why does managing energy well matter for South Africa's economy AND environment?
options: It keeps power reliable and affordable while cutting pollution and emissions
questions.expected: It keeps power reliable and affordable while cutting pollution and emissions
questions.memo: Reliable, efficient, cleaner energy supports industry and jobs (economy) and reduces pollution and climate impact (environment) together.

questions.question: A town cuts its peak electricity use through efficient lighting, solar geysers and awareness. Why is this good energy management?
options: It reduces demand and emissions and eases pressure on the grid without losing services
questions.expected: It reduces demand and emissions and eases pressure on the grid without losing services
questions.memo: Combining efficiency, renewables and behaviour change lowers demand and emissions while keeping services running — model energy management.

GEO.G12.MAP.A1.title: Synoptic & topographic map techniques
GEO.G12.MAP.A1.description: Synoptic and satellite data, grid referencing, magnetic declination, gradient, cross-sections and intervisibility — from given values.
GEO.G12.MAP.A1.recovery_strategy: Magnetic bearing = true bearing + magnetic declination (western declination). A compass points to MAGNETIC north, which drifts. Read synoptic maps: pressure cells → isobar spacing (wind) → station data → overall weather.

questions.question: On a topographic map, a six-figure grid reference gives a position accurate to about _______.
questions.memo: A four-figure reference locates a 1 km grid square; a six-figure reference narrows it to about 100 m within that square.

questions.question: A compass needle points towards _______ north.
questions.memo: A compass points to MAGNETIC north (the magnetic pole), which differs from true (geographic) north by the magnetic declination.

questions.question: The angle between true north and magnetic north is the magnetic _______.
questions.memo: Magnetic declination is the angular difference between true and magnetic north; it changes with place and slowly over time.

questions.question: A true bearing is 100° and the magnetic declination is 22° west. The magnetic bearing is _______. (Add a western declination.)
questions.memo: Magnetic bearing = true bearing + western declination = 100° + 22° = 122°.

questions.question: A learner subtracts a western magnetic declination instead of adding it. Why is this wrong?
options: For a western declination you ADD it to the true bearing to get the magnetic bearing
questions.expected: For a western declination you ADD it to the true bearing to get the magnetic bearing
questions.memo: In South Africa the declination is west, so magnetic bearing = true bearing + declination. Subtracting gives the wrong magnetic bearing.

questions.question: Magnetic declination in South Africa changes slightly each year, so it is given with an _______ rate of change.
questions.memo: Maps state the declination and its annual change so you can update it to the current year before converting bearings.

questions.question: On a synoptic map, an 'L' marks a _______.
questions.memo: L = low pressure (rising air, cloud and rain); H = high pressure (sinking air, clear and dry).

questions.question: Two points have a vertical interval of 200 m over a horizontal distance of 2 000 m. The gradient is _______.
Reading a synoptic map, you see tightly-packed isobars around a deep low. This means _______.
options: strong winds and stormy, wet weather
questions.expected: strong winds and stormy, wet weather
questions.memo: A deep low (rising air) brings cloud and rain; close isobars mean a steep pressure gradient and strong winds — stormy conditions.

questions.question: The order for systematically interpreting a synoptic map is _______.

items.text: Locate the high- and low-pressure cells
Check isobar spacing for wind strength
Read station models for local conditions

questions.memo: Big picture first (pressure cells), then wind (isobar spacing), then local detail (station models), then the overall weather summary.

questions.question: A satellite image shows a thick swirl of cloud over the ocean. On the synoptic map this most likely matches _______.
questions.memo: Dense, swirling cloud signals rising, moist air — a low-pressure system or cyclone — which the synoptic chart shows as a low with packed isobars.

questions.question: True north, magnetic north and grid north are three slightly different _______.
questions.memo: Maps reference three norths: TRUE (geographic pole), MAGNETIC (compass), and GRID (the map's grid lines). They differ by small angles.

questions.question: A line of equal pressure on a synoptic map is an _______.
questions.memo: Isobars join equal pressure (synoptic maps). Isotherms join equal temperature; isohyets join equal rainfall; contours join equal height.

questions.question: A road climbs from 100 m to 700 m over 12 km. The average gradient is _______.
Why must you update the magnetic declination to the current year before using it?
options: Declination changes a little each year, so an old value gives an inaccurate bearing
The map year does not matter
questions.expected: Declination changes a little each year, so an old value gives an inaccurate bearing
questions.memo: Because declination drifts annually, you apply the stated annual change for the years elapsed before converting between true and magnetic bearings.

questions.question: On a synoptic map of South Africa in winter, a cold front is approaching the Western Cape. What weather is expected?
options: Rain, wind and a drop in temperature as the front passes
questions.expected: Rain, wind and a drop in temperature as the front passes
questions.memo: Cold fronts in the winter-rainfall Western Cape bring bands of rain, gusty wind and cooler air behind them — read from the synoptic chart.

questions.question: A four-figure grid reference identifies _______.
options: an exact point to the metre
questions.memo: Four figures locate the 1 km square (eastings then northings); six figures pinpoint to ~100 m within it.

questions.question: Match each line/symbol to what it shows.
questions.memo: 1 Isobar → C equal pressure. 2 Contour → A equal height. 3 Isotherm → B equal temperature. (Prompt: 1=Isobar, 2=Contour, 3=Isotherm; A=equal height, B=equal temperature, C=equal pressure.)

questions.question: True or false: combining a synoptic map with a satellite image gives a fuller picture of current weather than either alone.
questions.memo: The synoptic map shows pressure, fronts and wind; the satellite image shows actual cloud — together they confirm and complete the weather picture.

questions.question: A hiker with a true bearing of 060° to a peak needs the compass (magnetic) bearing, given a 23° west declination. What should they set?
questions.memo: Western declination is ADDED to the true bearing: 060° + 23° = 083° on the compass.

GEO.G12.MAP.A2.title: GIS & photo interpretation
GEO.G12.MAP.A2.description: Vertical photos/orthophotos vs topographic maps, and GIS concepts (remote sensing, resolution, spatial/attribute data, raster/vector, buffering, querying).
GEO.G12.MAP.A2.recovery_strategy: GIS stores SPATIAL data (where) and ATTRIBUTE data (what) in layers. BUFFERING = a zone around a feature; QUERYING = asking the data to select features; INTEGRATION = combining layers. An orthophoto is corrected to true scale, so it can be measured like a map.

questions.question: In GIS, data about WHERE a feature is located is called _______ data.
questions.memo: Spatial data records location (coordinates/shape); attribute data records facts ABOUT the feature (name, population, type).

questions.question: In GIS, the table of facts about each feature (e.g. a town's name and population) is _______ data.
questions.memo: Attribute data describes the features; it is linked to the spatial data so you can map and query facts together.

questions.question: Creating a zone of a set distance around a feature (e.g. 1 km around a school) is called _______.
questions.memo: Buffering draws a zone of a chosen distance around points, lines or areas — used to find what lies within range of a feature.

questions.question: Asking the GIS to select all features that meet a condition (e.g. 'population over 10 000') is called _______.
questions.memo: A query interrogates the attribute data to pick out features matching set criteria — a core analytical power of GIS.

questions.question: A learner says buffering means deleting data. Correct them.
options: Buffering creates a zone around a feature; it does not delete anything
questions.expected: Buffering creates a zone around a feature; it does not delete anything
questions.memo: Buffering ADDS a distance zone around features (e.g. flood risk near a river). It is analysis, not deletion.

questions.question: Combining several GIS layers (e.g. roads, rivers, land use) to analyse them together is called data _______.
questions.memo: Data integration (overlay) stacks layers so relationships can be analysed — e.g. which houses lie in a flood zone near a road.

questions.question: Remote sensing means collecting data about the Earth _______.
options: from a distance, e.g. by satellite or aircraft
questions.expected: from a distance, e.g. by satellite or aircraft
questions.memo: Remote sensing gathers imagery and measurements without contact, feeding GIS with up-to-date data over large areas.

questions.question: An orthophoto map can be measured accurately because it is _______.
options: corrected to a uniform true scale
questions.expected: corrected to a uniform true scale
questions.memo: Orthophotos are geometrically corrected so scale is constant — unlike raw aerial photos, you can measure true distances on them.

questions.question: Sort each as SPATIAL data or ATTRIBUTE data.

items.text: The shape of a river drawn as a line
The river's name and length value
The crop grown on that farm

questions.memo: Spatial = location/shape (coordinates, lines, polygons). Attribute = facts about the feature (name, population, crop).

questions.question: Why is comparing an orthophoto with a topographic map of the same area useful?
options: The photo shows real detail; the map adds names, contours and symbols — together a fuller picture
Photos cannot be compared with maps
questions.expected: The photo shows real detail; the map adds names, contours and symbols — together a fuller picture
questions.memo: An orthophoto gives true-scale visual detail; the topographic map adds height, names and symbols. Side by side they complement each other.

questions.question: Match each GIS term to its meaning.
questions.memo: 1 Buffering → C zone around a feature. 2 Querying → D selecting by condition. 3 Integration → A overlaying layers. 4 Remote sensing → B sensing from a distance. (Prompt: 1=Buffering, 2=Querying, 3=Integration, 4=Remote sensing; A=overlay layers, B=sensing from distance, C=zone around feature, D=select by condition.)

questions.question: Data standardisation in GIS matters because it allows different datasets to _______.
questions.memo: Common formats and standards let agencies share and integrate data reliably; without them layers won't line up or combine correctly.

questions.question: Data security in GIS is important to _______.
options: protect sensitive information from misuse or unauthorised access
make data public to everyone always
questions.expected: protect sensitive information from misuse or unauthorised access
questions.memo: Some GIS data (personal, strategic or commercial) must be protected; security controls who can view and edit it.

questions.question: A government wants to find every household within 500 m of a planned new clinic. Which GIS tools fit best?
options: Buffer the clinic by 500 m, then query the households layer within it
questions.expected: Buffer the clinic by 500 m, then query the households layer within it
questions.memo: Buffering creates the 500 m zone; querying/overlaying the households layer selects those inside it — classic GIS analysis.

questions.question: True or false: a vertical aerial photo shows tops of features, while GIS lets you add and analyse data about them.
questions.memo: Photos provide the imagery; GIS layers add measurable, queryable data — together they support detailed spatial analysis.

questions.question: Higher spatial resolution in a satellite image means _______.
options: each pixel covers a smaller ground area (finer detail)
a larger ground area per pixel
questions.expected: each pixel covers a smaller ground area (finer detail)
questions.memo: Smaller ground area per pixel = higher spatial resolution = more detail visible.

questions.question: Government and private companies use GIS for tasks such as _______.
options: planning services, managing disasters and routing deliveries
questions.expected: planning services, managing disasters and routing deliveries
questions.memo: GIS supports town planning, emergency response, agriculture, conservation, logistics and weather/settlement analysis across many sectors.

questions.question: A learner mixes up spatial and attribute data, calling a town's population its 'spatial data'. Correct them.
options: Population is ATTRIBUTE data; spatial data is the town's location/shape
questions.expected: Population is ATTRIBUTE data; spatial data is the town's location/shape
questions.memo: Spatial = where it is; attribute = facts about it (like population). The learner confused the two.

questions.question: True or false: building a 'paper GIS' from tracing-paper layers demonstrates the layering and overlay idea behind digital GIS.
questions.memo: Stacking tracing-paper layers (roads, rivers, land use) and overlaying them models exactly how digital GIS combines data layers.

questions.question: Why is GIS so powerful for decision-making compared with a single printed map?
options: It can combine, query and analyse many data layers to answer complex spatial questions
It only shows one fixed picture
questions.expected: It can combine, query and analyse many data layers to answer complex spatial questions
questions.memo: GIS turns layered data into analysis — buffering, querying and overlaying to answer 'what, where and what-if' questions a static map cannot.

GEO.G12.T1.CLI.A1.title: Mid-latitude cyclones
GEO.G12.T1.CLI.A1.description: Characteristics, formation areas and conditions, stages of development, cold/warm/occluded fronts and their weather, and reading satellite/synoptic data.
GEO.G12.T1.CLI.A1.recovery_strategy: Mid-latitude cyclones form at ~30–60° where warm and cold air meet (the westerlies). COLD front = steep, sudden heavy rain then colder, clearer air. WARM front = gentle, prolonged lighter rain then warmer air. OCCLUDED = cold front catches the warm front. They bring the Western Cape winter rain.

questions.question: Mid-latitude cyclones form in the zone between about _______ latitude.
questions.memo: They form in the mid-latitudes (~30–60°) along the polar front, where warm subtropical air meets cold polar air.

questions.question: A mid-latitude cyclone forms where _______ air masses meet.
questions.memo: The contrast between warm tropical air and cold polar air along the polar front drives the cyclone's development.

questions.question: At a COLD front, cold air pushes UNDER warm air, giving _______.
options: steep uplift, brief heavy rain, then colder, clearer air
gentle uplift and long light rain
questions.expected: steep uplift, brief heavy rain, then colder, clearer air
questions.memo: The steep cold front forces warm air up sharply, causing short, intense rain/thunder, then cooler, clearer conditions behind it.

questions.question: At a WARM front, warm air rises GENTLY over cold air, giving _______.
options: a long spell of lighter, steady rain, then warmer air
questions.expected: a long spell of lighter, steady rain, then warmer air
questions.memo: The gentle warm-front slope produces widespread, prolonged lighter rain ahead of it, followed by milder, warmer air.

questions.question: When a cold front catches up with and lifts a warm front off the ground, an _______ front forms.
questions.memo: An occlusion forms in the cyclone's later stage as the faster cold front overtakes the warm front, lifting the warm air aloft.

questions.question: A learner says the WARM front brings sudden violent thunderstorms and a sharp temperature drop. Correct them.
options: That describes a COLD front; the warm front brings gentle, prolonged lighter rain then warmer air
questions.expected: That describes a COLD front; the warm front brings gentle, prolonged lighter rain then warmer air
questions.memo: Sudden heavy rain and a cold push behind = cold front. Gentle, lengthy lighter rain then warming = warm front. The learner swapped them.

questions.question: Order the stages of a mid-latitude cyclone's life.

items.text: Two air masses meet along the polar front
A wave/bend forms and pressure falls
The cyclone matures with clear warm and cold fronts
The cold front catches the warm front (occlusion) and it dies out

questions.memo: Front meets → wave forms → mature cyclone with both fronts → occlusion → decay. A clear life cycle.

questions.question: Look at the diagram of a mature mid-latitude cyclone. Which label shows the cold front?
options: A — the steeper front with the triangular barbs
B — the front with rounded bumps
D — the centre of high pressure
questions.expected: A — the steeper front with the triangular barbs
questions.memo: Cold fronts are drawn with triangles (A); warm fronts with semicircles (B). The warm sector (C) lies between them.

questions.question: The wedge of warm air between the cold and warm fronts is called the _______.
questions.memo: The warm sector is the mild, often clearer wedge of warm air between the advancing cold front and the leading warm front.

questions.question: Mid-latitude cyclones bring the Western Cape its rain mainly in _______.
questions.memo: In winter the westerlies and their cold fronts move north over the south-western Cape, giving it a winter-rainfall (Mediterranean) climate.

questions.question: Mid-latitude cyclones are steered across the oceans by the _______.
questions.memo: The prevailing westerlies carry these cyclones from west to east across the mid-latitude oceans.

questions.question: On a satellite image, a mature mid-latitude cyclone often appears as a _______.
questions.memo: The frontal cloud wrapping around the low gives the classic 'comma' shape on satellite imagery.

questions.question: True or false: a cold front usually moves faster than a warm front.
questions.memo: Cold fronts advance faster, which is why they eventually catch the slower warm front and form an occlusion.

questions.question: As a cold front passes a place, the temperature usually _______ and the pressure _______.
questions.memo: Behind a cold front, colder air moves in (temperature drops) and pressure rises as the low moves away.

questions.question: Which condition is necessary for a mid-latitude cyclone to form?
options: A strong temperature contrast between meeting air masses
questions.expected: A strong temperature contrast between meeting air masses
questions.memo: The energy comes from the contrast between warm and cold air along the polar front — no contrast, no cyclone.

questions.question: Steady, widespread, lighter rain over many hours ahead of the system suggests the approach of a _______.
questions.memo: Gentle uplift along a warm front spreads layered cloud and prolonged lighter rain well ahead of it.

questions.question: Why does a mid-latitude cyclone eventually 'die out' after occlusion?
options: Once the warm air is lifted off the surface, the temperature contrast driving it is lost
questions.expected: Once the warm air is lifted off the surface, the temperature contrast driving it is lost
questions.memo: Occlusion lifts the warm air aloft, removing the warm–cold contrast at the surface that fuelled the cyclone — so it weakens and decays.

questions.question: True or false: mid-latitude cyclones are low-pressure systems, so they bring cloud and rain rather than clear skies.
questions.memo: They are travelling lows: rising air along their fronts produces cloud, rain and wind, unlike the clear, dry weather of a high.

questions.question: On a synoptic map, a deepening low west of the Cape with packed isobars and a cold front warns of _______.
options: a coming cold front with rain, strong wind and cooler air
questions.expected: a coming cold front with rain, strong wind and cooler air
questions.memo: A deep low and cold front approaching from the west bring the Cape its characteristic frontal rain, gusty wind and a temperature drop.
