questions.question: Why do mid-latitude cyclones matter so much for the Western Cape but little for Durban?
options: The Cape lies in the winter westerly/cold-front belt; Durban's east coast gets summer rain from other systems
questions.expected: The Cape lies in the winter westerly/cold-front belt; Durban's east coast gets summer rain from other systems
questions.memo: Cold fronts from mid-latitude cyclones bring the south-western Cape its winter rain, while Durban's summer rain comes from other (easterly/convective) systems.

GEO.G12.T1.CLI.A2.title: Tropical cyclones
GEO.G12.T1.CLI.A2.description: Characteristics, formation areas/conditions, stages, weather, a southern-African case study, impacts and management.
GEO.G12.T1.CLI.A2.recovery_strategy: Tropical cyclones need WARM ocean water (≥26–27 °C), so they form over tropical seas and WEAKEN over land/cold water. The EYE is calm and clear; the EYE WALL has the strongest winds and heaviest rain. They bring extreme wind, rain, flooding and storm surge (e.g. Cyclone Idai).

questions.question: Tropical cyclones form over _______.
questions.memo: They need warm ocean water (about 26–27 °C or more) to supply the heat and moisture that power them.

questions.question: The minimum sea-surface temperature usually needed for a tropical cyclone to form is about _______.
questions.memo: Warm water of at least ~26–27 °C to a good depth provides the energy; this is why they form in tropical seas in the warm season.

questions.question: The calm, clear centre of a tropical cyclone is the _______.
questions.memo: The eye is a calm, clear core of sinking air; around it the eye wall has the most violent weather.

questions.question: The strongest winds and heaviest rain are found in the _______.
questions.memo: The eye wall, the ring of towering cloud around the eye, has the most destructive winds and rainfall.

questions.question: A learner says the strongest winds are in the eye. Correct them.
options: The eye is CALM; the strongest winds are in the surrounding eye wall
The eye has the heaviest rain
questions.expected: The eye is CALM; the strongest winds are in the surrounding eye wall
questions.memo: The eye is deceptively calm and clear; the violence is in the eye wall around it — a dangerous trap if people think the storm is over.

questions.question: What happens to a tropical cyclone when it moves over land?
options: It weakens because it loses its warm-ocean energy source
It turns into a high-pressure cell
questions.expected: It weakens because it loses its warm-ocean energy source
questions.memo: Cut off from warm water and slowed by friction over land, the cyclone weakens — though it can still cause severe flooding inland.

questions.question: Look at the cross-section of a tropical cyclone. Which label shows the eye?
options: A — the calm, clear central column
B — the towering cloud ring around the centre
questions.expected: A — the calm, clear central column
questions.memo: A eye (calm centre), B eye wall (worst weather), C spiral rain bands, D warm ocean (energy source).

questions.question: A wall of seawater pushed ashore by a tropical cyclone's winds and low pressure is a _______.
questions.memo: Storm surge — not an earthquake-driven tsunami — is the deadly coastal flooding caused by a cyclone's winds and low pressure raising the sea.

questions.question: A tropical cyclone that severely affected Mozambique, Zimbabwe and Malawi in 2019 was Cyclone _______.
questions.memo: Cyclone Idai (2019) caused catastrophic flooding and loss of life in southern Africa — the prescribed regional case study.

questions.question: Sort each as an IMPACT of a tropical cyclone or a PREPARATION/management strategy.

items.text: Roads, bridges and power lines damaged

questions.memo: Impacts = the damage (floods, deaths, destroyed infrastructure); strategies = how we prepare and respond (warnings, evacuation, building codes).

questions.question: Why do tropical cyclones NOT form right on the equator (0°)?
options: The Coriolis force is too weak there to start the spin
The Sun is too far away
questions.expected: The Coriolis force is too weak there to start the spin
questions.memo: Cyclones need some Coriolis force to begin rotating, so they form a few degrees away from the equator, not on it.

questions.question: Spiral bands of heavy cloud and rain rotating around the centre are called _______.
questions.memo: Spiral rain bands wheel around the eye, bringing bursts of heavy rain and strong gusts well before and after the eye wall.

questions.question: How does a tropical cyclone differ from a mid-latitude cyclone in its energy source?
options: Tropical: warm-ocean heat/moisture; mid-latitude: warm–cold air contrast
Both get energy from cold polar air
questions.expected: Tropical: warm-ocean heat/moisture; mid-latitude: warm–cold air contrast
questions.memo: Tropical cyclones are powered by latent heat from warm tropical oceans; mid-latitude cyclones by the temperature contrast at the polar front.

questions.question: True or false: the low pressure in a tropical cyclone's centre helps lift the sea surface, adding to the storm surge.
questions.memo: The very low central pressure raises the sea, and the winds pile water towards the coast — together producing the destructive storm surge.

questions.question: An ENVIRONMENTAL impact of a tropical cyclone is _______.
options: coastal erosion, flooding and damage to ecosystems
questions.expected: coastal erosion, flooding and damage to ecosystems
questions.memo: Cyclones erode beaches, flood wetlands, salt-poison farmland and damage reefs and forests — major environmental as well as human impacts.

questions.question: Which preparation step most directly SAVES LIVES before a cyclone strikes?
options: Timely warnings and evacuation to safe shelters
questions.expected: Timely warnings and evacuation to safe shelters
questions.memo: Accurate forecasts, clear warnings and organised evacuation move people out of harm's way — the biggest factor in reducing deaths.

questions.question: Why are poor coastal communities often hit hardest by tropical cyclones?
options: Weaker housing, low-lying exposed sites and limited warning/evacuation resources
They live on high, protected ground
questions.expected: Weaker housing, low-lying exposed sites and limited warning/evacuation resources
questions.memo: Vulnerability is social as well as physical: fragile homes, exposed locations and fewer resources to prepare or evacuate raise the toll — as seen with Idai.

questions.question: True or false: tropical cyclones generally form in the warm season when ocean temperatures are highest.
questions.memo: They need the warmest seas, so the cyclone season falls in and after the hottest months for each ocean basin.

questions.question: After the calm eye passes over a town, residents go outside — and are caught by renewed violent weather. Why?
options: The eye wall on the far side hits next, with winds from the opposite direction
The storm is definitely over after the eye
The eye is the most dangerous part
questions.expected: The eye wall on the far side hits next, with winds from the opposite direction
questions.memo: The calm eye is only the middle; the trailing eye wall brings a second round of extreme winds (from the opposite direction) — a deadly misconception.

questions.question: Using Cyclone Idai, why is disaster management across borders important for southern Africa?
options: One cyclone can devastate several countries at once, so warning and relief must be coordinated regionally
Cyclones only ever hit one country
Each country can ignore the others
questions.expected: One cyclone can devastate several countries at once, so warning and relief must be coordinated regionally
questions.memo: Idai struck Mozambique, Zimbabwe and Malawi together, showing the need for shared forecasting, warnings and cross-border relief.

GEO.G12.T1.CLI.A3.title: Subtropical anticyclones & South Africa's weather
GEO.G12.T1.CLI.A3.description: SA's high-pressure cells, anticyclonic circulation, travelling disturbances (moisture front, line thunderstorms, coastal lows, berg winds) and reading the synoptic maps.
GEO.G12.T1.CLI.A3.recovery_strategy: Three highs steer SA's weather: South Atlantic HP (west), South Indian HP (east), Kalahari/continental HP (interior, strong in winter). Anticyclonic (sinking) air = dry, stable. BERG WINDS blow from the interior to the coast, warming and drying as they descend — hot, dry coastal conditions.

questions.question: An anticyclone (high-pressure cell) is associated with _______.
options: sinking air and dry, stable, clear weather
questions.expected: sinking air and dry, stable, clear weather
questions.memo: In a high, air sinks and warms, suppressing cloud — giving the calm, clear, dry conditions typical of anticyclonic weather.

questions.question: The high-pressure cell off South Africa's WEST coast is the South _______ High.
questions.memo: The South Atlantic High sits off the west coast; the South Indian High off the east; and a continental (Kalahari) high develops over the interior, especially in winter.

questions.question: The high-pressure cell that strengthens over the interior of South Africa in winter is the _______ High.
questions.memo: In winter a strong continental (Kalahari) high settles over the cool interior, bringing dry, stable, sunny conditions to much of the country.

questions.question: In the southern hemisphere, air circulates around a high-pressure cell in which direction?
questions.memo: In the southern hemisphere anticyclonic flow is ANTICLOCKWISE (and clockwise around a low) — the reverse of the northern hemisphere.

questions.question: A berg wind is a wind that blows from the _______ towards the coast, becoming hot and dry.
questions.memo: Berg winds descend from the interior plateau to the coast; as they sink they warm and dry, giving unusually hot, dry coastal weather.

questions.question: Why is a berg wind hot and dry by the time it reaches the coast?
options: Descending air is compressed and warmed, and any moisture has been lost
It comes straight off cold water
questions.expected: Descending air is compressed and warmed, and any moisture has been lost
questions.memo: As air sinks from the high interior it is compressed and heated, and it is already dry — so it arrives at the coast hot and parched (high fire risk).

questions.question: A learner says berg winds bring cold, wet weather to the coast. Correct them.
options: Berg winds are HOT and DRY because the descending air warms and has lost its moisture
Berg winds blow from the sea
questions.expected: Berg winds are HOT and DRY because the descending air warms and has lost its moisture
questions.memo: Berg winds raise coastal temperatures sharply and lower humidity — hot and dry, not cold and wet.

questions.question: A narrow band of low pressure that moves along the coast ahead of a cold front is a _______.
questions.memo: Coastal lows travel along the South African coast, often signalling a change in weather (and frequently preceding a cold front).

questions.question: A line of thunderstorms that develops along a boundary of moist and dry air is a _______.
questions.memo: Where moist air meets drier air (a moisture front), uplift can trigger a line of thunderstorms — a travelling disturbance over the interior.

questions.question: Match each South African high-pressure cell to its position.
questions.memo: 1 South Atlantic High → B off the west coast. 2 South Indian High → C off the east coast. 3 Kalahari High → A over the interior. (Prompt: 1=South Atlantic, 2=South Indian, 3=Kalahari; A=interior, B=west coast, C=east coast.)

questions.question: Why does much of South Africa have dry, sunny winters?
options: The strong continental high brings sinking, stable, dry air over the interior
Cold fronts cross the whole country daily
questions.expected: The strong continental high brings sinking, stable, dry air over the interior
questions.memo: Winter's dominant Kalahari high gives clear, dry, sunny but cold days over the interior; only the winter-rainfall Cape gets frontal rain.

questions.question: Look at the synoptic map symbols. Which label marks a high-pressure cell?
options: A — the 'H' with isobars increasing inward
B — the 'L' with isobars decreasing inward
questions.expected: A — the 'H' with isobars increasing inward
questions.memo: A high is marked 'H' with pressure rising towards the centre; a low is 'L' with pressure falling towards the centre.

questions.question: Berg winds along the coast often raise the risk of _______.
questions.memo: Hot, dry, gusty berg winds dry out vegetation and fan flames, sharply increasing wildfire danger along the coast.

questions.question: True or false: in the southern hemisphere, winds blow clockwise around a low-pressure cell.
questions.memo: Southern hemisphere: clockwise around a LOW and anticlockwise around a HIGH — the opposite of the northern hemisphere.

questions.question: The general dryness of South Africa is partly explained by its position under the _______.
questions.memo: Lying near 30°S, much of SA sits under subsiding subtropical high pressure, which suppresses rainfall and keeps the country semi-arid.

questions.question: Which travelling disturbance often brings a welcome BREAK in hot, stable anticyclonic weather along the coast?
options: A coastal low (often ahead of a cold front)
questions.expected: A coastal low (often ahead of a cold front)
questions.memo: A passing coastal low can bring cloud, wind shifts and cooler, sometimes wetter conditions, breaking a hot, stable spell — frequently preceding a front.

questions.question: True or false: the anticyclones around South Africa shift their position with the seasons, changing the weather they bring.
questions.memo: The highs migrate seasonally (e.g. the continental high strengthens in winter), altering wind, temperature and rainfall patterns across the country.

questions.question: Why does sinking air in an anticyclone prevent cloud and rain?
options: Descending air warms and dries, so water vapour does not condense
Sinking air cools and condenses heavily
questions.expected: Descending air warms and dries, so water vapour does not condense
questions.memo: As air sinks it compresses and warms, lowering relative humidity — the opposite of the rising, cooling, condensing air in a low.

questions.question: A synoptic map shows a strong high over the interior and a berg-wind situation along the south coast. What weather is likely at the coast?
options: Unusually hot, dry, windy conditions with high fire risk
Thick coastal fog and calm air
questions.expected: Unusually hot, dry, windy conditions with high fire risk
questions.memo: Air sinking from the interior high blows seaward as a berg wind, warming and drying — giving hot, dry, fire-prone coastal weather.

questions.question: Why are South Africa's high-pressure cells central to understanding its climate?
options: They dominate the country's stable, dry conditions and steer the disturbances that bring change
They have no effect on weather
questions.expected: They dominate the country's stable, dry conditions and steer the disturbances that bring change
questions.memo: The subtropical anticyclones set SA's generally dry, stable background weather; the travelling disturbances moving around them deliver most of the day-to-day changes.

GEO.G12.T1.CLI.A4.title: Valley climates
GEO.G12.T1.CLI.A4.description: Valley micro-climates, slope aspect, anabatic/katabatic winds, inversions, frost pockets and radiation fog, and their influence on settlement and farming.
GEO.G12.T1.CLI.A4.recovery_strategy: ANABATIC winds blow UP-slope by DAY (warm air rises). KATABATIC winds drain cold dense air DOWN-slope at NIGHT, pooling on the valley floor → temperature INVERSION, FROST POCKETS and radiation fog. Farmers plant frost-sensitive crops on the warmer mid-slopes, not the cold floor.

questions.question: An anabatic wind blows _______.
options: up the valley slopes during the day
questions.expected: up the valley slopes during the day
questions.memo: By day the Sun heats the slopes; warm air becomes buoyant and flows UP-slope — an anabatic wind.

questions.question: A katabatic wind blows _______.
options: up the slopes during the day
questions.memo: At night the slopes cool; cold, dense air drains DOWN-slope into the valley floor — a katabatic wind.

questions.question: A learner says katabatic winds blow UP the valley during the day. Correct them.
options: Katabatic winds blow DOWN-slope at NIGHT; anabatic winds blow up by day
questions.expected: Katabatic winds blow DOWN-slope at NIGHT; anabatic winds blow up by day
questions.memo: Anabatic = up by day (warm, rising); katabatic = down at night (cold, sinking). The learner swapped them.

questions.question: Cold air draining to the valley floor at night can cause warmer air to sit ABOVE colder air. This is a temperature _______.
questions.memo: Normally air cools with height; an INVERSION reverses this — cold air pools below, warmer air sits above — common in valleys on calm clear nights.

questions.question: Where in a valley is frost most likely to form on a cold, clear night?
questions.memo: Cold dense air sinks and collects on the valley floor, creating a 'frost pocket' — the coldest spot, where frost forms first.

questions.question: Because of frost pockets, farmers often plant frost-sensitive crops (like fruit) on the _______.
questions.memo: The mid-slopes (thermal belt) stay warmer at night as cold air drains past them to the floor — the best place for frost-sensitive crops.

questions.question: Slope ASPECT refers to _______.
questions.memo: Aspect is the compass direction a slope faces; it strongly affects how much sun the slope receives and thus its micro-climate.

questions.question: In the southern hemisphere, which slope receives the MOST sunshine and is warmest?
questions.memo: In the southern hemisphere the Sun is in the northern sky, so NORTH-facing slopes get the most sun and are warmer and drier; south-facing slopes are cooler and shadier.

questions.question: Fog that forms on calm, clear nights as the ground cools is _______ fog.
questions.memo: Radiation fog forms when the surface radiates heat away on still, clear nights, cooling the air to its dew point — often pooling in valleys.

questions.question: Order what happens in a valley on a calm, clear night.

items.text: Slopes lose heat by radiation and cool
Cold, dense air drains down-slope (katabatic wind)
Cold air pools on the valley floor (inversion)
Frost and radiation fog form in the frost pocket

questions.memo: Slopes cool → katabatic drainage → cold air pools (inversion) → frost and fog form on the floor. A clear chain of cause and effect.

questions.question: Look at the valley cross-section. Which label shows the frost pocket?
options: C — the cold-air pool on the valley floor
A — the warm mid-slope thermal belt
questions.expected: C — the cold-air pool on the valley floor
questions.memo: C is the cold-air pool (frost pocket) on the floor; A is the warmer thermal belt on the mid-slope where farmers prefer to plant.

questions.question: Why do vineyards and orchards often AVOID the valley floor in frost-prone areas?
options: Cold air pools there at night, raising the risk of frost damage
questions.expected: Cold air pools there at night, raising the risk of frost damage
questions.memo: Frost pockets on the floor can kill frost-sensitive crops; the warmer mid-slope thermal belt is safer, which is why vineyards favour slopes.

questions.question: True or false: a temperature inversion can trap cold air and pollution near the valley floor.
questions.memo: The warm 'lid' above an inversion stops the cold air below from rising, trapping fog, smoke and pollutants near the surface.

questions.question: A south-facing slope (southern hemisphere) is generally _______ than a north-facing slope.
questions.memo: Facing away from the northern Sun, south-facing slopes receive less direct sunlight, so they are cooler, shadier and often more moist and vegetated.

questions.question: Anabatic and katabatic winds are examples of _______ winds caused by local heating and cooling.
questions.memo: These are local (mountain–valley) winds driven by the daily heating and cooling of slopes, separate from the global wind belts.

questions.question: Why does the valley floor warm up later in the morning than the slopes?
options: Cold air and fog pooled overnight take time to clear and warm
The floor is closer to the Sun
questions.expected: Cold air and fog pooled overnight take time to clear and warm
questions.memo: The overnight cold-air pool and radiation fog must disperse before the floor warms, so it lags behind the sun-warmed slopes in the morning.

questions.question: True or false: settlements may favour the warmer mid-slopes over a frosty, foggy valley floor.
questions.memo: Like crops, settlement and orchards often prefer the milder thermal belt on the mid-slope, avoiding the cold, foggy floor.

questions.question: Daytime anabatic winds form because slopes _______ faster than the air over the valley centre.
questions.memo: Sun-warmed slopes heat the air against them, which rises and flows up-slope (anabatic) — the reverse of the night-time katabatic drainage.

questions.question: Why does aspect strongly affect farming in a valley?
options: Sunnier slopes suit warmth-loving crops; shadier, moister slopes suit other uses
Aspect has no effect on crops
Only the floor can be farmed
questions.expected: Sunnier slopes suit warmth-loving crops; shadier, moister slopes suit other uses
questions.memo: The warmer, drier north-facing slope suits vines and fruit; the cooler, moister south-facing slope suits forestry or pasture — aspect guides land use.

questions.question: A wine farmer must choose where to plant frost-sensitive vines in a valley. Where and why?
options: On the warmer mid-slope thermal belt, above the frost pocket on the floor
questions.expected: On the warmer mid-slope thermal belt, above the frost pocket on the floor
questions.memo: Cold air drains past the mid-slope to pool on the floor; planting on the warmer thermal belt avoids frost damage — a direct use of valley-climate knowledge.

GEO.G12.T1.CLI.A5.title: Urban climates
GEO.G12.T1.CLI.A5.description: Why urban and rural climates differ, the urban heat island, pollution domes, and strategies to reduce the heat-island effect.
GEO.G12.T1.CLI.A5.recovery_strategy: Cities are WARMER than the countryside (urban HEAT ISLAND): dark concrete and tar absorb heat, buildings block wind, and cars/factories/air-conditioners release waste heat. A POLLUTION DOME traps dirty air over the city. Reduce it with parks, trees, green roofs and lighter, reflective surfaces.

questions.question: An urban heat island means a city is usually _______ than the surrounding countryside.
questions.memo: Cities trap and generate heat, so they are typically several degrees warmer than nearby rural areas — the urban heat island.

questions.question: Which feature of cities contributes MOST to the heat-island effect?
options: Dark concrete, tar and brick that absorb and store heat
questions.expected: Dark concrete, tar and brick that absorb and store heat
questions.memo: Built surfaces absorb solar heat by day and release it at night; combined with little vegetation and waste heat, they warm the city.

questions.question: A learner says the city centre is the COOLEST part of a region. Correct them.
options: The dense city centre is usually the WARMEST (peak of the heat island)
Temperature does not vary across a city
questions.expected: The dense city centre is usually the WARMEST (peak of the heat island)
questions.memo: The built-up core, with the most concrete and waste heat, is normally the hottest point — the peak of the urban heat island.

questions.question: Sort each as a CAUSE of the urban heat island or a STRATEGY to reduce it.

items.text: Waste heat from cars and air-conditioners
Few plants and little open water

questions.memo: Causes: heat-absorbing surfaces, waste heat, little vegetation. Strategies: trees, parks, reflective roofs and green roofs to cool the city.

questions.question: A dome of warm, polluted air that can sit over a city is called a _______.
questions.memo: A pollution dome forms when pollutants and warm air are trapped over a city, especially under calm conditions or an inversion.

questions.question: Why is air pollution often WORSE over a city on a calm night with a temperature inversion?
options: The warm 'lid' traps pollutants near the surface so they cannot disperse
Wind blows the pollution away faster
Pollution rises into space at night
questions.expected: The warm 'lid' traps pollutants near the surface so they cannot disperse
questions.memo: An inversion caps the cooler surface air, preventing the rising mixing that would normally disperse pollution — concentrating it in a dome.

questions.question: Which strategy directly REDUCES the urban heat-island effect?
options: Increasing green spaces, trees and reflective surfaces
questions.expected: Increasing green spaces, trees and reflective surfaces
questions.memo: Vegetation cools through shade and evapotranspiration, and light/reflective surfaces absorb less heat — both lower city temperatures.

questions.question: Trees cool cities partly through _______, releasing water vapour that absorbs heat.
questions.memo: Evapotranspiration from leaves uses heat energy to evaporate water, cooling the surrounding air — plus trees provide shade.

questions.question: Cities can also be slightly _______ than the countryside because dust gives extra surfaces for condensation.
questions.memo: Extra dust (condensation nuclei) and rising warm air can make cities a little cloudier and sometimes rainier, especially downwind.

questions.question: Wind speed in city centres is often _______ than in open countryside.
options: lower (buildings reduce it), though channelled gusts can occur
questions.expected: lower (buildings reduce it), though channelled gusts can occur
questions.memo: Buildings create friction that lowers average wind, but narrow streets can channel and speed up gusts (the 'canyon effect').

questions.question:
The table shows night temperatures across a city transect. What does it reveal?

| Location | Night temp (°C) |
|------|------|
| Rural edge | 14 |
| Suburb | 16 |
| City centre | 19 |
options: Temperature rises towards the city centre — a heat island
questions.expected: Temperature rises towards the city centre — a heat island
questions.memo: From 14 °C at the rural edge to 19 °C in the centre, the rising trend towards the core is the classic heat-island profile.

questions.question: Green roofs reduce the heat-island effect by _______.
options: insulating buildings and cooling through plants instead of bare hot roofs
questions.expected: insulating buildings and cooling through plants instead of bare hot roofs
questions.memo: Planting roofs replaces heat-absorbing surfaces with cooling vegetation, insulating the building and lowering surrounding air temperature.

questions.question: Why is the urban heat island usually STRONGEST at night?
options: Built surfaces slowly release the heat they absorbed all day, while rural areas cool quickly
Cities only heat up at night
The Sun shines at night in cities
Rural areas stay warmer at night
questions.expected: Built surfaces slowly release the heat they absorbed all day, while rural areas cool quickly
questions.memo: Concrete and tar store daytime heat and radiate it slowly overnight, keeping cities warm while open countryside cools rapidly — widening the gap at night.

questions.question: True or false: more vehicles, factories and air-conditioners add 'waste heat' that intensifies the urban heat island.
questions.memo: Human activity releases waste heat (engines, machinery, cooling systems), adding to the warming caused by heat-absorbing surfaces.

questions.question: An EFFECT of a strong pollution dome on city residents is _______.
options: more respiratory illness and reduced air quality
questions.expected: more respiratory illness and reduced air quality
questions.memo: Trapped pollutants worsen air quality, causing breathing problems, smog and health risks — a key reason to cut emissions and improve dispersal.

questions.question: Light-coloured, reflective roofs and pavements help because they _______.
options: reflect more sunlight (higher albedo), absorbing less heat
absorb more heat than dark ones
questions.expected: reflect more sunlight (higher albedo), absorbing less heat
questions.memo: High-albedo (light) surfaces bounce sunlight away instead of soaking it up, keeping the city cooler than dark tar and roofs.

questions.question: True or false: planning cities with parks, trees and water features can measurably lower urban temperatures.
questions.memo: Green and blue spaces cool through shade and evaporation, creating cooler 'islands' that reduce the overall heat-island effect.

questions.question: Why does a city centre with little vegetation get especially hot?
options: Without plants there is little shade or evaporative cooling, and surfaces absorb heat
questions.expected: Without plants there is little shade or evaporative cooling, and surfaces absorb heat
questions.memo: Vegetation normally cools by shading and transpiring; its absence in a built-up core removes that cooling, so heat-absorbing surfaces dominate.

questions.question: A heatwave hits a city with a strong heat island and pollution dome. Why are residents at greater risk than rural neighbours?
options: Higher city temperatures plus trapped pollution worsen heat stress and breathing
questions.expected: Higher city temperatures plus trapped pollution worsen heat stress and breathing
questions.memo: The heat island raises temperatures and the pollution dome traps dirty air, compounding heat stress and respiratory risk for city dwellers.

questions.question: A city plans more parks, tree-lined streets, green roofs and reflective surfaces. What is the goal and why will it work?
options: To cool the city — vegetation and reflective surfaces reduce heat absorption and add shade/evaporation
questions.expected: To cool the city — vegetation and reflective surfaces reduce heat absorption and add shade/evaporation
questions.memo: These measures attack the heat island at its source — replacing heat-absorbing surfaces with cooling vegetation and reflective materials lowers urban temperatures.

GEO.G12.T1.GEO.A1.title: Drainage systems in South Africa
GEO.G12.T1.GEO.A1.description: Drainage concepts, river types, drainage patterns, drainage density, stream order, and laminar vs turbulent flow.
GEO.G12.T1.GEO.A1.recovery_strategy: A DRAINAGE BASIN/CATCHMENT is the land drained by one river system; the WATERSHED is the high ground dividing basins. Patterns reflect rock: DENDRITIC (tree-like) on uniform rock; TRELLIS on tilted hard/soft rock; RADIAL (outward) off a dome; CENTRIPETAL (inward) into a basin.

questions.question: All the land drained by one river and its tributaries is called a _______.
questions.memo: A drainage basin (catchment) is the whole area whose water flows into one river system.

questions.question: The high ground separating two drainage basins is the _______.
questions.memo: A watershed (divide) is the ridge of high land separating one catchment from the next — water falls to one side or the other.

questions.question: The point where two rivers join is a _______.
questions.memo: A confluence is where a tributary meets the main river; the source is where a river begins and the mouth is where it ends (sea/lake).

questions.question: A smaller river or stream that flows INTO a larger one is a _______.
questions.memo: Tributaries feed the main river. (A distributary, by contrast, branches OUT, as in a delta.)

questions.question: A tree-like branching drainage pattern that forms on uniform rock is _______.
questions.memo: Dendritic patterns (like tree branches) develop where the underlying rock is uniform with no strong structural control.

questions.question: A rectangular, ladder-like pattern that forms on alternating bands of hard and soft tilted rock is _______.
questions.memo: Trellis drainage forms where tributaries follow soft-rock valleys and join the main stream at right angles, controlled by tilted strata.

questions.question: Rivers flowing OUTWARD in all directions from a central high point (like a dome or volcano) form a _______ pattern.
questions.memo: Radial drainage spreads outward from a high centre (dome/cone); centripetal drainage flows INWARD into a basin.

questions.question: Rivers flowing INWARD towards a central low point form a _______ pattern.
questions.memo: Centripetal drainage converges into a central basin or depression — the opposite of radial.

questions.question: Look at the diagram of drainage patterns. Which label shows the radial pattern?
options: C — streams spreading outward from a central peak
D — streams converging into a basin
questions.expected: C — streams spreading outward from a central peak
questions.memo: A dendritic, B trellis, C radial (outward from a peak), D centripetal (inward to a basin).

questions.question: A river that flows ALL YEAR round is described as _______.
questions.memo: Permanent rivers flow year-round; periodic flow seasonally; episodic flow only after rare heavy rain; exotic rivers cross dry areas fed from a wetter source.

questions.question: The Orange River, which crosses arid areas but is fed from the wetter Lesotho highlands, is an example of a/an _______ river.
questions.memo: An exotic river rises in a humid region and flows through a dry one, sustained by its distant source — like the Orange (and the Nile).

questions.question: Match each drainage pattern to its controlling condition.
questions.memo: 1 Dendritic → C uniform rock. 2 Trellis → A tilted hard/soft bands. 3 Radial → D a central dome/peak. 4 Centripetal → B an inland basin. (Prompt: 1=Dendritic, 2=Trellis, 3=Radial, 4=Centripetal; A=tilted hard/soft rock, B=inland basin, C=uniform rock, D=central dome.)

questions.question: Drainage DENSITY refers to _______.
options: the total length of streams in a given area
questions.expected: the total length of streams in a given area
questions.memo: Drainage density = stream length ÷ area. High density (many channels) suggests impermeable rock or steep, wet land; low density suggests permeable or dry ground.

questions.question: High drainage density (many close channels) usually indicates _______.
questions.memo: When water cannot soak in (impermeable rock) or there is a lot of it (high rainfall), many surface channels form — high drainage density.

questions.question: Smooth, orderly water flow in straight layers is _______ flow, while chaotic mixing is _______ flow.
questions.memo: Laminar flow is smooth and layered (slow, shallow water); turbulent flow is churning and mixing (faster, rougher water) — turbulent water erodes and transports more.

questions.question: A learner says the watershed is the main river channel. Correct them.
options: The watershed is the high ground DIVIDING basins, not the river itself
The watershed is the river mouth
questions.expected: The watershed is the high ground DIVIDING basins, not the river itself
questions.memo: A watershed is the boundary ridge between catchments; the river flows within the basin, not along the divide.

questions.question: Stream ORDER is a way of _______.
options: numbering streams by how many tributaries have joined
questions.expected: numbering streams by how many tributaries have joined
questions.memo: In stream ordering, the smallest headwater streams are 1st order; where two 1st-order streams meet they form a 2nd order, and so on — a measure of network size.

questions.question: True or false: a river type can be classified by how often it flows (permanent, periodic, episodic).
questions.memo: Rivers are classified by flow regime: permanent (always), periodic (seasonal), episodic (only after rare rain), plus exotic rivers fed from distant wet sources.

questions.question: Why does a region of hard, impermeable rock and high rainfall have many surface streams?
options: Water cannot infiltrate, so it runs off in numerous channels — high drainage density
questions.expected: Water cannot infiltrate, so it runs off in numerous channels — high drainage density
questions.memo: Impermeable rock forces water to flow over the surface; plentiful rain supplies it, so many channels develop — a high drainage density.

questions.question: On a topographic map you see streams spreading out from a central mountain. What pattern and underlying landform is this?
options: A radial pattern over a dome or volcanic cone
A trellis pattern on flat land
A centripetal pattern in a basin
A dendritic pattern on tilted rock
questions.expected: A radial pattern over a dome or volcanic cone
questions.memo: Streams flowing outward in all directions from a high centre indicate radial drainage over a dome or cone.

GEO.G12.T1.GEO.A2.title: Fluvial processes & landforms
GEO.G12.T1.GEO.A2.description: River profiles and stages, fluvial landforms, river grading, rejuvenation, river capture, and superimposed/antecedent drainage.
GEO.G12.T1.GEO.A2.recovery_strategy: UPPER course = steep, fast, eroding: V-valleys, waterfalls, rapids. LOWER course = gentle, depositing: meanders, oxbow lakes, floodplains, levees, deltas. An OXBOW LAKE forms when a meander loop is cut off. Rejuvenation (renewed erosion) gives knickpoints, terraces and incised meanders.

questions.question: In its UPPER course, a river mainly _______.
options: erodes downward, forming steep V-shaped valleys
deposits silt and builds a delta
questions.expected: erodes downward, forming steep V-shaped valleys
questions.memo: The steep upper course has fast, energetic water that cuts down, creating V-shaped valleys, waterfalls and rapids.

questions.question: In its LOWER course, a river mainly _______.
options: deposits material, forming meanders, floodplains and deltas
questions.expected: deposits material, forming meanders, floodplains and deltas
questions.memo: The gentle lower course has lots of water but low energy per load, so it deposits — building meanders, floodplains, levees and deltas.

questions.question: A large bend or loop in a river is a _______.
questions.memo: Meanders are sweeping bends that develop in the middle and lower course as the river erodes the outer bank and deposits on the inner bank.

questions.question: A curved lake left behind when a meander loop is cut off is an _______.
questions.memo: When the narrow neck of a meander is breached, the loop is abandoned, leaving a crescent-shaped oxbow lake.

questions.question: Order the formation of an oxbow lake.

items.text: A meander loop grows as the outer bank erodes
The neck of the loop narrows
The river breaks through the neck (often in a flood)
The old loop is sealed off as an oxbow lake

questions.memo: Loop grows → neck narrows → river cuts through the neck → abandoned loop becomes an oxbow lake.

questions.question: Look at the lower-course diagram. Which label shows a natural levee?
options: B — the raised bank of deposited material beside the channel
D — the fan of sediment at the mouth
questions.expected: B — the raised bank of deposited material beside the channel
questions.memo: A meander, B natural levee (raised bank built by repeated flooding), C oxbow lake, D delta.

questions.question: A fan-shaped deposit where a river enters the sea or a lake is a _______.
questions.memo: A delta forms where a river drops its load as it meets standing water, building up low, fertile, branching land at the mouth.

questions.question: When a river's energy is renewed (e.g. the land is uplifted or sea level falls), the process is called _______.
questions.memo: Rejuvenation gives a river renewed downcutting power, producing features like knickpoints, river terraces and incised meanders.

questions.question: A sudden break of slope (often a small waterfall) in a rejuvenated river's long profile is a _______.
questions.memo: A knickpoint marks where renewed downcutting has reached; it migrates upstream as a step or waterfall in the long profile.

questions.question: A learner says deltas form in the UPPER course. Correct them.
options: Deltas form in the LOWER course where the river meets the sea and deposits its load
questions.expected: Deltas form in the LOWER course where the river meets the sea and deposits its load
questions.memo: Deltas are lower-course depositional features at the mouth; the upper course is dominated by erosion (V-valleys, waterfalls).

questions.question: River CAPTURE (stream piracy) is when one river _______.
options: erodes back and diverts the flow of another river into itself
questions.expected: erodes back and diverts the flow of another river into itself
questions.memo: A more powerful river erodes headward, breaks into a neighbouring valley and 'captures' its water, diverting the flow into its own channel.

questions.question: The sharp bend where one river was diverted into another during river capture is the _______.
questions.memo: The elbow of capture marks the right-angle bend where the captured stream turns into the captor; downstream the abandoned valley holds a misfit stream and a wind gap.

questions.question: A river's long profile shows its slope from _______.
options: top to bottom of a hill
questions.memo: The longitudinal (long) profile is the lengthwise slope, steep at the source and flattening to the mouth — ideally a smooth, concave 'graded' curve.

questions.question: A 'graded' river is one whose profile is _______.
options: a smooth, balanced curve where erosion and deposition are in equilibrium
questions.expected: a smooth, balanced curve where erosion and deposition are in equilibrium
questions.memo: Grading is the river's tendency towards a smooth concave profile in balance; rejuvenation disturbs this, adding knickpoints until it re-grades.

questions.question: Match each landform to its river course.
questions.memo: 1 Waterfall → C upper course. 2 Meander → A middle course. 3 Delta → B lower course/mouth. (Prompt: 1=Waterfall, 2=Meander, 3=Delta; A=middle course, B=lower course/mouth, C=upper course.)

questions.question: Step-like benches of old floodplain left above a rejuvenated river are river _______.
questions.memo: When a river cuts down into its old floodplain after rejuvenation, remnants of the former floodplain are left as paired terraces along the valley sides.

questions.question: Why does the OUTER bank of a meander erode while the INNER bank gains a sandbank?
options: Faster water on the outside erodes; slower water on the inside deposits
questions.expected: Faster water on the outside erodes; slower water on the inside deposits
questions.memo: Flow is fastest on the outer bend (erosion, cutting a river cliff) and slowest on the inner bend (deposition, building a point bar) — which migrates the meander.

questions.question: A deeply cut, winding gorge that keeps the shape of old meanders shows _______.
questions.memo: Incised meanders form when a meandering river is rejuvenated and cuts down, entrenching its bends into the rock — evidence of renewed erosion.

questions.question: True or false: braided streams form where a river carries a heavy load and splits into many channels around sediment bars.
questions.memo: When a river is overloaded with sediment (e.g. variable flow), it deposits bars and divides into a braided network of shifting channels.

questions.question: A geographer finds a dry 'wind gap', an elbow bend and a small misfit stream in a large valley. What process explains this?
options: River capture — the original river was diverted, leaving these tell-tale features
The valley was made by wind only
questions.expected: River capture — the original river was diverted, leaving these tell-tale features
questions.memo: A wind gap (dry former valley), an elbow of capture and an undersized misfit stream are classic evidence that a river was captured and its flow diverted.

GEO.G12.T1.GEO.A3.title: Catchment & river management
GEO.G12.T1.GEO.A3.description: Why managing drainage basins matters, human impacts on catchments, and a South African catchment-management case study.
GEO.G12.T1.GEO.A3.recovery_strategy: A catchment is one connected system — what happens upstream (pollution, farming, alien plants, building) affects everyone downstream. Good management protects water QUALITY and QUANTITY: control pollution, clear alien plants, protect wetlands and coordinate users across the whole basin.

questions.question: Why is a catchment managed as ONE connected system?
options: What happens upstream affects water quality and quantity downstream
questions.expected: What happens upstream affects water quality and quantity downstream
questions.memo: Water links the whole basin, so upstream pollution, farming or abstraction directly affect downstream users — management must be catchment-wide.

questions.question: Pollution discharged upstream will _______.
options: stay only at the discharge point
questions.memo: Because the river carries it onward, upstream pollution harms downstream towns, farms and ecosystems — a core reason for catchment management.

questions.question: Invasive alien plants (like wattle) in a catchment are a problem because they _______.
options: use large amounts of water, reducing river flow
questions.expected: use large amounts of water, reducing river flow
questions.memo: Thirsty alien trees consume far more water than indigenous plants, cutting the water that reaches rivers and dams — clearing them (e.g. Working for Water) boosts flow.

questions.question: Wetlands in a catchment are valuable because they _______.
options: store water, filter pollutants and reduce flooding
questions.expected: store water, filter pollutants and reduce flooding
questions.memo: Wetlands act as natural sponges and filters — storing and slowly releasing water, cleaning it and buffering floods. Protecting them is key to catchment health.

questions.question: Sort each as a HUMAN IMPACT that harms a catchment or a MANAGEMENT action that helps it.

items.text: Dumping factory waste into a river

questions.memo: Harms: pollution, overgrazing, draining wetlands. Helps: clearing aliens, protecting wetlands, treating sewage. Management reduces harm and restores health.

questions.question: Removing natural vegetation in a catchment tends to _______.
options: increase runoff, erosion and flood risk
store more water in the soil
questions.expected: increase runoff, erosion and flood risk
questions.memo: Bare ground sheds water quickly, raising flood peaks and washing soil into rivers (siltation) — vegetation cover protects the catchment.

questions.question: A learner says pollution upstream does not affect downstream users. Correct them.
options: The river carries pollution downstream, so it DOES affect downstream users
questions.expected: The river carries pollution downstream, so it DOES affect downstream users
questions.memo: Catchments are connected; pollution travels with the flow, harming everyone downstream — the whole basin must be managed together.

questions.question: South Africa's 'Working for Water' programme manages catchments by _______.
options: clearing invasive alien plants to restore water flow (and creating jobs)
questions.expected: clearing invasive alien plants to restore water flow (and creating jobs)
questions.memo: Working for Water clears water-hungry alien plants, restoring streamflow and biodiversity while providing employment — a noted SA management case study.

questions.question: Why must different water users (farms, cities, industry) in a catchment be COORDINATED?
options: They share one limited water resource, so fair allocation and protection are needed
Each can take unlimited water with no effect
questions.expected: They share one limited water resource, so fair allocation and protection are needed
questions.memo: All users draw on the same finite catchment, so allocation, pollution control and conservation must be planned together to keep supply fair and sustainable.

questions.question: Building on or paving large areas of a catchment increases flood risk because it _______.
options: reduces infiltration and speeds runoff into rivers
questions.expected: reduces infiltration and speeds runoff into rivers
questions.memo: Hard surfaces stop water soaking in, so rain rushes off into rivers all at once, raising flood peaks — urban catchments need good stormwater management.

questions.question: True or false: protecting a catchment safeguards both the QUANTITY and the QUALITY of water downstream.
questions.memo: Good catchment management keeps flow reliable (quantity) and clean (quality) — both essential for towns, farms and ecosystems.

questions.question: Soil eroded from a poorly-managed catchment silts up dams, which _______.
questions.memo: Sediment fills dams over time, cutting how much water they can store and shortening their useful life — a downstream cost of upstream erosion.

questions.question: Riverbank ('riparian') vegetation helps a catchment by _______.
options: stabilising banks, filtering runoff and providing habitat
questions.expected: stabilising banks, filtering runoff and providing habitat
questions.memo: Plants along the banks hold the soil, trap pollutants and sediment before they reach the water, and shelter wildlife — so they are protected in good management.

questions.question: True or false: catchment management often needs cooperation across municipal and even national borders.
questions.memo: Rivers cross administrative and national boundaries (e.g. shared with neighbouring countries), so management requires cross-border cooperation.

questions.question:
The table shows river flow before and after clearing alien plants in a catchment. What does it show?

| Stage | Dry-season flow (Ml/day) |
|------|------|
| Before clearing | 12 |
| After clearing | 18 |
options: Clearing thirsty alien plants increased river flow
Alien plants add water to rivers
questions.expected: Clearing thirsty alien plants increased river flow
questions.memo: Flow rose from 12 to 18 Ml/day after clearing, showing how removing water-hungry aliens frees up water for the river — the Working for Water rationale.

questions.question: Managing a drainage basin well is especially important in South Africa because it is a _______ country.
questions.memo: With limited, variable water, SA must protect every catchment to secure reliable, clean supply — making catchment management a national priority.

questions.question: Why can over-abstraction (taking too much water) upstream harm a wetland or estuary downstream?
options: Reduced flow starves the wetland/estuary of the water it needs to function
questions.expected: Reduced flow starves the wetland/estuary of the water it needs to function
questions.memo: Taking too much upstream lowers downstream flow, degrading wetlands and estuaries that depend on it — so 'environmental flows' must be maintained.

questions.question: Which combination best describes integrated catchment management?
options: Controlling pollution, clearing aliens, protecting wetlands and coordinating all users
questions.expected: Controlling pollution, clearing aliens, protecting wetlands and coordinating all users
questions.memo: Integrated management combines pollution control, alien clearing, wetland protection and fair, coordinated water use across the whole basin.

questions.question: True or false: healthy catchments support farming, cities, industry AND ecosystems at the same time.
questions.memo: A well-managed catchment delivers reliable, clean water for all these users together — which is why protecting it benefits the whole region.

questions.question: A city downstream suffers dirty, unreliable water. Upstream there is pollution, alien trees and eroded farmland. What integrated plan would help?
options: Control pollution, clear aliens, restore vegetation/wetlands and coordinate water use basin-wide
Only treat water at the city, ignoring upstream
questions.expected: Control pollution, clear aliens, restore vegetation/wetlands and coordinate water use basin-wide
questions.memo: Because the problems are upstream and connected, the fix must be catchment-wide: cut pollution, clear aliens, restore cover and wetlands, and manage all users together.

GEO.G12.T2.SET.A1.title: Study of settlements
GEO.G12.T2.SET.A1.description: Settlement concept, site vs situation, rural and urban settlements, and classification by size, complexity, pattern and function.
GEO.G12.T2.SET.A1.recovery_strategy: SITE = the actual ground a settlement stands on (flat land, near water, defensible). SITUATION = where it sits relative to other places (on routes, near resources, central). Settlements are classified by SIZE, PATTERN (shape) and FUNCTION (what they mainly do).

questions.question: A settlement is _______.
options: a place where people live, from a single farm to a large city
questions.expected: a place where people live, from a single farm to a large city
questions.memo: Settlements range from a lone farmstead to a megacity; they are simply places where people live and carry out activities.

questions.question: The SITE of a settlement is _______.
options: the actual piece of land it is built on
its position relative to other places
the number of people in it
questions.expected: the actual piece of land it is built on
questions.memo: Site = the physical ground itself (flat, sheltered, near water, defensible). Situation = its position in relation to surrounding places.

questions.question: The SITUATION of a settlement describes _______.
options: its position relative to other places and routes
questions.expected: its position relative to other places and routes
questions.memo: Situation is about connections — near a port, on a route junction, central to a farming region — which strongly shapes how a settlement grows.

questions.question: A learner says 'near a major road junction' describes a settlement's SITE. Correct them.
options: That describes SITUATION (position relative to routes); site is the actual ground
questions.expected: That describes SITUATION (position relative to routes); site is the actual ground
questions.memo: Being near a junction is about relationships to other places = situation. Site is the land the settlement physically occupies.

questions.question: Which is an example of a good SITE factor for an early settlement?
options: Flat, well-drained land with a reliable water supply
Being far from any other town
questions.expected: Flat, well-drained land with a reliable water supply
questions.memo: Classic site factors: water, flat dry building land, shelter, defensible ground and local resources like fertile soil or building stone.

questions.question: Settlements can be classified by their _______.
questions.memo: Geographers classify settlements by SIZE (population), PATTERN (shape/layout) and FUNCTION (their main activity or role).

questions.question: The FUNCTION of a settlement refers to _______.
options: its main activity or purpose (e.g. mining, port, market)
questions.expected: its main activity or purpose (e.g. mining, port, market)
questions.memo: Function is what a settlement mainly does — many settlements are multifunctional, but a dominant role (mining, port, resort) often defines them.

questions.question: Sort each detail as describing SITE or SITUATION.

items.text: Built on flat, dry land beside a river
Located where two major roads cross
Central to a large farming region
Near a sheltered natural harbour serving trade routes

questions.memo: Site = the actual land (flat, dry, hilltop). Situation = relationships to other places and routes (junction, central, near a harbour/trade).

questions.question: A RURAL settlement is generally _______ than an urban one.
questions.memo: Rural settlements are smaller and tied to the land (farming, forestry, mining); urban settlements are larger with industry, services and commerce.

questions.question: As settlements grow in size, their FUNCTIONS usually become _______.
questions.memo: Larger settlements offer more and higher-order functions (specialist shops, hospitals, universities), reflecting their place in the urban hierarchy.

questions.question: Match each settlement to a likely dominant FUNCTION.
questions.memo: 1 Kimberley → C mining town. 2 Durban → A port/harbour city. 3 Stellenbosch → B university/wine town. (Prompt: 1=Kimberley, 2=Durban, 3=Stellenbosch; A=port city, B=university/wine town, C=mining town.)

questions.question: A defensible hilltop with steep sides was historically chosen as a SITE because it _______.
options: was easy to defend against attack
questions.expected: was easy to defend against attack
questions.memo: Defence was a major early site factor; high, steep ground let people see and resist attackers — a physical-land (site) advantage.

questions.question: True or false: a settlement's situation can become MORE important over time as new roads or railways connect it.
questions.memo: Improved connections (a new highway, railway or port) can transform a settlement's situation and trigger rapid growth — situation is dynamic.

questions.question: A 'multifunctional' settlement is one that _______.
options: performs several functions (e.g. administration, commerce and industry)
questions.expected: performs several functions (e.g. administration, commerce and industry)
questions.memo: Large cities are typically multifunctional, combining government, business, industry, services and culture rather than a single role.

questions.question: Why did many old towns develop at a river crossing point (a 'bridging point')?
options: It combined a crossing of the river with trade routes meeting there (good situation)
Rivers have no effect on towns
questions.expected: It combined a crossing of the river with trade routes meeting there (good situation)
questions.memo: A bridging/fording point concentrates routes and trade, giving an excellent situation — many historic towns grew at such crossings.

questions.question: True or false: settlement size, pattern and function are linked — bigger settlements tend to have more complex patterns and functions.
questions.memo: Larger settlements usually have more elaborate layouts and a wider range of functions and services than small villages.

questions.question: A 'dormitory' (commuter) town mainly functions to _______.
options: house people who travel to work in a nearby larger city
questions.expected: house people who travel to work in a nearby larger city
questions.memo: Commuter/dormitory towns are residential settlements whose workers commute to a bigger centre nearby — a function created by good transport links.

questions.question: Which best shows the difference between site and situation for a port city?
options: Site = a sheltered deep-water bay; situation = its links to shipping routes and a productive hinterland
Site and situation are identical for ports
Site = its trade routes; situation = the bay
questions.expected: Site = a sheltered deep-water bay; situation = its links to shipping routes and a productive hinterland
questions.memo: The bay itself is the SITE; its position on global shipping lanes and behind a rich inland region is the SITUATION that lets it thrive.

questions.question: True or false: studying site and situation helps explain WHY a settlement is where it is and how it has grown.
questions.memo: Site explains the original choice of spot; situation explains connections and growth — together they account for a settlement's location and development.

questions.question: A town began on flat land by a ford, then boomed when a railway junction was built there. Identify the site and situation factors.
options: Site = flat land by the ford; situation = the route/railway junction that boosted growth
Site = the railway; situation = the flat land
questions.expected: Site = flat land by the ford; situation = the route/railway junction that boosted growth
questions.memo: The physical spot (flat land at the ford) is the site; the meeting of routes and the railway junction is the situation that drove its expansion.

GEO.G12.T2.SET.A2.title: Rural settlements
GEO.G12.T2.SET.A2.description: How site and situation affect rural location, classification by pattern and function, settlement shapes, and rural land use.
GEO.G12.T2.SET.A2.recovery_strategy: NUCLEATED = houses clustered together (often around water or a crossroads); DISPERSED = scattered farmsteads. Shapes follow the cause: LINEAR along a road/river/valley; CROSS-ROAD or T-SHAPED at junctions; ROUND/clustered around a central point like a water source.

questions.question: A NUCLEATED rural settlement is one where houses are _______.
questions.memo: Nucleated (clustered) settlements group houses together, often around a water source, crossroads or church; dispersed ones are spread out.

questions.question: A DISPERSED rural settlement has houses that are _______.
questions.memo: Dispersed settlements are scattered farmsteads spread across the land, common where farms are large and water is widely available.

questions.question: A village strung out along a road or river is a _______ settlement.
questions.memo: Linear settlements form a line along a route, river or valley because building follows that feature.

questions.question: Look at the diagram of settlement shapes. Which label shows a cross-road settlement?
options: C — buildings clustered where two roads meet at a crossing
A — a line of houses along one road
B — houses around a central point
questions.expected: C — buildings clustered where two roads meet at a crossing
questions.memo: A linear (along a road), B round/clustered, C cross-road (at a road crossing), D dispersed/isolated.

questions.question: Why might a rural settlement form a LINEAR shape along a river?
options: People build near the water and transport route, so houses line up along it
Linear shapes form for no reason
Rivers force houses into a circle
questions.expected: People build near the water and transport route, so houses line up along it
questions.memo: Access to water and the river as a routeway draws building alongside it, producing a long, thin (linear) settlement.

questions.question: A learner calls scattered farmsteads a 'nucleated' settlement. Correct them.
options: Scattered farmsteads are DISPERSED; nucleated means clustered together
questions.expected: Scattered farmsteads are DISPERSED; nucleated means clustered together
questions.memo: Dispersed = scattered; nucleated = clustered. The learner used the wrong term for spread-out farms.

questions.question: A round (clustered) settlement often forms around a central _______.
options: feature such as a water source, well or market square
questions.expected: feature such as a water source, well or market square
questions.memo: People cluster around a shared central feature — a well, water point, church or market — giving a roughly round, nucleated shape.

questions.question: Match each settlement shape to its likely cause.
questions.memo: 1 Linear → C built along a road/river. 2 Round → A clustered around a central water point. 3 Cross-road → B grew where two routes meet. (Prompt: 1=Linear, 2=Round, 3=Cross-road; A=central water point, B=route junction, C=along a road/river.)

questions.question: Which is a typical FUNCTION of a rural settlement?
questions.memo: Rural settlements are usually tied to primary activities — crop and livestock farming, forestry, fishing or mining.

questions.question: Good water supply, fertile soil and gentle land are _______ factors favouring a rural settlement's location.
questions.memo: These are qualities of the physical land itself — site factors — that make a spot suitable to settle and farm.

questions.question: Being close to a market town and a main road is a _______ factor favouring a rural settlement.
questions.memo: Connections to markets and routes are about position relative to other places — situation factors that help a settlement prosper.

questions.question: Dispersed settlement (scattered farms) is most likely where _______.
options: farms are large and water is widely available
everyone shares one tiny water point
questions.expected: farms are large and water is widely available
questions.memo: Large farms and plentiful, evenly-spread water let families live separately on their own land, producing a dispersed pattern.

questions.question: Nucleated settlement (clustering) is encouraged where _______.
options: water is found only at certain points, or people group for defence/services
every house has its own borehole
questions.expected: water is found only at certain points, or people group for defence/services
questions.memo: Limited water points, defence, and the convenience of shared services pull houses together into nucleated settlements.

questions.question: True or false: the shape of a rural settlement often reflects the physical features (roads, rivers, relief) around it.
questions.memo: Settlement shape responds to the land: linear along routes/rivers, round around water, cross-road at junctions — geography drives the form.

questions.question: Land use in a rural settlement is dominated by _______.
options: agriculture (fields, grazing) with some homes and services
questions.expected: agriculture (fields, grazing) with some homes and services
questions.memo: Most rural land is farmland (crops, pasture), with a small built-up area of homes, a school, shop or church.

questions.question: A T-shaped settlement most likely formed because _______.
options: a side road joins a main road, and building followed both
questions.expected: a side road joins a main road, and building followed both
questions.memo: Where a minor road meets a main road in a T, houses line both, giving the settlement a T shape — a route-controlled form.

questions.question: Why might a rural settlement decline if its only road is bypassed by a new highway?
options: Losing through-traffic worsens its situation, cutting trade and access
Roads have no effect on settlements
It would instantly become a city
questions.expected: Losing through-traffic worsens its situation, cutting trade and access
questions.memo: A bypass can damage a settlement's situation by removing passing trade and easy access — sometimes causing shops to close and the town to shrink.

questions.question: True or false: rural settlements can also be classified by function, e.g. a farming village, a mining village or a fishing village.
questions.memo: Like urban places, rural settlements have functions — most are agricultural, but some are mining, fishing, forestry or tourism villages.

questions.question: A surveyor maps a village where every house lies along one valley road beside a stream. Name the pattern and shape, and why.
options: Nucleated and linear — building followed the road and water along the valley
Dispersed and round — for no reason
questions.expected: Nucleated and linear — building followed the road and water along the valley
questions.memo: Houses grouped along a single route and stream give a nucleated, linear settlement shaped by the valley's road and water.

questions.question: Why do site and situation TOGETHER explain a rural settlement best?
options: Site explains the original spot; situation explains its links and whether it grows or declines
questions.expected: Site explains the original spot; situation explains its links and whether it grows or declines
questions.memo: Site gives the reason for the original location (water, land); situation (connections to markets and routes) shapes its later fortunes — both are needed.

GEO.G12.T2.SET.A3.title: Rural settlement issues
GEO.G12.T2.SET.A3.description: Rural-urban migration, causes and consequences of rural depopulation, a case study, and social-justice issues (land reform).
GEO.G12.T2.SET.A3.recovery_strategy: Rural DEPOPULATION = the countryside losing people, mainly young working-age adults moving to cities for jobs and services. This leaves an ageing population, labour shortages and closed schools/shops. Land reform and rural development aim to address the inequalities driving it.

questions.question: Rural depopulation means the countryside is _______.
questions.memo: Depopulation is a decline in rural population, mainly as people move away to towns and cities.

questions.question: The movement of people from the countryside to cities is called _______.
questions.memo: Rural-urban migration is the main driver of both rural depopulation and urban growth in developing countries.

questions.question: Which group is MOST likely to leave rural areas?
questions.memo: The young and able leave for jobs and education, so depopulation strips out the working-age group, leaving an ageing rural population.

questions.question: A learner says rural depopulation means too many people in the countryside. Correct them.
options: Depopulation is the LOSS of people; over-crowding is the opposite
questions.expected: Depopulation is the LOSS of people; over-crowding is the opposite
questions.memo: De-population = losing people. The learner confused it with overpopulation or over-crowding.

questions.question: Which is a PUSH factor driving people out of rural areas?
options: Few jobs, low wages and poor services
questions.expected: Few jobs, low wages and poor services
questions.memo: Push factors are rural problems people flee (unemployment, low income, drought, poor schools/clinics); city attractions are pull factors.

questions.question: Sort each as a CAUSE of rural depopulation or a CONSEQUENCE of it.

items.text: Lack of jobs in rural areas

questions.memo: Causes push/pull people away (no jobs, poor services, city wages); consequences are what's left behind (ageing population, closures, labour shortages).

questions.question: A CONSEQUENCE of rural depopulation for the local economy is _______.
options: fewer workers and customers, so businesses and services close
questions.expected: fewer workers and customers, so businesses and services close
questions.memo: As people leave, demand and labour fall; shops, schools and clinics close, making the area even less attractive — a downward spiral.

questions.question: Remittances (money sent home by migrants) can HELP rural source areas by _______.
options: supporting families and funding food, schooling and small projects
questions.expected: supporting families and funding food, schooling and small projects
questions.memo: Migrants often send money home, easing rural poverty and funding needs — a positive link between the city and the countryside.

questions.question: In South Africa, land reform aims to _______.
options: redress past unequal access to land and support rural development
questions.expected: redress past unequal access to land and support rural development
questions.memo: Land reform addresses the historical injustice of unequal land ownership, aiming to give more people access to productive land and improve rural livelihoods.

questions.question: A social-justice issue in many rural areas is unequal access to _______.
options: land, water, services and economic opportunities
questions.expected: land, water, services and economic opportunities
questions.memo: Rural social justice concerns fair access to land, water, healthcare, education and jobs — long-standing inequalities the state seeks to address.

questions.question: How can improving rural areas REDUCE depopulation?
options: Better jobs, services and infrastructure reduce the reasons to leave
questions.expected: Better jobs, services and infrastructure reduce the reasons to leave
questions.memo: Tackling the push factors — creating rural jobs and improving schools, clinics, roads and electricity — keeps more people in the countryside.

questions.question:
The table shows a rural district's population. What is happening?

| Year | Population | % aged 15–40 |
|------|------|------|
| 2000 | 50 000 | 38 |
| 2020 | 36 000 | 22 |
options: Depopulation, with young adults leaving (ageing population)
questions.expected: Depopulation, with young adults leaving (ageing population)
questions.memo: Total population fell and the young-adult share dropped from 38% to 22% — classic depopulation through out-migration of working-age people.

questions.question: Why does rural depopulation often make farm production HARDER?
options: A shrinking, ageing workforce means fewer people to work the land
questions.expected: A shrinking, ageing workforce means fewer people to work the land
questions.memo: Losing young labour leaves farms short of workers, which can cut production and leave land underused — a real consequence of depopulation.

questions.question: True or false: rural depopulation in the source area and rapid urban growth in the city are two sides of the same migration.
questions.memo: The same rural-urban migration empties the countryside and swells the cities — linked processes to be managed together.

questions.question: Investing in rural infrastructure (roads, electricity, water, internet) helps by _______.
options: making rural areas more liveable and economically viable
questions.expected: making rural areas more liveable and economically viable
questions.memo: Better infrastructure attracts business, supports farming and improves life, helping retain people and even draw some back.

questions.question: A NEGATIVE social consequence of depopulation can be _______.
options: loss of community life as people and services leave
questions.expected: loss of community life as people and services leave
questions.memo: As numbers fall, social life weakens — clubs, churches and schools close and community ties fray, especially for those left behind.

questions.question: Why is land reform considered both an economic and a social-justice issue?
options: It addresses past unfairness in land ownership AND aims to make land productive for livelihoods
It has no link to the economy
questions.expected: It addresses past unfairness in land ownership AND aims to make land productive for livelihoods
questions.memo: Land reform seeks to right historical injustice (social justice) while enabling people to earn a living from the land (economic development) — both together.

questions.question: True or false: depopulation can become a 'vicious cycle' where people leave, services close, and that makes even more people leave.
questions.memo: Out-migration triggers closures and decline, which push still more people out — a self-reinforcing downward spiral that intervention must break.

questions.question: A rural village loses its clinic and high school as families leave for the city. Suggest a strategy to address the underlying problem.
options: Create local jobs and restore services so people have reasons to stay
questions.expected: Create local jobs and restore services so people have reasons to stay
questions.memo: Tackling the push factors — jobs, services and infrastructure — addresses why people leave, helping to stabilise and even reverse depopulation.

questions.question: Why must rural issues be tackled to ease pressure on cities too?
options: Improving rural areas slows migration, reducing overcrowding and informal settlements in cities
Rural and urban areas are unconnected
questions.expected: Improving rural areas slows migration, reducing overcrowding and informal settlements in cities
questions.memo: Because rural push and urban pull are linked, strengthening rural areas reduces the flood of migrants and the strain on city housing and services.

GEO.G12.T2.SET.A4.title: Urban settlements
GEO.G12.T2.SET.A4.description: Origin and development of urban settlements, urbanisation, site and situation, and classification by function.
GEO.G12.T2.SET.A4.recovery_strategy: Urban FUNCTION = a town's main job: PORT/break-of-bulk (goods change transport), JUNCTION (route crossing), GATEWAY/GAP (controls a route through a barrier), SPECIALISED (mining, university, resort), CENTRAL PLACE (services for a surrounding area).

questions.question: Urbanisation is the increase in the _______ of people living in towns and cities.
questions.memo: Urbanisation is the growing share of a population that lives in urban areas, driven by migration and city growth.

questions.question: A town whose main function is to handle goods changing from one transport type to another (e.g. ship to rail) is a _______ point.
questions.memo: At a break-of-bulk point goods are unloaded and reloaded onto a different transport (e.g. a port) — a key trade/transport function.

questions.question: A learner says a break-of-bulk point is where a city runs out of land. Correct them.
options: It is where goods change transport mode (e.g. ship to rail), not where land runs out
It is a type of farm
questions.expected: It is where goods change transport mode (e.g. ship to rail), not where land runs out
questions.memo: Break-of-bulk = transferring cargo between transport types (often at a port). The learner misread the term.

questions.question: A town that grew where several transport routes meet is a _______ town.
questions.memo: Junction towns develop where routes (roads, railways, rivers) cross, concentrating trade and movement.

questions.question: A town that controls a route through a natural barrier (like a mountain pass) is a _______ town.
questions.memo: A gap or gateway town sits where a route passes through a barrier (a mountain gap or river valley), giving it strategic control of movement.

questions.question: Match each town to its function.
questions.memo: 1 Durban → C port/break-of-bulk. 2 Kimberley → A mining (specialised). 3 Sun City → D resort. 4 a route-crossing town → B junction. (Prompt: 1=Durban, 2=Kimberley, 3=Sun City, 4=route-crossing town; A=mining, B=junction, C=port, D=resort.)

questions.question: A 'central place' is a settlement that mainly _______.
options: provides goods and services to a surrounding area
questions.expected: provides goods and services to a surrounding area
questions.memo: A central place serves the needs (shops, services, markets) of the population in the area around it — the basis of central-place theory.

questions.question: A specialised city is one dominated by a single major function, such as _______.
options: mining, a university or a resort
questions.expected: mining, a university or a resort
questions.memo: Specialised cities are defined by one dominant role — a mining town, a university town, a resort or an administrative capital.

questions.question: Most early cities developed where the SITE and SITUATION offered _______.
options: water, defence, trade routes and a productive surrounding area
questions.expected: water, defence, trade routes and a productive surrounding area
questions.memo: Cities arose where good site (water, defence, building land) met good situation (trade routes, a rich hinterland to supply and serve).

questions.question: The area that a town serves and draws customers/resources from is its _______.
questions.memo: The hinterland (or sphere of influence) is the surrounding region a town serves and depends on — larger for bigger towns.

questions.question: Sort each town by its main FUNCTION.
questions.memo: Trade/transport functions move and exchange goods (port, junction, break-of-bulk); specialised towns centre on one activity (mining, resort, university).

questions.question: Why have the world's urban populations grown so rapidly in the last century?
options: Industrialisation and rural-urban migration drew people to cities for jobs
