questions.expected: Industrialisation and rural-urban migration drew people to cities for jobs
questions.memo: Industrial jobs and services pulled people from rural areas; today most of humanity lives in urban areas — the result of sustained urbanisation.

questions.question: A town located where a railway is forced to cross a river is benefiting from its _______.
questions.memo: Its position controlling a crossing of routes is a situation advantage that concentrates movement and trade there.

questions.question: True or false: a port city is a type of break-of-bulk point because cargo transfers between ships and land transport there.
questions.memo: At a port, goods are unloaded from ships onto trucks/trains (and vice versa) — a classic break-of-bulk function.

questions.question: Larger cities have larger spheres of influence because they _______.
options: offer more high-order goods and services that attract people from further away
questions.expected: offer more high-order goods and services that attract people from further away
questions.memo: Big cities provide specialist, high-order services (major hospitals, universities, airports) that draw people from a wide region — a large sphere of influence.

questions.question: A mining town may decline when _______.
options: the mineral runs out or its price collapses
questions.expected: the mineral runs out or its price collapses
questions.memo: Single-function mining towns are vulnerable: when the resource is exhausted or prices crash, jobs vanish and the town can become a 'ghost town'.

questions.question: True or false: most large cities are multifunctional, combining trade, industry, services and administration.
questions.memo: While a city may have started with one function, large cities grow to perform many roles at once — they are multifunctional.

questions.question: Why did many South African cities originally develop near the coast or on the goldfields?
options: Coastal sites offered ports/trade; the goldfields offered mineral wealth — both strong location factors
questions.expected: Coastal sites offered ports/trade; the goldfields offered mineral wealth — both strong location factors
questions.memo: Ports (Cape Town, Durban) grew on trade situation; Johannesburg grew on the gold-bearing Witwatersrand — site/situation resources shaped SA's urban map.

questions.question: A break-of-bulk port, a junction and a gateway town all share which underlying advantage?
options: A strong situation that concentrates movement, trade and people
questions.expected: A strong situation that concentrates movement, trade and people
questions.memo: All three owe their growth to favourable situation — controlling or concentrating the flow of goods and people through that point.

questions.question: A coastal town has a deep sheltered bay, sits on global shipping routes, and unloads cargo onto railways inland. Classify its function and explain.
options: A port / break-of-bulk town — its site (bay) and situation (routes) make it a trade and transport hub
A mining town — for the minerals
A dormitory town with no trade
questions.expected: A port / break-of-bulk town — its site (bay) and situation (routes) make it a trade and transport hub
questions.memo: The sheltered bay (site) plus position on shipping lanes and cargo transfer to rail (situation) define a port and break-of-bulk trade/transport function.

GEO.G12.T2.SET.A5.title: Urban hierarchies
GEO.G12.T2.SET.A5.description: Urban hierarchy, central place, threshold population, sphere of influence, range of goods, and low/high-order functions and centres.
GEO.G12.T2.SET.A5.recovery_strategy: LOW-ORDER goods/services are cheap, bought often, with a small THRESHOLD and short RANGE (bread, spaza). HIGH-ORDER goods are expensive, bought rarely, needing a large threshold and long range (specialist hospital, university). Hence: many small centres, few big ones.

questions.question: An urban hierarchy arranges settlements by their _______.
options: size and the range of functions/services they offer
questions.expected: size and the range of functions/services they offer
questions.memo: The hierarchy runs from many small hamlets/villages up to a few large cities, with size and the level of services increasing up the order.

questions.question: The minimum number of customers needed to support a service is its _______ population.
questions.memo: Threshold = the minimum market needed for a service to survive. High-order services need large thresholds; low-order ones need small thresholds.

questions.question: The maximum distance people will travel to buy a good or use a service is its _______.
questions.memo: Range = how far customers will travel for it. People travel far for high-order goods (rarely bought) but only short distances for low-order goods (daily needs).

questions.question: A loaf of bread is a _______ good.
questions.memo: Low-order goods are cheap and bought frequently (bread, milk), needing only a small threshold and short range — found in many small centres.

questions.question: A university or specialist hospital is a _______ service.
questions.memo: High-order services are expensive and rarely needed, requiring a large threshold and long range — so they are found only in a few big centres.

questions.question: A learner calls a daily loaf of bread a 'high-order good'. Correct them.
options: Bread is LOW-order — cheap, bought often, with a small threshold and short range
Order does not apply to bread
questions.expected: Bread is LOW-order — cheap, bought often, with a small threshold and short range
questions.memo: Frequently-bought everyday items are low-order. High-order goods are expensive and bought rarely (cars, specialist care).

questions.question: There are MANY small low-order centres but FEW large high-order centres because _______.
options: high-order services need large thresholds, so only a few big centres can support them
questions.expected: high-order services need large thresholds, so only a few big centres can support them
questions.memo: Big thresholds mean only a few centres have enough customers for high-order services, while low-order services (small thresholds) are everywhere — shaping the hierarchy.

questions.question: The area served by a central place is its _______.
questions.memo: The sphere of influence is the surrounding region a central place serves; bigger, higher-order centres have larger spheres.

questions.question: Match each centre to its likely service level.
questions.memo: 1 Village → C low-order (spaza, primary school). 2 Town → B middle-order (supermarket, clinic). 3 City → A high-order (university, specialist hospital). (Prompt: 1=Village, 2=Town, 3=City; A=high-order services, B=middle-order, C=low-order.)

questions.question: Why will people travel FURTHER for a high-order good than a low-order one?
options: High-order goods are expensive and bought rarely, so the long trip is worthwhile
Range is the same for all goods
questions.expected: High-order goods are expensive and bought rarely, so the long trip is worthwhile
questions.memo: For a costly, infrequent purchase (a car, a specialist appointment) a long journey is justified; for daily bread it is not — so high-order goods have a longer range.

questions.question: A spaza shop survives in a small township because bread and airtime have a _______ threshold.
questions.memo: Low-order goods need only a small market to be viable, so small centres can support shops selling them.

questions.question: A learner says a small village can support a specialist hospital. Why is this unlikely?
options: A specialist hospital is high-order and needs a large threshold the village cannot provide
questions.expected: A specialist hospital is high-order and needs a large threshold the village cannot provide
questions.memo: High-order services require many customers (a large threshold); a small village lacks the population, so such services locate in cities.

questions.question:
The table ranks centres. Which would have the FEWEST in a region?

| Centre | Order of services |
|------|------|
| Hamlet | Lowest |
| Town | Middle |
| City | Highest |
questions.memo: The higher the order, the fewer the centres: many hamlets, fewer towns, very few cities — the classic hierarchy pyramid.

questions.question: True or false: as you go UP the urban hierarchy, settlements become fewer but offer more and higher-order services.
questions.memo: Up the hierarchy: fewer settlements, larger size, bigger thresholds, longer ranges and more high-order functions.

questions.question: If the range of a service is SHORTER than its threshold area, the service will _______.
options: fail, because not enough customers can reach it
questions.expected: fail, because not enough customers can reach it
questions.memo: For a service to survive, its range (how far people travel) must be large enough to capture its threshold market; if not, it cannot get enough customers.

questions.question: Higher-order centres have LARGER spheres of influence because _______.
options: their high-order services draw people from a wide area
questions.expected: their high-order services draw people from a wide area
questions.memo: Specialist services attract customers from far away, so big centres serve large regions — a wide sphere of influence.

questions.question: Which list is in the correct order from LOWEST to HIGHEST in the urban hierarchy?
questions.memo: Smallest to largest: hamlet → village → town → city (→ conurbation), with services increasing up the order.

questions.question: Online shopping and delivery can change central-place patterns by _______.
options: extending the range of goods so people no longer need to travel to a centre
questions.expected: extending the range of goods so people no longer need to travel to a centre
questions.memo: E-commerce lets even high-order goods reach customers anywhere, effectively increasing range and challenging the traditional need to travel to higher-order centres.

questions.question: True or false: threshold, range and sphere of influence together explain why settlements form a hierarchy.
questions.memo: These concepts explain which services a centre can support and how far it serves — producing the pattern of many small and few large centres.

questions.question: A new specialist eye hospital is planned. Using hierarchy concepts, where should it go and why?
options: In a large city, because its high threshold needs a big population and wide sphere of influence
questions.expected: In a large city, because its high threshold needs a big population and wide sphere of influence
questions.memo: A high-order service requires a large threshold market, so it locates in a big city that can supply enough patients and draw them from a wide region.

GEO.G12.T2.SET.A6.title: Urban structure & patterns
GEO.G12.T2.SET.A6.description: Land-use zones, urban profile, factors shaping morphology, models of urban structure (incl. the South African city), and changing SA urban patterns.
GEO.G12.T2.SET.A6.recovery_strategy: The CBD (central business district) has the highest land values, tallest buildings and best accessibility. Land value generally FALLS outwards. The SOUTH AFRICAN city is distinctive: apartheid planning placed townships and 'buffer zones' that separated communities — patterns that still shape cities today.

questions.question: The CBD (central business district) of a city is usually characterised by _______.
options: the highest land values, tallest buildings and best accessibility
the cheapest land and lowest buildings
questions.expected: the highest land values, tallest buildings and best accessibility
questions.memo: The CBD is the commercial heart: most accessible, highest land values, tall buildings and a concentration of shops and offices.

questions.question: Land values in a city generally _______ with distance from the CBD.
questions.memo: Land is most valuable in the accessible centre and generally falls in value outward — a key influence on the pattern of land use.

questions.question: Different areas of a city used for housing, industry, shops, etc., are called land-use _______.
questions.memo: Cities are divided into land-use zones (CBD, residential, industrial, etc.), each with characteristic activities and land values.

questions.question: Look at the urban model diagram. Which label shows the CBD?
options: A — the central core with tall buildings
C — the industrial zone by the railway
questions.expected: A — the central core with tall buildings
questions.memo: A CBD (centre), B suburbs, C industry (often along transport routes), D rural-urban fringe at the edge.

questions.question: Which factor strongly influences a city's internal structure (morphology)?
options: Land values, accessibility, history and planning decisions
questions.expected: Land values, accessibility, history and planning decisions
questions.memo: City shape is moulded by land value, transport/accessibility, relief, history and planning (including, in SA, apartheid planning).

questions.question: The South African city model is DISTINCTIVE because of the lasting effects of _______.
questions.memo: Apartheid laws forced racial segregation, placing townships far from the centre and separating areas with 'buffer zones' — a pattern still visible today.

questions.question: A 'buffer zone' in the apartheid city was _______.
options: open land (or a road/railway) separating segregated residential areas
the city's main park for all
questions.expected: open land (or a road/railway) separating segregated residential areas
questions.memo: Buffer zones (open land, highways, industry) were deliberately used to keep racially-defined areas apart — a defining feature of the SA city.

questions.question: A learner says the CBD has the lowest land values and tallest trees. Correct them.
options: The CBD has the HIGHEST land values and tallest buildings, not trees
questions.expected: The CBD has the HIGHEST land values and tallest buildings, not trees
questions.memo: The CBD is the high-value, high-rise commercial core — the learner described the opposite.

questions.question: Heavy industry in many cities locates _______.
options: along railways, rivers or main roads, often near the edge or in zones away from housing
in the very centre of the CBD
on top of the tallest buildings
questions.expected: along railways, rivers or main roads, often near the edge or in zones away from housing
questions.memo: Industry needs transport links and large, cheaper land, so it clusters along routes and in zones — usually separated from high-quality housing.

questions.question: In the apartheid-era SA city, townships were typically located _______.
options: far from the CBD and jobs, on the urban periphery
next to all the best services
questions.expected: far from the CBD and jobs, on the urban periphery
questions.memo: Townships were placed on the edges, far from work and services, forcing long, costly commutes — a spatial injustice still being addressed.

questions.question: The 'urban profile' refers to _______.
options: the changing height of buildings across the city (e.g. tall in the CBD, lower outward)
questions.expected: the changing height of buildings across the city (e.g. tall in the CBD, lower outward)
questions.memo: The urban profile is the skyline cross-section — buildings are tallest where land values are highest (the CBD) and lower towards the edges.

questions.question: Match each urban zone to its typical feature.
questions.memo: 1 CBD → C tall buildings, highest land value. 2 Inner city → A older, denser, mixed/poorer housing. 3 Suburbs → D lower-density housing outward. 4 Rural-urban fringe → B city meets countryside. (Prompt: 1=CBD, 2=Inner city, 3=Suburbs, 4=Rural-urban fringe; A=older dense housing, B=city meets countryside, C=high-rise core, D=low-density suburbs.)

questions.question: Since 1994, South African cities have been changing through _______.
options: desegregation, new housing and attempts at more integrated planning
questions.expected: desegregation, new housing and attempts at more integrated planning
questions.memo: Post-apartheid, cities are slowly desegregating, with RDP/new housing, upgrading and integration efforts — though apartheid's spatial legacy persists.

questions.question: True or false: the wealthiest residential suburbs in many cities are found away from heavy industry and pollution.
questions.memo: High-income areas tend to locate in pleasant, less-polluted areas (often upwind/uphill), away from industry — a common pattern in city models.

questions.question: Why are tall buildings concentrated in the CBD?
options: High land values make builders go upward to use the expensive space intensively
questions.expected: High land values make builders go upward to use the expensive space intensively
questions.memo: Where land is most expensive and accessible, building UP maximises floor space per square metre — hence skyscrapers cluster in the CBD.

questions.question: The 'rural-urban fringe' is _______.
options: the transition zone at the edge of the city where it meets the countryside
the very centre of the city
questions.expected: the transition zone at the edge of the city where it meets the countryside
questions.memo: The fringe is the mixed zone of new housing, smallholdings and open land where urban gives way to rural — often where cities expand.

questions.question: Why do apartheid-era spatial patterns still cause problems in SA cities today?
options: Many poor communities remain far from jobs and services, facing long, costly commutes
Segregation has fully ended in space
Townships are now in the CBD
questions.expected: Many poor communities remain far from jobs and services, facing long, costly commutes
questions.memo: The peripheral location of townships, fixed in the built environment, still imposes long commutes and limits access to opportunity — a lasting spatial injustice.

questions.question: Models like the multiple-nuclei model suggest cities grow around _______.
options: several separate centres (nuclei), not just one CBD
questions.expected: several separate centres (nuclei), not just one CBD
questions.memo: The multiple-nuclei model recognises that modern cities have several specialised centres (CBD, industrial areas, out-of-town malls) rather than growing from one core.

questions.question: True or false: urban models are simplified — real cities are shaped by their own relief, history and planning.
questions.memo: Models are useful generalisations, but each real city is modified by its physical setting, history (e.g. apartheid) and planning choices.

questions.question: A planner wants a more INTEGRATED post-apartheid city. Which approach fits?
options: Build affordable housing closer to jobs and transport, and bridge old buffer zones
Move all housing further from the centre
Concentrate services in one wealthy area
questions.expected: Build affordable housing closer to jobs and transport, and bridge old buffer zones
questions.memo: Integration means bringing housing, jobs and transport together and breaking down apartheid-era separation — densifying and connecting rather than pushing the poor outward.

GEO.G12.T2.SET.A7.title: Urban settlement issues
GEO.G12.T2.SET.A7.description: Recent SA urbanisation, issues of rapid urbanisation, informal settlements, and case studies of managing urban challenges.
GEO.G12.T2.SET.A7.recovery_strategy: Rapid urbanisation outpaces housing and services, producing INFORMAL SETTLEMENTS, overcrowding, traffic and strained water/sanitation. The cause is structural — too little affordable housing and deep inequality — not personal choice. Responses: upgrade settlements, integrated housing, better transport and services.

questions.question: An informal settlement is an area of _______.
options: self-built housing on land without formal planning or services
questions.expected: self-built housing on land without formal planning or services
questions.memo: Informal settlements (shack areas) are unplanned, often lacking secure tenure, formal services and infrastructure.

questions.question: Rapid urbanisation often outpaces the supply of _______.
questions.memo: When people arrive faster than cities can provide homes, water, sanitation and jobs, shortages and informal settlements result.

questions.question: A learner says informal settlements exist because people refuse formal housing. Correct them.
options: They exist mainly because there is too little affordable housing, not by choice
questions.expected: They exist mainly because there is too little affordable housing, not by choice
questions.memo: Informal settlements are a response to housing shortages, poverty and inequality — a structural problem, not a personal preference.

questions.question: Sort each as an ISSUE of rapid urbanisation or a STRATEGY to manage it.

items.text: Building integrated affordable housing near jobs

questions.memo: Issues are the problems (housing shortage, congestion, weak services); strategies are the responses (upgrading, transport, integrated housing).

questions.question: A common problem in fast-growing cities is traffic _______.
questions.memo: Too many vehicles for the road network causes congestion, wasting time and fuel and worsening air pollution — a major urban issue.

questions.question: Upgrading an informal settlement 'in situ' means _______.
options: improving it where it is with services, roads and secure tenure
demolishing it and moving everyone far away
questions.expected: improving it where it is with services, roads and secure tenure
questions.memo: In-situ upgrading installs water, sanitation, roads and tenure without uprooting the community, keeping people near jobs and networks — often better than relocation.

questions.question: Why do informal settlements often have poor sanitation and health risks?
options: High density without formal water, toilets and refuse services spreads disease
questions.expected: High density without formal water, toilets and refuse services spreads disease
questions.memo: Crowding plus a lack of clean water, toilets and waste removal allows diseases like cholera and TB to spread — a key reason to provide services.

questions.question:
The table shows a city's growth. What challenge does it imply?

| Year | City population | Houses built (cumulative) |
|------|------|------|
| 2010 | 1,0 m | 250 000 |
| 2020 | 1,6 m | 300 000 |
options: Population grew much faster than housing — a worsening housing shortage
questions.expected: Population grew much faster than housing — a worsening housing shortage
questions.memo: Population rose 60% while houses rose only 20% — demand far outstripped supply, the classic driver of informal settlement growth.

questions.question: In South Africa, government housing projects (e.g. RDP houses) aim to _______.
options: provide formal, serviced housing for low-income families
questions.expected: provide formal, serviced housing for low-income families
questions.memo: State housing programmes deliver basic formal homes with services to reduce the housing backlog — though demand still outpaces supply.

questions.question: An effective response to traffic congestion is _______.
questions.memo: Good, affordable public transport (like Bus Rapid Transit) moves more people with fewer vehicles, easing congestion and pollution.

questions.question: Why is providing services to informal settlements often better than demolishing them?
options: It keeps people near jobs and networks while improving health and dignity
Demolition is always cheaper and kinder
People prefer to be relocated far away
questions.expected: It keeps people near jobs and networks while improving health and dignity
questions.memo: Upgrading respects existing livelihoods and social networks and is often more sustainable than forced removals to distant, poorly-located sites.

questions.question: Rapid urbanisation puts pressure on 'service provision', which means _______.
options: supplying water, electricity, sanitation and refuse removal
questions.expected: supplying water, electricity, sanitation and refuse removal
questions.memo: Basic municipal services struggle to keep up with fast growth, leaving many without reliable water, power, sanitation or waste collection.

questions.question: True or false: building affordable housing CLOSE to jobs and transport helps reduce both poverty and long commutes.
questions.memo: Well-located housing cuts transport costs and time and improves access to work — addressing the apartheid legacy of poor people living far from opportunity.

questions.question: Informal settlements on floodplains or steep slopes are especially risky because _______.
options: they face flooding, fire and landslide hazards with little protection
questions.expected: they face flooding, fire and landslide hazards with little protection
questions.memo: Limited land choices push settlements onto hazardous sites; combined with dense, flammable shacks and poor drainage, this raises disaster risk.

questions.question: Overcrowding in cities is a direct result of _______.
options: too many people for the available housing and space
questions.expected: too many people for the available housing and space
questions.memo: When population outpaces housing, people crowd into limited space — many in one room or shack — straining services and health.

questions.question: True or false: rapid urbanisation has both costs (overcrowding, informal settlements) and potential benefits (jobs, services, opportunity).
questions.memo: Cities offer real opportunities AND serious challenges; good management aims to capture the benefits while reducing the costs.

questions.question: Densifying a city (building more homes within the existing area) helps by _______.
options: housing more people near jobs and services without endless sprawl
questions.expected: housing more people near jobs and services without endless sprawl
questions.memo: Densification (e.g. flats, infill) uses land efficiently, supports public transport and keeps people close to opportunity — countering wasteful sprawl.

questions.question: A city addresses environmental, economic AND social-justice concerns when it _______.
options: upgrades settlements with services, creates jobs and locates housing fairly near opportunity
questions.expected: upgrades settlements with services, creates jobs and locates housing fairly near opportunity
questions.memo: Holistic urban management improves the environment (services, sanitation), the economy (jobs) and fairness (access to opportunity) together.

questions.question: True or false: the growth of informal settlements is closely linked to rural-urban migration and the shortage of affordable housing.
questions.memo: Migrants arriving faster than affordable housing can be built end up in informal settlements — the two trends are tightly connected.

questions.question: A South African city has a fast-growing informal settlement near the centre, with poor sanitation and flooding. Propose a sound management approach.
options: Upgrade in situ — install water, sanitation, drainage and tenure, and improve transport — rather than distant relocation
Demolish it and move everyone to the far periphery
Fence it off and provide nothing
questions.expected: Upgrade in situ — install water, sanitation, drainage and tenure, and improve transport — rather than distant relocation
questions.memo: In-situ upgrading keeps residents near jobs while fixing services and hazards; forced removal to the periphery repeats apartheid-era injustices and worsens commutes.

GEO.G12.T3.ECO.A1.title: Structure of the economy
GEO.G12.T3.ECO.A1.description: Economic sectors (primary, secondary, tertiary, quaternary), their contribution by value and employment, and using statistical/graphical data.
GEO.G12.T3.ECO.A1.recovery_strategy: PRIMARY = extracting raw materials (farming, mining, fishing). SECONDARY = manufacturing (factories). TERTIARY = services (shops, banks, transport). QUATERNARY = knowledge/research (IT, R&D). In SA the tertiary sector dominates GDP; sectors can differ in their share of VALUE versus EMPLOYMENT.

questions.question: The PRIMARY sector of the economy involves _______.
options: extracting raw materials (farming, mining, fishing, forestry)
questions.expected: extracting raw materials (farming, mining, fishing, forestry)
questions.memo: Primary activities take raw materials directly from nature — farming, mining, fishing, forestry.

questions.question: The SECONDARY sector involves _______.
options: manufacturing and processing raw materials into goods
questions.expected: manufacturing and processing raw materials into goods
questions.memo: Secondary activities turn raw materials into products — factories, construction, processing.

questions.question: The TERTIARY sector provides _______.
questions.memo: Tertiary activities are services — retail, finance, transport, health, education, tourism.

questions.question: The QUATERNARY sector involves _______.
questions.memo: Quaternary activities are knowledge-based — research and development, IT, consultancy — the most advanced sector.

questions.question: A learner calls a car factory a primary-sector activity. Correct them.
options: Manufacturing cars is SECONDARY; primary is extracting raw materials
questions.expected: Manufacturing cars is SECONDARY; primary is extracting raw materials
questions.memo: Making cars processes materials into goods = secondary. Primary would be mining the iron ore used to make the steel.

questions.question: Sort each activity into its economic sector.
questions.memo: Primary = extract (mining, maize); secondary = make (cars, clothing); tertiary = serve (banking, tourism).

questions.question: Which sector contributes the LARGEST share of South Africa's GDP?
questions.memo: Services (finance, trade, transport, government) dominate SA's GDP, as in most modern economies, while primary's share has fallen.

questions.question:
The table shows two sectors. What does it reveal about value vs employment?

| Sector | % of GDP | % of jobs |
|------|------|------|
| Mining | 8 | 5 |
| Agriculture | 3 | 15 |
options: Agriculture employs many but adds little value; mining adds more value with fewer workers
Both add equal value and jobs
questions.expected: Agriculture employs many but adds little value; mining adds more value with fewer workers
questions.memo: A sector's share of VALUE (GDP) can differ from its share of EMPLOYMENT — agriculture is labour-intensive but low-value here; mining the reverse.

questions.question: As economies develop, employment usually shifts FROM the primary sector TOWARDS _______.
questions.memo: Development typically moves workers from farming/mining into manufacturing and especially services as the economy modernises.

questions.question: Match each job to its sector.
questions.memo: 1 Fisher → C primary. 2 Steel worker → A secondary. 3 Software developer → D quaternary. 4 Shop assistant → B tertiary. (Prompt: 1=Fisher, 2=Steel worker, 3=Software developer, 4=Shop assistant; A=secondary, B=tertiary, C=primary, D=quaternary.)

questions.question: True or false: a sector can have a small share of jobs but a large share of GDP value (and vice versa).
questions.memo: Capital-intensive sectors (e.g. mining) can produce high value with few workers; labour-intensive ones (e.g. small-scale farming) the opposite.

questions.question: Processing raw materials before export (beneficiation) shifts activity from the primary to the _______ sector.
questions.memo: Turning ore into metal or crops into food is secondary-sector manufacturing — it adds value and jobs at home rather than exporting raw materials.

questions.question: Why do governments study the structure of the economy by sector?
options: To see where value and jobs come from and plan development and skills
questions.expected: To see where value and jobs come from and plan development and skills
questions.memo: Knowing each sector's contribution guides policy — where to invest, what skills to train and how to grow and diversify the economy.

questions.question: A bar graph shows GDP shares of 60% tertiary, 20% secondary, 20% primary. This is typical of a/an _______ economy.
questions.memo: A large tertiary share is the signature of a modern, developed-style economy where services dominate output.

questions.question: True or false: the primary sector still matters in South Africa for export earnings and employment, even though its GDP share is smaller than services.
questions.memo: Mining and agriculture remain important for exports, foreign exchange and rural jobs, despite services leading GDP.

questions.question: Which is a QUATERNARY-sector example?
questions.memo: Research and high-level knowledge work (R&D, IT, consultancy) is quaternary — the most advanced, knowledge-based sector.

questions.question: Why might a country want to GROW its secondary and tertiary sectors rather than rely on the primary sector?
options: They add more value, create varied jobs and reduce dependence on raw-material prices
questions.expected: They add more value, create varied jobs and reduce dependence on raw-material prices
questions.memo: Manufacturing and services add value, diversify the economy and create skilled jobs, reducing vulnerability to volatile commodity prices.

questions.question: True or false: graphs and statistics (like sector shares of GDP) are essential tools for analysing an economy's structure.
questions.memo: Statistical and graphical data let geographers compare sectors, track change over time and inform economic decisions.

questions.question: A tourism business (lodge, tours, restaurants) belongs to which sector?
questions.memo: Tourism provides services — accommodation, guiding, food, transport — so it is a tertiary-sector activity, important for SA's economy.

questions.question: A country exports raw ore and imports finished metal goods. How could it restructure its economy to gain more?
options: Develop secondary industry to process (beneficiate) the ore locally, adding value and jobs
questions.expected: Develop secondary industry to process (beneficiate) the ore locally, adding value and jobs
questions.memo: Building secondary-sector processing captures the value currently added abroad and creates jobs — moving up the value chain rather than just exporting raw materials.

GEO.G12.T3.ECO.A2.title: Agriculture
GEO.G12.T3.ECO.A2.description: Agriculture's contribution, small- vs large-scale farmers, products and markets, factors favouring/hindering farming, and food security.
GEO.G12.T3.ECO.A2.recovery_strategy: FOOD SECURITY = all people having reliable ACCESS to enough safe, nutritious food — depends on availability, affordability AND access, not just production. SA farming is limited by low, variable rainfall and limited arable land, and shaped by the history of land ownership; large commercial and small-scale farmers play different roles.

questions.question: Agriculture is part of which economic sector?
questions.memo: Farming extracts food and raw materials directly from the land, so it is a primary-sector activity.

questions.question: Large-scale COMMERCIAL farming is mainly aimed at _______.
options: producing crops/livestock for sale (markets and export)
questions.expected: producing crops/livestock for sale (markets and export)
questions.memo: Commercial farms produce for the market and export, using capital and technology; subsistence/small-scale farming focuses on feeding the family.

questions.question: Small-scale (subsistence) farmers mainly produce _______.
options: food for their own families, with any surplus sold locally
questions.expected: food for their own families, with any surplus sold locally
questions.memo: Subsistence farmers grow mainly to feed themselves, selling only small surpluses — important for rural livelihoods and local food.

questions.question: Food security means _______.
options: all people having reliable access to enough safe, nutritious food
growing the most food in the world
questions.expected: all people having reliable access to enough safe, nutritious food
questions.memo: Food security depends on availability AND affordability AND access for everyone — not just how much food a country produces overall.

questions.question: A learner says a country with big farms automatically has food security. Correct them.
options: Production alone isn't enough — people must also be able to AFFORD and ACCESS the food
Big farms guarantee everyone is fed
questions.expected: Production alone isn't enough — people must also be able to AFFORD and ACCESS the food
questions.memo: A country can produce plenty yet have hungry people if food is unaffordable or inaccessible — security is about access, not just output.

questions.question: Which is a factor that HINDERS agriculture in much of South Africa?
options: Low and unreliable rainfall with limited arable land
questions.expected: Low and unreliable rainfall with limited arable land
questions.memo: Only a small share of SA's land is arable, and rainfall is low and variable — major constraints on farming, alongside the history of land ownership.

questions.question: Sort each as a factor that FAVOURS or HINDERS South African agriculture.

items.text: A range of climates for varied crops
Good transport and ports for export

questions.memo: Favours: fertile areas, varied climate, export infrastructure. Hinders: drought, limited water, soil degradation.

questions.question: South Africa exports agricultural products such as _______.
questions.memo: SA is a notable exporter of citrus, wine, table grapes, deciduous fruit and (in good years) maize — earning foreign exchange.

questions.question: Agriculture's contribution to the SA economy includes _______.
options: food, jobs, export earnings and raw materials for industry
questions.expected: food, jobs, export earnings and raw materials for industry
questions.memo: Beyond a modest GDP share, farming provides food security, rural employment, export income and inputs for food processing and other industries.

questions.question: Why is WATER such a critical factor for South African farming?
options: The country is water-scarce, so reliable water (rain or irrigation) limits what can be farmed where
Water has no effect on crops
questions.expected: The country is water-scarce, so reliable water (rain or irrigation) limits what can be farmed where
questions.memo: With low, uneven rainfall, water availability determines which crops can grow where; much high-value farming depends on irrigation.

questions.question: The 'home market' for SA produce refers to _______.
questions.memo: The home (domestic) market is local consumers within SA; the export market is sales to other countries. Farmers serve both.

questions.question: A factor that FAVOURS commercial farming in a region is _______.
options: good soils, reliable water and access to markets and transport
questions.expected: good soils, reliable water and access to markets and transport
questions.memo: Successful commercial farming needs suitable climate and soil, reliable water, capital, and transport links to markets and ports.

questions.question: The history of land ownership affects SA agriculture today because _______.
options: past dispossession left land ownership very unequal, which land reform now seeks to address
ownership has no effect on farming
questions.expected: past dispossession left land ownership very unequal, which land reform now seeks to address
questions.memo: Apartheid-era land dispossession concentrated farmland, leaving deep inequality; land reform aims to broaden access and support emerging farmers.

questions.question: How can supporting SMALL-scale and emerging farmers improve food security?
options: More producers and local food supply improve availability, access and rural incomes
It has no effect on food security
questions.expected: More producers and local food supply improve availability, access and rural incomes
questions.memo: Backing small farmers (with training, inputs, land and markets) boosts local food supply, incomes and access — strengthening food security from the ground up.

questions.question:
The table shows rainfall and farming type. What link does it suggest?

| Area | Rainfall (mm) | Main farming |
|------|------|------|
| West coast interior | 200 | Extensive sheep grazing |
| Mpumalanga | 800 | Crops (maize) |
options: Lower rainfall suits extensive grazing; higher rainfall allows crop farming
Rainfall has no effect on farming
Dry areas grow the most maize
Wet areas can only graze sheep
questions.expected: Lower rainfall suits extensive grazing; higher rainfall allows crop farming
questions.memo: Dry areas (200 mm) support only extensive grazing; wetter areas (800 mm) allow rain-fed crops — rainfall strongly shapes land use.

questions.question: True or false: climate change (more droughts and heat) is a growing threat to South Africa's food production.
questions.memo: Hotter, drier and more variable conditions threaten yields, water supply and livestock — a rising risk to food security that farming must adapt to.

questions.question: Why can a wealthy country with little farmland still be food-secure?
options: It can afford to import the food its people need
questions.expected: It can afford to import the food its people need
questions.memo: Food security is about ACCESS; a rich country can import food reliably, while a poorer farming country may still have hungry people — access and affordability are key.

questions.question: Large commercial farms tend to be more _______ than small subsistence farms.
questions.memo: Commercial farms use machinery, irrigation and inputs to produce large quantities for sale; subsistence farms rely more on family labour.

questions.question: True or false: agriculture supplies raw materials for South Africa's food-processing and textile industries.
questions.memo: Farm products (grain, fruit, wool, cotton, hides) feed secondary industries like milling, canning, textiles and leather — linking the sectors.

questions.question: A region faces drought, eroded soils and many households unable to afford food. Suggest measures to improve food security.
options: Water-wise farming, soil conservation, support for small farmers, and help with food access/affordability
questions.expected: Water-wise farming, soil conservation, support for small farmers, and help with food access/affordability
questions.memo: Boosting production sustainably (drought-tolerant crops, soil care, supporting small farmers) AND improving access/affordability together tackle food insecurity.

GEO.G12.T3.ECO.A3.title: Mining
GEO.G12.T3.ECO.A3.description: Mining's contribution and significance, factors favouring/hindering it, and a case study of one major SA mineral.
GEO.G12.T3.ECO.A3.recovery_strategy: Mining built SA's economy (gold, platinum, coal, diamonds) — foreign exchange and jobs. BUT minerals are FINITE and prices swing; mining also damages the environment (acid mine drainage, dust, land), risks health and creates reliance on one sector. Diversifying reduces the risk.

questions.question: Mining belongs to which economic sector?
questions.memo: Mining extracts raw minerals from the earth, so it is a primary-sector activity.

questions.question: Which mineral was central to the founding of Johannesburg and SA's industrial economy?
questions.memo: The discovery of gold on the Witwatersrand (1886) created Johannesburg and powered SA's industrialisation; the country was long the world's top gold producer.

questions.question: South Africa is the world's leading producer of _______.
questions.memo: SA holds most of the world's platinum-group metals (in the Bushveld Complex) and is the leading producer — a major export earner.

questions.question: Mining contributes to the SA economy through _______.
options: export earnings, jobs and inputs for industry
questions.expected: export earnings, jobs and inputs for industry
questions.memo: Mining earns vital foreign exchange, employs many workers and supplies materials (coal, ore) for energy and manufacturing.

questions.question: Which is a factor that FAVOURS mining in South Africa?
questions.memo: SA's exceptional mineral wealth, plus established infrastructure, skills and capital, favour mining; high costs, depth and labour issues can hinder it.

questions.question: Sort each as a BENEFIT or a COST of mining.
questions.memo: Benefits: exports, jobs, infrastructure. Costs: water and land pollution, health risks. Mining is a major but double-edged industry.

questions.question: Acid mine drainage is a problem in which _______ flows from mines into water.
questions.memo: Water reacting with exposed sulphide minerals in old mines becomes acidic and toxic; when it reaches rivers and groundwater it is a serious pollution problem.

questions.question: A learner says mining has no downside for communities or the environment. Correct them.
options: Mining causes pollution, land damage and health risks, alongside its benefits
questions.expected: Mining causes pollution, land damage and health risks, alongside its benefits
questions.memo: Mining brings jobs and income BUT also acid mine drainage, dust, sinkholes, land degradation and miner health risks — real costs to weigh.

questions.question: Why is over-dependence on mining a RISK for an economy?
options: Minerals are finite and prices swing, so reliance on them leaves the economy vulnerable
questions.expected: Minerals are finite and prices swing, so reliance on them leaves the economy vulnerable
questions.memo: Finite reserves and volatile world prices make single-sector dependence risky; diversifying into manufacturing and services builds resilience.

questions.question: Which factor can HINDER mining in South Africa?
options: Deep, costly ore bodies, labour disputes and electricity/water constraints
questions.expected: Deep, costly ore bodies, labour disputes and electricity/water constraints
questions.memo: SA's gold is now very deep and expensive to mine; labour relations, power supply, water and safety all add challenges.

questions.question: Coal is especially significant in South Africa because it _______.
options: fuels most of the country's electricity generation
questions.expected: fuels most of the country's electricity generation
questions.memo: Coal underpins SA's energy supply (thermal power stations) as well as being a major export — central to the economy but a big source of emissions.

questions.question: Mining historically shaped SA's settlement and labour patterns by _______.
options: drawing migrant workers to mines and creating mining towns
questions.expected: drawing migrant workers to mines and creating mining towns
questions.memo: The migrant-labour system pulled men from rural areas and neighbouring countries to the mines, founding towns and shaping society for over a century.

questions.question: A health risk long associated with deep-level and dusty mining is _______.
questions.memo: Dust inhalation causes silicosis and raises TB risk; mining also carries accident and heat risks — major occupational-health concerns.

questions.question:
The table shows a mineral's price and the economy. What risk does it illustrate?

| Year | World price (index) | Mining GDP |
|------|------|------|
| 2018 | 100 | High |
| 2020 | 60 | Sharp drop |
options: A price crash sharply cuts mining income — the risk of commodity dependence
questions.expected: A price crash sharply cuts mining income — the risk of commodity dependence
questions.memo: When the world price fell from 100 to 60, mining income dropped sharply — showing how dependence on a single, price-volatile commodity is risky.

questions.question: Rehabilitating mined land means _______.
options: restoring it (e.g. re-shaping, re-vegetating) after mining ends
building a mine dump on it
questions.expected: restoring it (e.g. re-shaping, re-vegetating) after mining ends
questions.memo: Rehabilitation repairs the environment after mining — reshaping land, treating water and replanting — to reduce lasting damage.

questions.question: True or false: beneficiating minerals (processing them locally) adds value and creates more jobs than exporting raw ore.
questions.memo: Refining and manufacturing from minerals at home (e.g. jewellery, catalytic converters) captures more value and employment than exporting raw ore.

questions.question: Why do many former mining towns face hardship when a mine closes?
options: Their economy depended on the mine, so closure brings job losses and decline
Closing a mine always enriches a town
questions.expected: Their economy depended on the mine, so closure brings job losses and decline
questions.memo: Single-industry mining towns can collapse when the mine closes (resource exhaustion or low prices), causing unemployment and population loss.

questions.question: True or false: mining provides important inputs (coal, iron ore, platinum) for South Africa's energy and manufacturing industries.
questions.memo: Mining links to other sectors: coal for power, iron ore for steel, platinum for catalytic converters — fuelling energy and industry.

questions.question: A sustainable approach to mining tries to _______.
options: limit environmental harm, protect workers and plan for life after the mine
exhaust resources as fast as possible
questions.expected: limit environmental harm, protect workers and plan for life after the mine
questions.memo: Responsible mining controls pollution, ensures safety, rehabilitates land and helps communities diversify for when the resource runs out.

questions.question: A mining region worries about its future as ore runs low and prices fall. What strategy reduces the risk?
options: Diversify the local economy and beneficiate minerals so it does not depend on raw mining alone
Mine even faster with no plan
Rely entirely on the one mineral
questions.expected: Diversify the local economy and beneficiate minerals so it does not depend on raw mining alone
questions.memo: Building processing industries and other economic activities lessens dependence on finite, price-volatile raw mining — protecting jobs for the future.

GEO.G12.T3.ECO.A4.title: Secondary & tertiary sectors
GEO.G12.T3.ECO.A4.description: Contribution of secondary/tertiary sectors, types of industry, factors influencing industrial location, and SA's main industrial regions.
GEO.G12.T3.ECO.A4.recovery_strategy: RAW-MATERIAL-oriented industries (heavy, bulky inputs that lose weight, e.g. steel) locate near the raw material; MARKET-oriented industries (products bulky/perishable, e.g. bread) locate near customers. FOOTLOOSE industries (electronics, IT) can locate almost anywhere. Gauteng (PWV) is SA's largest industrial region.

questions.question: The secondary sector is also called the _______ sector.
questions.memo: Secondary = manufacturing/processing, turning raw materials into finished goods.

questions.question: A 'heavy industry' is one that _______.
options: uses large, bulky materials and equipment (e.g. iron and steel)
questions.expected: uses large, bulky materials and equipment (e.g. iron and steel)
questions.memo: Heavy industries (steel, chemicals, heavy machinery) handle bulky inputs and products; light industries make smaller goods (clothing, electronics).

questions.question: A RAW-MATERIAL-oriented industry locates near _______.
options: its raw materials (especially if they are bulky or lose weight in processing)
questions.expected: its raw materials (especially if they are bulky or lose weight in processing)
questions.memo: When raw materials are heavy or lose mass when processed (e.g. ore to metal), it is cheaper to locate the industry near the source — raw-material orientation.

questions.question: A MARKET-oriented industry locates near _______.
options: its customers (especially if products are bulky, fragile or perishable)
questions.expected: its customers (especially if products are bulky, fragile or perishable)
questions.memo: When the product is costly to transport (bulky/perishable, e.g. bread, soft drinks), the industry locates near the market.

questions.question: A learner says a heavy steel works should locate FAR from its raw materials. Correct them.
options: Heavy, weight-losing industries locate NEAR their raw materials to cut transport costs
Location does not matter for steel
questions.expected: Heavy, weight-losing industries locate NEAR their raw materials to cut transport costs
questions.memo: Steel-making uses huge amounts of heavy iron ore and coal that lose weight when processed, so locating near them (and transport) saves cost — not far away.

questions.question: A FOOTLOOSE industry is one that _______.
options: can locate almost anywhere (e.g. electronics, IT)
questions.expected: can locate almost anywhere (e.g. electronics, IT)
questions.memo: Footloose industries are not tied to raw materials or heavy transport; light, high-value products (electronics, software) let them locate freely.

questions.question: A learner says a footloose industry must be near a mine. Correct them.
options: Footloose industries are NOT tied to raw materials and can locate almost anywhere
questions.expected: Footloose industries are NOT tied to raw materials and can locate almost anywhere
questions.memo: 'Footloose' means free to choose location; such industries (IT, electronics) do not depend on being near a mine or specific raw material.

questions.question: South Africa's LARGEST industrial region is _______.
questions.memo: Gauteng (the old PWV — Pretoria-Witwatersrand-Vereeniging) is SA's industrial heartland, built on gold, a large market, labour and infrastructure.

questions.question: Which factor influences where industries locate?
options: Raw materials, labour, transport, markets and energy
questions.expected: Raw materials, labour, transport, markets and energy
questions.memo: Industrial location depends on access to raw materials, labour, transport infrastructure, markets, energy/water, capital and government policy.

questions.question: Match each industry to its likely location factor.
questions.memo: 1 Iron & steel → C near raw materials. 2 Bakery → A near the market. 3 Software firm → B footloose (anywhere). (Prompt: 1=Iron & steel, 2=Bakery, 3=Software firm; A=near market, B=footloose, C=near raw materials.)

questions.question: A 'bridge' (break-of-bulk) industry locates where _______.
options: goods change transport mode (e.g. a port), saving handling costs
questions.expected: goods change transport mode (e.g. a port), saving handling costs
questions.memo: Locating at a break-of-bulk point (like a port) lets an industry process goods where they are already being unloaded/reloaded, cutting transport costs.

questions.question: Which is one of SA's major coastal industrial regions?
questions.memo: SA's main industrial regions are Gauteng (PWV), Durban-Pinetown, Port Elizabeth-Uitenhage (Gqeberha) and the south-western Cape — the last three benefiting from ports.

questions.question: The Port Elizabeth-Uitenhage (Gqeberha) region is known especially for _______.
questions.memo: This coastal region is a centre of SA's automotive industry, benefiting from its port for importing parts and exporting vehicles.

questions.question: Why did Gauteng become SA's industrial core?
options: Gold wealth, a large labour force and market, plus transport links concentrated industry there
questions.expected: Gold wealth, a large labour force and market, plus transport links concentrated industry there
questions.memo: Gold first drew capital, people and infrastructure to the Witwatersrand; this built a huge market and labour pool that attracted further industry — a core region.

questions.question: Sort each as a factor that ATTRACTS industry or a CHALLENGE for industry.

items.text: High transport costs to distant markets

questions.memo: Attracts: transport, skilled labour, markets, energy. Challenges: unreliable power, distance to markets, water shortages.

questions.question: The tertiary sector's growing share of the economy reflects the rise of _______.
options: services like finance, retail, tourism and transport
questions.expected: services like finance, retail, tourism and transport
questions.memo: As economies mature, services expand — finance, retail, ICT, tourism and transport now dominate SA's GDP and employment growth.

questions.question: A 'ubiquitous' industry is one that _______.
options: is found almost everywhere because it serves local markets (e.g. bakeries)
questions.expected: is found almost everywhere because it serves local markets (e.g. bakeries)
questions.memo: Ubiquitous industries (bread, bricks, soft drinks) serve nearby markets and so are found in nearly every town — a market-oriented pattern.

questions.question: True or false: improving transport infrastructure can attract new industry to a region.
questions.memo: Better roads, rail, ports and reliable power lower costs and improve market access, making a region more attractive to industry.

questions.question: Why might a fruit-canning factory locate in a fruit-growing region rather than in a city?
options: The raw fruit is bulky and perishable, so processing it near the source saves cost and waste
questions.expected: The raw fruit is bulky and perishable, so processing it near the source saves cost and waste
questions.memo: Perishable, bulky raw materials favour processing close to where they are grown — a raw-material-oriented location decision.

questions.question: A government wants to attract a new electronics (footloose) factory to a struggling town. Which incentive fits best?
options: Since it can locate anywhere, offer reliable power, good transport, skills and tax incentives
Force it to locate at a distant mine
Offer nothing, since it must come anyway
Insist it use only bulky raw materials
questions.expected: Since it can locate anywhere, offer reliable power, good transport, skills and tax incentives
questions.memo: Footloose industries choose freely, so towns compete by offering infrastructure, skilled labour and incentives — exactly what regional-development policy provides.

GEO.G12.T3.ECO.A5.title: Strategies for industrial development
GEO.G12.T3.ECO.A5.description: Apartheid and post-apartheid industrial strategies, Industrial Development Zones (IDZs), Spatial Development Initiatives (SDIs), and centralisation vs decentralisation.
GEO.G12.T3.ECO.A5.recovery_strategy: DECENTRALISATION spreads industry AWAY from crowded cores to develop poorer regions and ease congestion; CENTRALISATION concentrates it for shared infrastructure and markets. IDZs offer incentives to attract export industry (often near ports); SDIs (e.g. the Maputo Corridor) develop transport routes to unlock a region's potential.

questions.question: Industrial DECENTRALISATION means _______.
options: spreading industry away from major centres to other regions
concentrating all industry in one city
questions.expected: spreading industry away from major centres to other regions
questions.memo: Decentralisation moves industry out to poorer or less-crowded regions to spread development and ease pressure on the core.

questions.question: Industrial CENTRALISATION means _______.
questions.memo: Centralisation clusters industry in core regions (like Gauteng) to share infrastructure, labour and markets — but can worsen congestion and regional inequality.

questions.question: A learner says decentralisation means concentrating industry in one big city. Correct them.
options: That is CENTRALISATION; decentralisation SPREADS industry away from the core
questions.expected: That is CENTRALISATION; decentralisation SPREADS industry away from the core
questions.memo: Decentralisation disperses industry; centralisation concentrates it. The learner swapped them.

questions.question: An Industrial Development Zone (IDZ) is _______.
options: a special area, often near a port, with incentives to attract export-oriented industry
questions.expected: a special area, often near a port, with incentives to attract export-oriented industry
questions.memo: IDZs (e.g. Coega near Gqeberha) offer infrastructure and incentives, usually near ports/airports, to draw export industries and create jobs.

questions.question: A learner says an SDI is a type of mineral. Correct them.
options: An SDI is a Spatial Development Initiative — a programme to develop a region along a transport route
An SDI is a type of farm
questions.expected: An SDI is a Spatial Development Initiative — a programme to develop a region along a transport route
questions.memo: SDIs develop economic potential along corridors (transport routes), e.g. the Maputo Development Corridor — not a mineral.

questions.question: The Maputo Development Corridor is an example of a/an _______.
questions.memo: The Maputo Corridor links Gauteng to the port of Maputo, developing industry, trade and infrastructure along the route — a flagship SDI.

questions.question: An aim of industrial decentralisation in South Africa is to _______.
options: create jobs and development in poorer, peripheral regions
questions.expected: create jobs and development in poorer, peripheral regions
questions.memo: Decentralisation spreads economic opportunity to lagging regions, reducing inequality and easing pressure on the overcrowded core.

questions.question: Sort each as an ADVANTAGE of CENTRALISATION or of DECENTRALISATION.

items.text: Shared infrastructure and a big local market
Easy access to skilled labour in one place
Less congestion and pollution in the core
Firms benefit from being close together

questions.memo: Centralisation: shared infrastructure, labour, market, clustering benefits. Decentralisation: regional jobs, less core congestion, balanced development.

questions.question: Apartheid-era industrial policy used decentralisation partly to _______.
options: place industry near the former 'homelands' to support segregation
questions.expected: place industry near the former 'homelands' to support segregation
questions.memo: Apartheid decentralisation (growth points near homeland borders) was tied to segregation policy; post-apartheid strategy aims at genuine, equitable development.

questions.question: Post-apartheid industrial strategy aims to _______.
options: grow industry, create jobs and reduce regional and social inequality
questions.expected: grow industry, create jobs and reduce regional and social inequality
questions.memo: Democratic-era policy (IDZs, SDIs, special economic zones) seeks inclusive industrial growth, jobs and more balanced regional development.

questions.question: A DISADVANTAGE of heavy industrial centralisation in one region is _______.
options: congestion, pollution and worsening regional inequality
questions.expected: congestion, pollution and worsening regional inequality
questions.memo: Concentrating industry strains the core (traffic, pollution, housing) and leaves other regions poor — the case for some decentralisation.

questions.question: IDZs are usually located near ports or airports because _______.
options: export industries need fast, cheap access to international transport
it is required by law to be inland
questions.expected: export industries need fast, cheap access to international transport
questions.memo: Being at a port/airport lets IDZ firms import inputs and export products efficiently — key for export-oriented industrialisation.

questions.question: A development CORRIDOR (like an SDI) concentrates investment along a _______.
questions.memo: Corridors develop the economic potential along a key route (road/rail to a port), linking production areas to markets and attracting investment.

questions.question: Match each strategy/term to its description.
questions.memo: 1 IDZ → C port-based zone with incentives for export industry. 2 SDI → A development along a transport corridor. 3 Decentralisation → B spreading industry to other regions. (Prompt: 1=IDZ, 2=SDI, 3=Decentralisation; A=corridor development, B=spreading industry, C=port export zone.)

questions.question: Incentives offered to attract industry to a development zone might include _______.
options: tax breaks, cheap serviced land and good infrastructure
questions.expected: tax breaks, cheap serviced land and good infrastructure
questions.memo: Governments lure investment with tax incentives, ready infrastructure, serviced land and streamlined processes in IDZs/special economic zones.

questions.question: True or false: decentralisation can help reduce the gap between a wealthy core region and poorer peripheral regions.
questions.memo: By taking jobs and investment to lagging regions, decentralisation can narrow regional inequality — a key development goal.

questions.question: Why might decentralised 'growth points' sometimes FAIL to thrive?
options: Without enough infrastructure, skills and markets nearby, firms struggle to be profitable
questions.expected: Without enough infrastructure, skills and markets nearby, firms struggle to be profitable
questions.memo: Industry needs supporting conditions; growth points lacking infrastructure, skilled labour or access to markets may not attract or keep firms once incentives end.

questions.question: True or false: an SDI like the Maputo Corridor can benefit more than one country.
questions.memo: The Maputo Corridor links South Africa and Mozambique, boosting trade, transport and development on both sides of the border.

questions.question: Why does the government use BOTH incentives (IDZs) and corridors (SDIs) in its strategy?
options: IDZs attract export firms to set spots while SDIs develop whole regions along routes — together driving broader growth
One alone always works for everything
questions.expected: IDZs attract export firms to set spots while SDIs develop whole regions along routes — together driving broader growth
questions.memo: IDZs target investment at specific zones; SDIs unlock the wider potential of a corridor — combined, they spread industrial development more effectively.

questions.question: A poor coastal region with a port but little industry seeks jobs. Which strategy fits and why?
options: Establish an IDZ/SDI using the port to attract export industry with incentives and infrastructure
Centralise all industry in distant Gauteng
questions.expected: Establish an IDZ/SDI using the port to attract export industry with incentives and infrastructure
questions.memo: Its port is an asset; an IDZ (incentives near the port) or corridor SDI can attract export-oriented industry and create local jobs — exactly this policy's purpose.

GEO.G12.T3.ECO.A6.title: Informal sector
GEO.G12.T3.ECO.A6.description: Concept and characteristics of informal employment, reasons for its size in SA, and the challenges it faces.
GEO.G12.T3.ECO.A6.recovery_strategy: The INFORMAL sector is unregistered, untaxed, small-scale work (street vendors, spaza shops, casual labour) — no contracts, benefits or job security. It is large in SA because of high unemployment and limited formal jobs. It provides vital income and goods but faces low pay, insecurity and little legal protection.

questions.question: The informal sector consists of work that is _______.
options: unregistered, untaxed and small-scale (e.g. street vendors, spaza shops)
questions.expected: unregistered, untaxed and small-scale (e.g. street vendors, spaza shops)
questions.memo: Informal-sector work is outside formal registration and tax — street trading, spaza shops, casual labour, home enterprises.

questions.question: A key characteristic of informal employment is _______.
options: no formal contract, benefits or job security
questions.expected: no formal contract, benefits or job security
questions.memo: Informal workers usually lack contracts, benefits, paid leave or protection — making the work insecure and low-paid.

questions.question: A learner says a street vendor pays company tax and has a formal contract. Correct them.
options: A street vendor is in the INFORMAL sector — usually no contract, registration or company tax
questions.expected: A street vendor is in the INFORMAL sector — usually no contract, registration or company tax
questions.memo: Street vendors typically operate informally without registration, contracts or formal taxation — the opposite of the learner's claim.

questions.question: Why is the informal sector LARGE in South Africa?
options: High unemployment and too few formal jobs push people into informal work
questions.expected: High unemployment and too few formal jobs push people into informal work
questions.memo: With high unemployment and limited formal-sector jobs, many people earn a living informally as a survival strategy.

questions.question: Sort each as a CHARACTERISTIC of the FORMAL or the INFORMAL sector.
questions.memo: Formal = registered, taxed, contracts, benefits. Informal = unregistered, no contract or security (vendors, spazas).

questions.question: A BENEFIT of the informal sector is that it _______.
options: provides income, jobs and affordable goods/services where formal jobs are scarce
questions.expected: provides income, jobs and affordable goods/services where formal jobs are scarce
questions.memo: The informal sector is a vital safety net — income for millions, cheap goods and services, and entrepreneurial opportunity.

questions.question: A CHALLENGE facing informal workers is _______.
options: low, irregular income with no protection or benefits
questions.expected: low, irregular income with no protection or benefits
questions.memo: Informal work is precarious — uncertain income, no benefits, vulnerability to harassment or removal, and little access to credit.

questions.question: A learner says the informal sector provides no benefit to the economy. Correct them.
options: It provides vital income, jobs and goods/services for millions of people
questions.expected: It provides vital income, jobs and goods/services for millions of people
questions.memo: Far from useless, the informal sector keeps many households afloat, supplies affordable goods and absorbs workers the formal economy cannot — a major economic role.

questions.question: Informal traders often struggle to grow their businesses because they lack _______.
options: access to credit, secure premises and training
questions.expected: access to credit, secure premises and training
questions.memo: Without bank credit, secure trading sites or business skills, informal enterprises find it hard to expand — barriers that support could address.

questions.question: How could government SUPPORT the informal sector?
options: Provide trading space, micro-loans, skills training and basic services
questions.expected: Provide trading space, micro-loans, skills training and basic services
questions.memo: Supportive policy — designated markets, micro-finance, training and services — helps informal businesses survive, grow and even formalise.

questions.question: True or false: many people are in the informal sector out of necessity rather than choice.
questions.memo: With few formal jobs, informal work is often a survival strategy — a response to unemployment rather than a free choice.

questions.question: Informal-sector activity is hard to measure because it is _______.
options: unregistered and not fully recorded in official statistics
questions.expected: unregistered and not fully recorded in official statistics
questions.memo: Because it is unregistered and cash-based, the informal economy is partly invisible to official data, so its true size is often underestimated.

questions.question: Which is an example of informal-sector work?
options: A car-guard or a backyard mechanic
questions.expected: A car-guard or a backyard mechanic
questions.memo: Car-guards, backyard mechanics, street vendors, hawkers and casual day-labourers typify informal-sector work — outside formal registration.

questions.question: Why does high formal-sector unemployment tend to GROW the informal sector?
options: People without formal jobs create their own informal income to survive
questions.expected: People without formal jobs create their own informal income to survive
questions.memo: When formal jobs are scarce, people turn to self-created informal work (trading, services) to earn a living — so the two move together.

questions.question: Match each feature to the FORMAL or INFORMAL sector.
questions.memo: 1 Pays income tax → B formal. 2 No written contract → A informal. 3 Regulated and registered → B formal. 4 Cash-only street stall → A informal. (Prompt: 1,2,3,4 as above; A=informal, B=formal.)

questions.question: True or false: informal businesses can sometimes grow and 'formalise' into registered enterprises over time.
questions.memo: With success and support, some informal traders register, grow and join the formal economy — a path that good policy encourages.

questions.question: A social benefit of the informal sector is that it _______.
options: reduces poverty and keeps families afloat where there are no formal jobs
questions.expected: reduces poverty and keeps families afloat where there are no formal jobs
questions.memo: By providing income and affordable goods, the informal sector cushions poverty and supports households the formal economy leaves out.

questions.question: Why might informal traders be vulnerable to eviction or harassment?
options: They often lack secure rights to trade in their location
They are always protected by law
questions.expected: They often lack secure rights to trade in their location
questions.memo: Without secure trading rights or premises, informal traders can be moved on or harassed — a key insecurity that designated markets help address.

questions.question: True or false: the informal sector is a major source of employment in South Africa, especially for those excluded from formal jobs.
questions.memo: Millions of South Africans rely on informal work for income, making it a crucial part of the economy and a buffer against unemployment.

questions.question: A city wants to help its many street traders earn more securely. Which approach fits best?
options: Provide proper market stalls, storage, micro-loans and training rather than removing traders
questions.expected: Provide proper market stalls, storage, micro-loans and training rather than removing traders
questions.memo: Supporting informal traders with infrastructure, finance and skills raises their incomes and security and can help businesses grow — far better than removals.
